Name: belief_coherence_geometry
Title: Do LLM Beliefs Obey Logic? Measuring and Enforcing Deductive Coherence in Internal Belief Representations
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's internal belief representations (the linear 'truth directions' extracted from hidden states) should update in a logically coherent way when the model is presented with in-context evidence: believing a premise and a rule should raise the internal belief in the entailed conclusion, and believing a proposition should lower the internal belief in its negation. We hypothesize that LLM internal beliefs are systematically *incoherent* under deductive constraints, that this incoherence is measurable via probes, and that a lightweight inference-time intervention along truth directions can enforce coherence and improve downstream factual and reasoning reliability.
Related Work: Prior work extracts linear 'truth/belief directions' from LLM activations (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023) and shows probes can be more calibrated than outputs (Liu et al. 2023). Schouten et al. (2024) show belief directions are context-sensitive and that moving a premise along the truth direction can influence entailed sentences. However, existing work (a) treats each statement's belief in isolation or studies single premise-conclusion pairs qualitatively, and (b) never quantifies coherence as a graded, testable *logical* property across structured propositional networks (modus ponens, contraposition, negation, transitivity, De Morgan). Freedman & Toni (2025) study probabilistic-belief coherence but only at the output level, not internal representations. Our proposal is the first to (1) define and measure a deductive coherence score over internal belief geometry across a structured constraint set, and (2) derive an inference-time steering objective that projects internal beliefs onto the manifold of logically consistent belief assignments, testing whether this improves multi-hop reasoning and hallucination resistance.
Abstract: Large language models internally encode a graded representation of whether a statement is true, recoverable as linear 'truth directions' in hidden states. Yet a belief is only meaningful if it is coherent: if a model internally believes 'A' and 'A implies B', it should also internally believe 'B'. We ask whether LLM internal belief representations obey elementary rules of logic under in-context evidence. We construct BeliefLogic, a controlled dataset of propositional networks (facts, negations, implications, contrapositives, De Morgan pairs, and transitive chains) instantiated over both synthetic and real-world knowledge. Using difference-in-means and logistic probes to read a scalar 'internal belief' for any proposition at every layer, we define a Deductive Coherence Score measuring the fraction of logical constraints the model's internal beliefs satisfy after being presented with supporting evidence in-context. We find where and how internal beliefs violate logic (e.g., failing modus ponens, or believing both a proposition and its negation), how coherence varies by layer, model scale, and evidence framing, and whether output-level answers inherit the internal incoherence. We then introduce Coherence Steering, an inference-time intervention that nudges activations along truth directions to minimize violated constraints, projecting internal beliefs toward the nearest logically consistent assignment. We evaluate whether Coherence Steering (i) increases the coherence score, (ii) improves multi-hop entailment accuracy, and (iii) reduces hallucination on factual QA, without harming general capability. Our results characterize the logical structure of LLM beliefs and offer a cheap, data-efficient tool to make model beliefs more internally consistent.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build BeliefLogic, a set of propositional constraint networks. For each network, define base facts (with known truth values), and derived constraints from logical rules: negation (belief(A)+belief(not A)=1), modus ponens (A, A->B => B), contraposition (A->B <=> not B -> not A), transitivity (A->B, B->C => A->C), and De Morgan. Instantiate with (a) synthetic abstract symbols and (b) real-world statements from existing true/false datasets (e.g., cities, elements, animal facts) plus their negations and constructed implications. Provide, per item, the in-context evidence (premises) and the target proposition to probe.

Belief readout: For 3-5 open models spanning scale (e.g., Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), extract hidden states at the final token of each probed proposition. Train difference-in-means and logistic-regression truth probes per layer on a held-out set of simple true/false statements (following Marks & Tegmark). Convert probe scores to a scalar internal belief in [0,1] via Platt scaling. Validate probe transfer to BeliefLogic statements.

Coherence measurement: For each constraint type, define a violation metric (e.g., |belief(A)+belief(not A)-1|; for modus ponens, measure whether belief(B) rises when premises are in-context vs. absent, and whether it exceeds a threshold). Compute a per-layer, per-model Deductive Coherence Score = fraction of constraints satisfied. Report coherence broken down by rule type, layer, model scale, and evidence framing (first- vs third-person, explicit vs implicit rule statement). Compare internal-belief coherence to output-level coherence (asking the model directly).

Causal analysis: Test whether internal beliefs are causal by activation patching: move the premise's representation along the truth direction and measure the change in the conclusion's internal belief and in the output answer, replicating and extending Schouten et al. across the full constraint set.

Coherence Steering intervention: At inference, define an objective that projects the vector of internal beliefs for a proposition network onto the nearest point on the logically-consistent belief polytope (e.g., via a few gradient steps minimizing total constraint violation, translated into additive shifts along the per-proposition truth directions in a chosen layer, ITI-style). Apply during generation.

Downstream evaluation: Measure (i) post-steering Deductive Coherence Score, (ii) accuracy on multi-hop entailment tasks (e.g., ProofWriter, EntailmentBank subsets) and on synthetic transitive-chain QA, (iii) hallucination/factuality on TruthfulQA and a factual-recall QA set, and (iv) general capability retention on MMLU and a fluency/perplexity check. Compare against baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truthfulness steering, and chain-of-thought prompting.

Ablations: intervention layer choice, steering strength vs. capability tradeoff, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), synthetic vs real-world constraints, and generalization to unseen constraint types not used to define the steering objective.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Truth/belief probes may not linearly capture beliefs for complex or context-laden propositions, so measured incoherence could partly reflect probe error rather than genuine internal inconsistency; we mitigate with multiple probe types and causal patching validation.
Defining a single 'internal belief' scalar for a proposition depends on token/position choices; results may be sensitive to these design decisions and require careful robustness checks.
Coherence Steering along truth directions could degrade fluency or general capability if steering is too strong; the coherence-capability tradeoff must be characterized.

The logically-consistent polytope projection assumes the model represents each proposition with a comparable, calibrated belief scale; miscalibration across propositions could make the projection ill-posed.
Findings may vary substantially across model families and scales, limiting the universality of conclusions; we address this by testing multiple models.

Name: belief_source_provenance
Title: Where Did That Belief Come From? Probing and Steering the Parametric-vs-Contextual Provenance of LLM Beliefs
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM internally represents a proposition as true, its hidden states also encode WHY it believes it: whether the belief derives from parametric memory (pretraining) or from in-context evidence. We hypothesize this 'provenance' is linearly decodable and dissociable from the belief's truth-value, that belief-truth and belief-provenance can conflict (e.g., high internal belief in a false statement asserted in context), and that a lightweight steering intervention on the provenance direction can control whether the model trusts context vs. memory, mitigating both sycophantic context-following and rigid memory-clinging.
Related Work: Prior work extracts linear 'truth directions' from activations (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023) and shows probes predict correctness/retraction (Yang & Jia 2025). Knowledge-conflict work studies when models follow context vs. parametric memory behaviorally and via steering (SI-FACT 2025; Simulated Adoption / 'Orthogonal Interference' 2026; Layer of Truth 2025). Xiros et al. (2026) disentangle knowledge from verbalization. However, none disentangle a belief's *provenance* (parametric vs. contextual source) as a distinct linear axis orthogonal to its truth-value, nor test whether provenance and truth conflict, nor use a provenance direction as a targeted knob for calibrated context-trust. Existing conflict work measures which side wins behaviorally or steers a truth/context direction; we introduce a two-axis (truth x provenance) decomposition of internal beliefs and a provenance-specific intervention. This is a genuinely new lens rather than an extension of truth-probing.
Abstract: Large language models internally represent whether a statement is true, but a belief is characterized not only by its content and confidence but also by its source. We ask whether an LLM's hidden states encode the *provenance* of a belief: does the model 'believe' a proposition because it recalls it from pretraining (parametric) or because it was just told so in context (contextual)? We construct BeliefSource, a dataset of propositions crossed along two axes: truth-value (true/false by world knowledge) and evidence provenance (asserted in context / absent from context), including deliberate conflicts (false statements asserted in context; true statements contradicted in context). Using difference-in-means and logistic probes on hidden states, we test whether (1) a linear truth direction and a linear provenance direction both exist, (2) they are approximately orthogonal and separately decodable, and (3) internal belief-truth and belief-provenance dissociate under conflict. We map how each axis evolves across layers and model scale, and validate causality via activation patching. Finally, we introduce Provenance Steering: nudging activations along the provenance direction to make the model rely more (or less) on in-context evidence. We evaluate whether this calibrates context-trust, reducing sycophantic acceptance of false injected claims while improving legitimate context updating (RAG-style faithfulness), without harming general capability. Our two-axis account gives a sharper picture of LLM beliefs and a cheap, interpretable knob for the memory-versus-context tradeoff that underlies hallucination and sycophancy.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build BeliefSource with propositions crossed on truth-value (true/false per world knowledge) and provenance (evidence present in context vs. absent), using real-world facts (cities, elements, science, biographies) plus their negations. Four core cells: (T,parametric-only), (F,parametric-only), (T,context-supported), (F,context-asserted i.e. injected falsehood), plus conflict cells (T-fact contradicted in context; F-fact never asserted). Control surface form to avoid lexical shortcuts.

Probe training and axis discovery: For 4-5 open models (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), extract final-token hidden states per proposition per layer. Train (a) a truth probe on (T vs F) with provenance balanced, and (b) a provenance probe on (context-present vs absent) with truth balanced, using difference-in-means and logistic regression. Report per-layer accuracy of each probe and cross-axis leakage (does the truth probe accidentally decode provenance and vice versa).

Orthogonality analysis: Measure cosine similarity between the truth and provenance directions per layer; test whether provenance is decodable in the subspace orthogonal to the truth direction (project out truth direction, re-probe provenance). Report whether the two axes are dissociable.

Conflict dissociation: On conflict cells, measure internal belief-truth scalar vs. provenance scalar. Test the hypothesis that injected falsehoods produce high contextual-provenance and elevated belief while remaining decodable as 'false' along the truth axis in earlier layers, with the axes diverging by layer. Compare to output-level answers.

Causal validation: Activation patching / directional steering: move activations along the provenance direction and measure changes in (a) the provenance probe readout, (b) the output answer's reliance on context, holding truth direction fixed; confirm provenance is causal and separable from truth.
Provenance Steering intervention: At inference, add a scaled provenance-direction vector at a chosen layer to increase or decrease context reliance (ITI-style). Sweep steering strength.

Downstream evaluation: (i) Sycophancy/misinformation robustness: fraction of injected-false-claims accepted (lower is better) under negative provenance steering; (ii) Legitimate context updating: accuracy on RAG-style QA where correct answers require trusting new context (e.g., updated facts, counterfactual-but-authoritative contexts), under positive steering; (iii) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity; (iv) TruthfulQA. Baselines: no steering, truth-direction (ITI) steering, prompt-based instructions to trust/distrust context.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type, steering strength vs. capability tradeoff, generalization to unseen domains and to multi-sentence contexts, and whether a single provenance direction transfers across topics.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The provenance probe might exploit trivial cues (e.g., whether the statement's tokens recently appeared in the prompt) rather than a genuine belief-source representation; we mitigate with paraphrased context, distractor contexts, and cross-domain generalization tests.

Truth and provenance directions may be entangled in some models, weakening the two-axis claim; the orthogonality and project-out analyses directly test this and negative results are still informative.
Provenance Steering could trade off sycophancy reduction against legitimate context updating; we explicitly measure both to characterize the frontier.
Scalar readouts depend on token/position choices and probe calibration, which may affect conflict-cell interpretation; robustness checks across positions and probe types are included.
Findings may vary across model families and scales, limiting universality; we test multiple models.

Name: belief_ghost_revision
Title: Belief Ghosts: Do Superseded Beliefs Persist in LLM Activations After In-Context Revision?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM revises its internal belief about a world fact after being given new, contradicting in-context evidence, the superseded (old) belief is not fully erased from hidden states: a decodable 'belief ghost' persists. We hypothesize that (1) the strength of this ghost is measurable via probes, (2) ghost strength causally predicts downstream failures such as relapsing to the old answer under mild pressure, inconsistency across paraphrases, and hallucinated recall of the outdated fact, and (3) a lightweight inference-time intervention that suppresses the old-belief direction ('belief erasure steering') stabilizes revised beliefs and reduces backsliding without harming legitimate memory.
Related Work: Prior work extracts linear truth/belief directions from activations (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023) and studies context-vs-parametric knowledge conflict behaviorally (SI-FACT 2025) and via steering. Knowledge editing work (ROME, MEMIT; REACT 2025) studies persistence of edits in weights, not the transient representational dynamics of in-context revision. Nguyen et al. (2026, DToM-Track) show LLMs struggle to retrieve PRIOR belief states after updates in third-party Theory-of-Mind, but only at the output level and for others' beliefs, not the model's own first-order world belief and not in the representation space. Our proposal is the first to ask whether an LLM's OWN superseded belief about a world fact leaves a persistent, decodable trace in hidden states after in-context revision, to quantify this 'belief ghost' as a graded representational quantity, to show it causally predicts backsliding/relapse and hallucination, and to introduce a targeted erasure intervention. This is a new representational-dynamics lens on belief revision, not an extension of static truth-probing or output-level ToM.
Abstract: Large language models are routinely asked to update their beliefs in context: told a fact is now outdated, corrected, or superseded by fresh evidence. When such a revision occurs, does the model truly overwrite its prior belief, or does a trace of the superseded belief linger in its internal representations? We hypothesize the existence of 'belief ghosts': after in-context revision, the old belief remains partially decodable from hidden states even when the model's output has switched to the new belief. We construct BeliefRevise, a controlled dataset of world facts, each paired with an in-context revision that flips the correct answer (e.g., 'The capital of X is now officially Y'), spanning factual, numerical, and relational domains. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes trained on independent true/false statements, we read a scalar internal belief for both the old and new proposition after revision, defining a Belief Ghost Score that measures residual activation of the superseded belief across layers and model scale. We then test whether ghost strength causally predicts failure: relapse to the old answer under mild adversarial pressure or long context, inconsistency across paraphrased queries, and spontaneous hallucination of the outdated fact. We validate causality via activation patching along the old-belief direction. Finally, we introduce Belief Erasure Steering, an inference-time intervention that projects out the residual old-belief direction, and evaluate whether it stabilizes revised beliefs and reduces backsliding while preserving legitimate parametric memory and general capability. Our results reveal the hidden persistence of superseded beliefs and offer a cheap tool for reliable in-context belief updating.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build BeliefRevise. Each item = (a) an original fact F_old with known correct answer A_old from world knowledge, (b) an in-context revision statement asserting the new correct answer A_new (a controlled counterfactual or plausible update), and (c) a query probing the current belief. Cover factual (capitals, leaders), numerical (populations, dates), and relational (X is a member of Y) domains. Include control items with no revision, and paraphrase sets per query. Ensure surface forms of A_old and A_new are matched to avoid lexical shortcuts.

Belief readout setup: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an independent set of simple true/false statements, following Marks & Tegmark. Platt-scale probe outputs to scalar beliefs in [0,1]. After presenting a revision in context, at the query position read the internal belief in proposition 'answer = A_old' and 'answer = A_new'.

Belief Ghost Score: Define ghost(item) = internal belief in A_old after revision, measured only on items where the model's OUTPUT has correctly switched to A_new. Report per-layer, per-domain, per-model ghost strength; compare to no-revision baselines and to pre-revision belief. Track how the old and new belief scalars diverge across layers.

Predictive validity: Test whether Belief Ghost Score predicts downstream failure at the item level. Failure metrics: (i) Relapse rate = fraction where the model reverts to A_old under mild pressure (appended distractor text, longer context, or a leading question); (ii) Paraphrase inconsistency = variance of answer across paraphrased queries; (iii) Hallucinated recall = fraction where later in the same conversation the model spontaneously states A_old. Report correlation/AUC of ghost score for predicting each failure.

Causal validation: Activation patching. Add or subtract the old-belief direction (difference-in-means vector for A_old) at chosen layers and measure changes in (a) the old-belief probe readout and (b) the probability of relapsing to A_old at the output, holding the new-belief direction fixed. Confirm the ghost is causal.

Belief Erasure Steering: At inference, after the revision is in context, project activations at selected layers orthogonal to the residual old-belief direction (or subtract a scaled old-belief vector), ITI-style. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduction in Belief Ghost Score, (ii) reduction in relapse rate and paraphrase inconsistency, (iii) reduction in hallucinated recall of A_old, (iv) preservation of legitimate parametric memory on unrelated facts and no-revision controls, and (v) general capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, and prompt-based instruction to 'forget the old fact'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type, steering strength vs. capability tradeoff, factual vs numerical vs relational domains, plausibility of the revision (counterfactual vs realistic update), context length between revision and query (test whether ghosts strengthen or fade over distance), and generalization to unseen domains.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The old-belief probe direction may leak into lexical/positional cues (e.g., A_old tokens appearing earlier), so a decodable 'ghost' could reflect surface memory rather than a genuine residual belief; mitigate with paraphrases, surface-form matching, and cross-domain generalization.
Truth probes may not linearly capture beliefs for numerical or relational propositions, so ghost measurement could partly reflect probe error; use multiple probe types and causal patching validation.
Belief Erasure Steering could inadvertently erase legitimate parametric memory of the fact or degrade fluency; we explicitly measure memory preservation on controls and capability retention.
Scalar belief readouts depend on token/position choices; robustness checks across positions and probe types are included.
Findings may vary across model families and scales, limiting universality; we test multiple models and report negative results as informative.

Name: premature_belief_commitment
Title: Jumping to Conclusions: When Do LLMs Commit to a Belief Before Reading the Evidence?
Short Hypothesis: As an LLM reads a statement token by token, its internal belief about the statement's truth forms progressively; we hypothesize that models frequently 'commit' to a truth-value at a token position BEFORE the disambiguating evidence has been read, that the earliness of this commitment (a 'premature commitment' signal) causally predicts factual errors and hallucinations, and that a cheap inference-time intervention that resets or delays commitment until the evidence position improves reliability.
Related Work: Prior work extracts static linear 'truth directions' from final-token activations (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023) and shows probes predict correctness (Liu et al. 2023) and hallucination via intrinsic signals (Turkish white-box benchmark 2026). World-model work studies latent 'belief states' as compressed history for next-token prediction (NextLat 2025; LSE-MTP 2026) but at the sequence-modeling level, not the truth-value of factual claims. Crucially, all belief-probing work reads a belief at a single (usually final) position and treats belief as static. None studies the TEMPORAL/POSITIONAL trajectory of a factual belief across the input tokens of a single statement, nor asks whether the model commits before the evidence token, nor uses commitment timing as a predictor of error, nor intervenes on it. Our contribution is a token-resolved dynamics view of belief formation: measuring per-position belief trajectories, defining a premature-commitment metric relative to the location of disambiguating evidence, testing its predictive and causal link to errors, and introducing a commitment-delaying intervention.
Abstract: Large language models are usually treated as forming a belief about a statement only after reading it in full. But belief formation is a process that unfolds token by token. We study the temporal dynamics of factual belief within a single statement and ask a simple question: does an LLM commit to a truth-value before it has read the evidence that should decide it? We construct BeliefTiming, a dataset of factual statements engineered so that the token position of the disambiguating evidence (the word that determines whether the statement is true or false) is precisely controlled and can be placed early or late in the sentence. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes applied at every token position, we trace a per-position belief trajectory and define a Commitment Point (the earliest position after which the probe's belief stably matches the model's final output) and a Premature Commitment Score (how far the Commitment Point precedes the evidence position). We test three hypotheses: (1) models commit early on a nontrivial fraction of items, often anchoring on surface priors before the evidence; (2) larger Premature Commitment Scores predict factual errors, paraphrase inconsistency, and hallucination at the item level; and (3) commitment is causal, verified by activation patching at the commitment position. We then introduce Commitment Delay Steering, an inference-time intervention that dampens the truth direction at pre-evidence positions to prevent early lock-in, and evaluate whether it improves factual accuracy and calibration without harming fluency or general capability. Our results recast LLM belief as a temporal process and expose 'jumping to conclusions' as a measurable, fixable failure mode.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build BeliefTiming, factual statements where a single disambiguating token/phrase determines truth, with controllable position. Two designs: (a) Late-evidence templates, e.g., 'The capital of the country whose flag is red and white and located in [region] is [City]', where the correct answer hinges on a token near the end; (b) Early-evidence templates where the deciding token appears near the start. For each item annotate the evidence position, ground-truth label, and construct a strong 'surface prior' (a plausible-but-wrong completion the model might anchor on). Include true and false variants and paraphrase sets. Match surface forms to avoid trivial cues.

Belief readout across positions: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an independent set of simple true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to [0,1]. Apply the probe at EVERY token position while reading each BeliefTiming statement to obtain a per-position belief trajectory (choose a mid/late layer, with a layer sweep).

Commitment metrics: Define Commitment Point = earliest position p such that the belief trajectory stays within epsilon of the model's final-position belief for all positions >= p. Define Premature Commitment Score = (evidence_position - Commitment_Point), positive when the model commits before the evidence. Report distributions across items, models, and template types; compare early- vs late-evidence templates.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether Premature Commitment Score predicts (i) factual error (output disagrees with ground truth), (ii) paraphrase inconsistency (variance of answer across paraphrases), and (iii) confident-wrong hallucination. Report AUC/correlation of the commitment score for predicting each failure, and compare against baselines like output-token entropy and final-position probe confidence.

Anchoring analysis: Test whether early commitment corresponds to locking onto the surface prior: measure whether the pre-evidence committed belief matches the surface-prior completion rather than the evidence-consistent answer. Quantify the fraction of premature commitments that are prior-driven.

Causal validation: Activation patching at the Commitment Point. (a) Ablate/patch the truth direction at pre-evidence positions and measure whether the final output flips toward the evidence-consistent answer; (b) inject the correct-belief direction at the evidence position and measure recovery. Confirm the commitment is causal, not epiphenomenal.

Commitment Delay Steering: Inference-time intervention that reduces the projection onto (or scales down updates along) the truth direction at positions before the evidence token, delaying lock-in until evidence is read. Since evidence position is unknown at deployment, implement a position-agnostic variant that dampens the truth direction whenever the trajectory's slope indicates premature commitment (rate-of-change gating). Sweep strength and layer.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) factual accuracy on BeliefTiming late-evidence sets, (ii) calibration (ECE) and paraphrase consistency, (iii) accuracy on external factual QA where the answer depends on late-arriving context (multi-hop / RAG-style items), (iv) general capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, and chain-of-thought prompting (which may naturally delay commitment).

Ablations: layer and epsilon choices for the Commitment Point, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), template type, model scale, robustness of the position-agnostic gating, and generalization to naturally occurring late-evidence questions not used in tuning.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Per-position probe readouts may reflect ongoing syntactic parsing rather than a stable truth belief; the Commitment Point could be sensitive to epsilon and layer choices. We mitigate with layer/epsilon sweeps, multiple probe types, and causal patching to distinguish genuine commitment from probe artifacts.

Controlling the exact 'evidence position' is nontrivial for real language; some items may have distributed evidence. We use templated, single-disambiguator constructions and validate with human annotation, and separately test naturally occurring items.

The position-agnostic Commitment Delay Steering may fail to identify premature commitment without knowing the evidence location, and could dampen legitimate early-correct beliefs, hurting easy items; we explicitly measure the accuracy tradeoff across easy vs hard items.

Premature commitment may correlate with, but not exceed, simpler baselines (entropy, final confidence) as an error predictor; if so, the value is in the mechanistic/causal insight rather than a new predictor, which we report honestly.
Findings may vary across model families and scales, limiting universality; we test multiple models and report negative results as informative.

Name: metabelief_alignment
Title: Does the Model Believe It Believes? Measuring First-Order vs Second-Order Belief Alignment in LLM Activations
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM internally represents a proposition P as true (a first-order belief), its internal representation of the self-referential proposition 'I believe P' (a second-order belief) should agree. We hypothesize that LLM first-order and second-order beliefs are systematically MISALIGNED in their internal representations, that this metabelief misalignment is linearly decodable and dissociable from first-order belief, that misalignment causally predicts miscalibrated verbalized confidence and hedging behavior, and that a lightweight inference-time intervention aligning the two axes improves confidence calibration.
Related Work: Introspection/metacognition work asks whether models can predict their own behavior (Binder et al. 2024) or self-report confidence (Ackerman 2025), and finds limited or negative privileged self-access at the OUTPUT level (Song et al. 2025; Ashuach et al. 2026). Functional-metacognition steering (Li et al. 2026) decodes states like evaluation-awareness and self-assessed capability but not the alignment between a belief and the belief-about-that-belief. Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023) reads only first-order beliefs. No prior work compares, within activations, the model's first-order belief in P against its second-order (self-referential) belief in 'I believe P', treats their mismatch as a graded decodable quantity, links it causally to verbalized confidence miscalibration, or intervenes to align them. This is a new representational lens on introspective consistency rather than an extension of behavioral self-prediction or static truth probing.
Abstract: A belief is more than an assertion about the world; a rational agent that believes a proposition P should also, when asked, represent itself as believing P. We investigate whether large language models maintain this metacognitive consistency inside their activations. We distinguish a first-order belief (the internal truth-value the model assigns to P) from a second-order belief (the internal truth-value the model assigns to the self-referential statement 'I believe that P'). Using difference-in-means and logistic probes on hidden states, we read scalar first-order and second-order beliefs for matched propositions and define a Metabelief Misalignment Score. We test four hypotheses: (1) first- and second-order beliefs are both linearly decodable and constitute distinct, dissociable axes; (2) they are systematically misaligned for a nontrivial fraction of propositions, especially uncertain or false ones; (3) misalignment causally predicts output-level pathologies such as overconfident hedging, underconfident correct answers, and inconsistency between an answer and a follow-up 'Do you believe that?' query; and (4) an inference-time intervention that steers the second-order axis toward the first-order axis improves verbalized-confidence calibration. We map both axes across layers and model scale, validate causality with activation patching, and evaluate downstream calibration and consistency. Our results reveal whether LLMs 'believe that they believe' consistently, offering a sharper account of machine introspection and a cheap tool for aligning models' stated confidence with their internal evidence.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build MetaBelief, a set of propositions P drawn from real-world facts (cities, science, biographies, etc.) plus their negations, spanning three regimes: (a) confidently-true (well-known facts), (b) confidently-false, and (c) uncertain/borderline (obscure or ambiguous facts the model is genuinely unsure about, validated by high output entropy). For each P, construct the matched second-order framing 'I believe that P' (and controls: third-person 'It is believed that P', and 'The statement P is true'). Match surface forms to avoid the second-order probe merely detecting the phrase 'I believe'.

Probe training and axis discovery: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), extract final-token hidden states per proposition per layer. Train a first-order truth probe on plain true/false statements and a second-order probe on 'I believe that <true/false statement>' items, using difference-in-means and logistic regression. Platt-scale to [0,1]. Report per-layer decoding accuracy of each probe and cross-axis leakage.

Dissociation/orthogonality analysis: Measure cosine similarity between the first- and second-order directions per layer; project out the first-order direction and test whether the second-order axis remains decodable. Test whether the two axes are genuinely distinct or collapse to one, controlling with the 'I believe' phrase-only baseline (does the second-order direction just detect self-referential phrasing?).

Misalignment measurement: Define Metabelief Misalignment(P) = |first-order belief(P) - second-order belief('I believe P')|. Report the distribution across the three regimes, layers, and models. Test the hypothesis that misalignment is largest for false and uncertain propositions and smallest for confident-true ones. Compare against output-level metabelief (asking the model 'Is P true?' then 'Do you believe P?').

Causal validation: Activation patching. Steer activations along the second-order direction and measure changes in (a) the second-order probe readout, (b) the model's verbalized answer to 'Do you believe that P?', holding the first-order axis fixed; and vice versa. Confirm the two axes are causally separable.

Predictive validity for calibration: At the item level, test whether Metabelief Misalignment predicts output-level pathologies: (i) overconfident hedging (confident verbalized 'I believe' on items the first-order axis marks uncertain), (ii) underconfident hedging on confident-correct items, and (iii) answer/belief inconsistency (model asserts P but denies believing P, or vice versa). Report AUC/correlation, compared against baselines like output-token entropy and first-order probe confidence.

Metabelief Alignment Steering: At inference, add a scaled vector that moves the second-order representation toward the first-order belief value at a chosen layer (ITI-style), i.e., align 'what it says it believes' with 'what its evidence indicates'. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduction in Metabelief Misalignment, (ii) verbalized-confidence calibration (ECE) on factual QA where the model states confidence, (iii) answer/belief consistency across the P-then-'do you believe P' probe, and (iv) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, first-order (ITI truth) steering, prompt-based 'be well-calibrated' instructions.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type, steering strength vs calibration/capability tradeoff, robustness to the surface-form controls (phrase-only vs genuine second-order), generalization to unseen domains, and whether a single second-order direction transfers across topics.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The second-order probe may merely detect the self-referential phrase 'I believe' rather than a genuine belief-about-belief; we mitigate with surface-form controls (third-person and 'the statement is true' framings), phrase-only baselines, and cross-domain generalization tests, and treat a purely phrase-detecting result as an informative negative.

First- and second-order directions may be entangled or collapse into one axis in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality and project-out analyses directly test this and negative results are still valuable.

Truth-style probes may not linearly capture beliefs for borderline/uncertain propositions, so misalignment could partly reflect probe error; we use multiple probe types, validate on confidently-true/false items, and confirm with causal patching.
Metabelief Alignment Steering could trade off calibration against capability or fluency; we characterize the tradeoff explicitly and compare to prompt-based baselines.
Findings may vary across model families and scales, and post-training (RLHF) may already shape metacognitive framing; we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects.

Name: belief_drift_context_dilution
Title: Belief Drift: Do LLM Internal Beliefs Erode as Context Grows, Even Without Contradiction?
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's internal belief in a proposition established early in a context silently degrades as more (topically-unrelated, non-contradicting) tokens accumulate between the establishing evidence and the query point. We hypothesize this 'belief drift' is a measurable, monotonic-ish function of intervening context length, is dissociable from mere attention/recency effects, causally predicts context-length-induced factual failures (the 'lost in the middle' phenomenon at the belief level), and can be counteracted by a cheap inference-time re-anchoring intervention along the belief direction.
Related Work: Prior work extracts static linear truth/belief directions from activations (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023) at a single query position. 'Lost in the middle' (Liu et al. 2023) documents position-dependent retrieval failures at the OUTPUT level, and long-context degradation is well studied behaviorally. Belief-tracking work (T3, Zou et al. 2025) studies belief deviation in multi-turn agent RL at the state/action level, not internal representations. No prior work traces how the internal belief scalar for a FIXED proposition changes as unrelated context accumulates, treats this erosion as a graded representational quantity, dissociates it from recency/attention baselines, links it causally to long-context errors, or re-anchors it via steering. Our contribution is a representational-dynamics account of context-induced belief erosion: measuring belief-vs-distance curves, testing predictive/causal links to failures, and introducing a re-anchoring intervention.
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed with long contexts, yet facts established early in a context often seem to fade by the time they are needed. We ask whether this fading is visible inside the model's beliefs: does the internal belief in a proposition, once established by in-context evidence, erode as unrelated, non-contradicting tokens accumulate between the evidence and the query? We construct BeliefDrift, a controlled dataset where a target fact is asserted in context and then followed by a variable amount of topically-unrelated filler text (0 to thousands of tokens), after which the belief is probed. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes on hidden states, we read a scalar internal belief in the target proposition at the query position and trace a Belief Drift Curve as a function of intervening distance, across layers and model scale. We test four hypotheses: (1) internal belief in the established fact declines as intervening context grows even absent any contradiction; (2) this drift is dissociable from generic recency effects by comparing to distance-matched but semantically-anchored controls; (3) drift magnitude causally predicts item-level factual failures underlying 'lost in the middle'; and (4) a lightweight inference-time re-anchoring intervention that adds back the belief direction restores accuracy. We validate causality with activation patching and evaluate downstream long-context QA accuracy, calibration, and capability retention. Our results reframe long-context degradation as measurable belief erosion and offer a cheap tool to stabilize established beliefs.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build BeliefDrift. Each item = (a) a target fact F asserted in context with a clear correct answer, (b) a controlled amount of intervening filler text of varying length (0, 128, 512, 1k, 2k, 4k tokens) that is topically unrelated and does NOT contradict or reference F, and (c) a query probing belief in F. Include true and false variants of F, paraphrase sets, and a 'distractor-dense' vs 'neutral filler' condition. Control filler content (coherent prose, random-topic facts, repeated boilerplate) to separate content effects from length effects.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open long-context models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an independent set of simple true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to [0,1]. At the query position after the filler, read the internal belief scalar in proposition 'answer to F = A_correct'.

Belief Drift Curve: Plot internal belief in F vs intervening distance, per layer, per model, per filler condition. Fit decay curves and report a Belief Drift Score = decline from distance-0 belief to belief at max distance. Compare drift across model scales and filler types.

Recency/attention dissociation: Add semantically-anchored control items where a cue near the query gently re-references the topic of F (without restating the answer); test whether belief drift is reduced, distinguishing genuine erosion from pure positional/recency decay. Compare belief drift to attention mass on the F tokens and to output-token confidence to show it is not merely an attention artifact.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether Belief Drift Score predicts (i) factual error at that distance (output disagrees with A_correct), (ii) paraphrase inconsistency, and (iii) confident-wrong hallucination. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (attention mass on F, output entropy, raw distance).

Causal validation: Activation patching. Add a scaled belief-direction vector (difference-in-means for F's correct answer) at the query position across layers and measure whether the output recovers the correct answer at long distances; conversely subtract it at short distances to induce failure. Confirm drift is causal, not epiphenomenal.

Re-anchoring intervention: At inference, add back a scaled belief-direction vector for the established fact at selected layers when the query is issued (ITI-style re-anchoring). Since the belief direction is fact-specific, implement a practical variant that re-anchors along the general truth direction gated by detected drift (belief scalar falling below a threshold relative to the distance-0 estimate). Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduction in Belief Drift Score, (ii) long-context QA accuracy where the needed fact is placed far from the query (single-fact needle-in-haystack and multi-fact variants), (iii) calibration (ECE) and paraphrase consistency, (iv) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, and prompt-based re-statement of the fact.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), filler content type, true vs false facts, model scale, position of F (beginning vs middle), and generalization to naturally occurring long documents not used in tuning.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Belief drift could reflect probe sensitivity to activation-norm changes over long contexts rather than genuine belief erosion; we mitigate with normalization, multiple probe types, and causal patching.

Drift may be confounded with pure recency/attention decay; the semantically-anchored control and attention-mass comparison directly test this, and a null (drift = recency) is still an informative finding.
The fact-specific re-anchoring vector is not available at deployment for arbitrary facts; the drift-gated general-truth-direction variant may be less effective, and we honestly characterize this gap.
Re-anchoring could over-strengthen false or superseded beliefs or harm fluency; we include false-fact and contradiction-later controls and measure capability retention.
Findings may vary across model families, scales, and context-window training; we test multiple models and report scale effects and negative results as informative.

Name: belief_contagion_interference
Title: Belief Contagion: Do LLM Beliefs Spuriously Bleed Across Associatively-Related but Logically-Independent Propositions?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM's internal belief in a proposition A is established or shifted by in-context evidence, the internal belief in a logically-independent but associatively-related proposition B changes in the same direction, even though A carries no logical information about B. We hypothesize this 'belief contagion' is a measurable, graded function of the semantic/associative distance between A and B, is dissociable from legitimate logical updating, causally predicts a characteristic hallucination mode (fabricating or endorsing related falsehoods after true context), and can be reduced by an inference-time intervention that isolates the target belief.
Related Work: Prior work extracts linear truth/belief directions from activations (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Bao et al. 2025) and shows they are context sensitive: Schouten et al. (2024) demonstrate that supporting/contradicting premises shift the truth-direction position of *entailed or contradicted* hypotheses, and note that 'contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact probe outputs' — but they study logically related sentences and treat off-target effects as a nuisance rather than characterizing them as a graded associative phenomenon. Logical-coherence work (my prior belief_coherence proposal) targets logically entailed conclusions; belief-drift work targets *unrelated* filler causing decay. None isolates the specific case where a belief spuriously spreads to logically-independent but semantically/associatively-linked propositions, quantifies it as a function of association strength, ties it causally to a related-falsehood hallucination mode, or intervenes to contain it. Concept-cone (Yu et al. 2025) and impossibility-vs-falsehood (Lee 2026) work concerns geometry of static truth, not cross-proposition contagion. Our contribution is a new representational lens: beliefs are 'sticky' and leak along association links, a distinct, testable, and fixable failure mode.
Abstract: A rational agent that comes to believe a fact should not thereby change its confidence in unrelated facts. We ask whether large language models obey this basic separation inside their belief representations. We hypothesize 'belief contagion': establishing or shifting the internal belief in a proposition A via in-context evidence spuriously shifts the internal belief in a logically-independent but associatively-related proposition B in the same direction. We construct BeliefContagion, a controlled dataset of proposition pairs (A, B) that are (i) logically independent (A neither entails nor contradicts B) yet (ii) span a controlled range of associative/semantic relatedness (e.g., same entity different attribute, same category, co-occurring topics), plus unrelated control pairs and truly-entailed pairs as anchors. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes, we read a scalar internal belief in B before and after presenting evidence that raises or lowers belief in A, defining a Contagion Score as the induced shift in B's belief. We test four claims: (1) contagion is nonzero and increases with associative relatedness but not with logical relevance; (2) it is dissociable from legitimate entailment-driven updating; (3) contagion magnitude causally predicts a related-falsehood hallucination mode — endorsing or fabricating plausible-but-false statements adjacent to true in-context content; and (4) a lightweight inference-time intervention that projects the evidence's activation shift onto the target-belief direction (containing spillover) reduces contagion and the associated hallucinations without harming legitimate updating or general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on factual QA. Our results reveal beliefs as leaky along association links and offer a cheap tool to contain them.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build BeliefContagion. Each item is a triple (evidence E for proposition A, target proposition B, relatedness label). Construct pairs so that A and B are logically independent (verified by construction: differing entities/attributes with no entailment or contradiction), across a graded relatedness axis: (r1) same entity, different independent attribute (e.g., A: 'Paris has a population over 2M'; B: 'Paris was founded before 300 BC'); (r2) same category, different entity (A about element X, B about element Y); (r3) topically co-occurring but distinct; (r4) unrelated control (different domain). Add anchor conditions: entailed pairs (A logically implies B) and contradictory pairs to calibrate the probe's legitimate updating. Include both belief-raising and belief-lowering evidence for A, and true/false variants of B. Match surface forms and control lexical overlap between E and B to avoid trivial cues; validate logical independence and relatedness labels with human annotation and an embedding-based relatedness score.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an independent set of simple true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to [0,1]. For each item, read the internal belief in B (a) with no evidence (baseline) and (b) after evidence E establishing/shifting belief in A. Confirm E moves belief in A as intended (manipulation check).

Contagion Score: Define Contagion(item) = belief_in_B(after E) - belief_in_B(baseline), signed by the direction E pushes A. Report per-layer, per-model Contagion Score as a function of relatedness (r1-r4) and compare to the entailed anchor (legitimate updating). Test the hypothesis that contagion decreases with associative distance and is near-zero for unrelated controls, while entailed pairs show large legitimate shifts. Compare internal contagion to output-level contagion (asking the model directly about B after E).

Dissociation from logical updating and lexical overlap: Regress Contagion on (a) embedding-based relatedness, (b) lexical overlap between E and B, and (c) a logical-relevance indicator (0 for independent pairs). Show contagion is driven by associative relatedness, not lexical overlap or genuine logical relevance. Include a paraphrase control (relatedness preserved, wording changed) to rule out surface cues.

Causal validation: Activation patching. Take the residual-stream shift induced by E (difference between activations with and without E at the B-query position) and (a) patch only its projection onto A's belief direction vs (b) patch its projection onto B's belief direction; measure the resulting change in B's probe readout and output. Confirm that the spillover component along B's direction causally drives the contagion and is separable from the intended A update.

Related-falsehood hallucination link: At the item level, test whether Contagion Score predicts a related-falsehood hallucination mode: after true evidence E about A, does the model endorse or fabricate a plausible-but-false B (false variant)? Metrics: (i) false-B endorsement rate, (ii) confident-wrong rate, (iii) spontaneous fabrication of related facts in open generation seeded by E. Report AUC/correlation of Contagion Score for predicting each, vs baselines (embedding relatedness alone, output entropy).

Contagion Containment intervention: At inference, decompose the evidence-induced activation shift at selected layers into the component along A's belief direction (keep) and components along other belief-relevant directions (dampen), i.e., project the update to contain spillover. A practical deployment variant dampens shifts orthogonal to the currently-queried target's truth direction. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduction in Contagion Score for independent pairs, (ii) preservation of legitimate updating on entailed-anchor pairs (must NOT be suppressed), (iii) reduction in related-falsehood endorsement/fabrication, (iv) factual QA accuracy on a mixed set with associative distractors, and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'only update beliefs justified by evidence'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), relatedness level, belief-raising vs belief-lowering evidence, true vs false B, model scale, and generalization to naturally-occurring associative pairs (e.g., from knowledge-base neighbors) not used in tuning.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent contagion could reflect lexical/co-occurrence priming captured by the probe rather than a genuine belief shift; we mitigate with lexical-overlap controls, paraphrase controls, embedding-vs-overlap regression, and causal patching that isolates the belief-direction component.

It may be hard to guarantee strict logical independence for real-world A/B pairs (subtle implicatures); we use human annotation, construct pairs from disjoint attributes, and include a spectrum so partial-dependence items can be filtered.
Truth probes may imperfectly capture beliefs for some B propositions, so contagion could partly reflect probe noise; we use multiple probe types, manipulation checks on A, and causal validation.

The Containment intervention could inadvertently suppress legitimate entailment-driven updating or harm fluency; we explicitly measure preservation on entailed anchors and capability retention, characterizing the tradeoff.

Contagion might correlate with but not exceed simple embedding-relatedness as a hallucination predictor; if so, the value is the mechanistic/causal insight and the containment tool, which we report honestly.
Findings may vary across model families, scales, and post-training; we test multiple models and report scale effects and negative results as informative.

Name: suppositional_belief_partitioning
Title: Believing Under Supposition: Do LLMs Internally Separate Hypothetical Beliefs From Actual Beliefs?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM reasons under a supposition it does not actually accept (e.g., 'Suppose the Earth had two moons; then tides would be stronger'), it must transiently adopt a hypothetical belief in the antecedent and its consequences while keeping its actual belief intact. We hypothesize that (1) an LLM's internal belief representation encodes a *suppositional* belief that is dissociable from its *actual* belief, (2) the two frequently fail to stay separated so that supposing a false premise contaminates the model's actual belief (a measurable 'supposition leak'), (3) leak magnitude causally predicts a failure mode where the model conflates hypothetical with actual after the supposition is withdrawn, and (4) a lightweight inference-time intervention that quarantines the suppositional shift reduces leak and improves counterfactual-reasoning reliability without harming genuine hypothetical inference.
Related Work: Truth/belief directions are extracted from activations (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023) and shown to be context-sensitive when real supporting/contradicting evidence is present (Schouten et al. 2024). Levinson (2026) finds belief-state simplex geometries via SAEs. Layer of Truth (Churina et al. 2025) tracks belief flips under pretraining poisoning. Counterfactual reasoning work (DeLorean, Qin et al. 2020) and ToM counterfactual-intervention analyses (Mohanty et al. 2026) operate at the output or third-party-belief level. Crucially, no prior work distinguishes, inside the model's own first-order belief representation, a belief held *under a supposition the model rejects* from the belief it *actually* holds, quantifies how suppositions leak into actual beliefs, ties this leak causally to hypothetical-actual conflation, or intervenes to quarantine it. This differs from my prior proposals: coherence studies logical updating under accepted evidence; provenance separates parametric vs contextual sources; ghosts study residue of superseded beliefs; contagion studies spillover across independent propositions. Suppositional partitioning is a new axis: the co-existence of a rejected-but-entertained belief alongside the endorsed belief.
Abstract: Rational reasoning requires the ability to entertain a supposition without believing it: to explore 'if X were true, then Y' while keeping one's actual convictions untouched. We ask whether large language models maintain this separation inside their belief representations. We distinguish an *actual belief* (the truth-value the model endorses for a proposition) from a *suppositional belief* (the truth-value the model represents for that proposition while reasoning under a hypothesis it does not accept). We construct SupposeBelief, a controlled dataset in which a supposition contrary to fact is introduced ('Suppose that P', where P is false), consequences Q are queried inside the suppositional scope, and the model's actual belief in P and Q is probed both inside and after the supposition is withdrawn. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes on hidden states, we read scalar suppositional and actual beliefs and define a Supposition Leak Score measuring how much entertaining a false P shifts the model's post-supposition actual belief in P (and its consequences). We test whether (1) suppositional and actual beliefs are dissociable linear quantities, (2) leak is nonzero and grows with supposition depth and plausibility, (3) leak causally predicts a hypothetical-actual conflation failure (the model later asserts the supposed falsehood as fact), and (4) a Supposition Quarantine intervention that confines the hypothetical shift to the suppositional scope reduces leak and conflation while preserving valid counterfactual inference. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on counterfactual QA, calibration, and capability retention. Our results reveal whether LLM beliefs respect the boundary between imagining and believing, and provide a cheap tool to enforce it.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build SupposeBelief. Each item = (a) an actual-world proposition P that is FALSE by world knowledge (e.g., 'The Earth has two moons'), (b) a supposition framing that opens a hypothetical scope ('Suppose that P. ...'), (c) one or more consequence propositions Q that would follow if P held (some true-under-P/false-in-actual-world, some independent), and (d) query points both INSIDE the supposition scope and AFTER the scope is explicitly closed ('Now, back to the real world: is P true?'). Include: true-P controls (supposing something already true), pure-imagination framings ('Imagine', 'In a story where') vs logical suppositions ('Assume for argument'), variable supposition depth (chains of nested/consequential supposings), and plausibility levels (mildly vs wildly counterfactual). Match surface forms to avoid the probe merely detecting the words 'suppose/imagine'.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an independent set of simple true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to [0,1]. Read the internal belief in P and Q at three positions: baseline (no supposition), inside the supposition scope, and after the scope is withdrawn. Manipulation check: confirm the model behaviorally reasons correctly under the supposition (output-level).

Dissociation analysis: Define suppositional-belief = probe readout inside scope, actual-belief = readout at baseline / after withdrawal. Test whether these are dissociable: inside a valid supposition the suppositional belief in a false P should rise while the actual (post-withdrawal) belief should ideally return to baseline. Measure cosine geometry: is there a distinct 'suppositional-mode' component, and can suppositional belief be decoded in the subspace orthogonal to the actual-truth direction? Include the 'suppose/imagine' phrase-only baseline to rule out phrase detection.

Supposition Leak Score: Define Leak(item) = actual-belief-in-P after withdrawal minus baseline actual-belief-in-P (signed toward the supposed value). Also measure consequence leak (residual belief in Q after scope closes). Report per-layer, per-model leak as a function of supposition depth, plausibility, and framing (imagine vs assume). Test the hypotheses that leak is nonzero, grows with depth and plausibility, and is larger for imaginative than logical framings. Compare internal leak to output-level leak (does the model later assert P as fact?).

Causal validation: Activation patching. Take the activation shift induced by entering the supposition scope; (a) patch its projection onto P's truth direction into the post-withdrawal state and measure whether the model's actual belief/output flips toward the falsehood; (b) subtract the suppositional shift and measure restoration. Confirm the leak component along the truth direction causally drives hypothetical-actual conflation and is separable from the intended suppositional reasoning.

Predictive validity for conflation failures: At the item level, test whether Leak Score predicts (i) post-scope conflation (model asserts the supposed falsehood as actual fact when later asked), (ii) inconsistency across paraphrased 'back to reality' queries, and (iii) contamination of downstream unrelated factual answers within the same conversation. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (output entropy, actual-truth probe confidence, supposition-plausibility score).

Supposition Quarantine intervention: At inference, detect the suppositional shift as the residual-stream component along the relevant truth direction that appears within the supposition scope, and at scope-closure subtract (quarantine) that component from later positions, ITI-style, so the actual belief re-anchors to baseline. Provide a scope-agnostic deployment variant that quarantines shifts introduced under explicit hypothetical markers. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduction in Leak Score, (ii) reduction in post-scope conflation and paraphrase inconsistency, (iii) PRESERVATION of valid counterfactual reasoning inside the scope (must NOT be suppressed) on counterfactual-QA benchmarks (e.g., counterfactual story revision, 'what-if' science questions), (iv) calibration (ECE) on actual-fact QA after hypothetical excursions, and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, and prompt-based instruction to 'clearly separate hypotheticals from facts'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), supposition depth and plausibility, imagine vs assume framing, true-P control (should show near-zero problematic leak), model scale, distance between scope-closure and the actual query, and generalization to naturally occurring hypothetical passages not used in tuning.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent leak could reflect the probe detecting lexical residue of the supposed proposition rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with phrase-only baselines, surface-form matching, paraphrase controls, and causal patching that isolates the truth-direction component.

Truth probes may imperfectly capture beliefs for counterfactual or consequence propositions, so suppositional readouts could carry probe noise; use multiple probe types, behavioral manipulation checks that the model reasons correctly under supposition, and validate on true-P controls.

Distinguishing 'suppositional belief' from 'actual belief' assumes a stable comparable belief scale across positions; scalar readouts depend on token/position choices, so we include position and layer robustness checks.

Supposition Quarantine could over-suppress and impair legitimate counterfactual reasoning inside the scope, or harm fluency; we explicitly measure counterfactual-QA preservation and capability retention, characterizing the tradeoff.

Leak may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (supposition plausibility, output entropy) for conflation failures; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal insight and the quarantine tool, which we report honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may already encourage hypothetical framing); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: belief_evidence_weighting
Title: Do LLM Beliefs Weigh Evidence? Testing Bayesian Sensitivity of Internal Belief Strength to Evidence Quantity and Reliability
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's internal belief strength for a proposition should update in a graded, Bayesian-like manner as it accumulates in-context evidence: more independent supporting pieces should raise internal belief, more reliable sources should raise it more than unreliable ones, and mixed evidence should produce intermediate belief. We hypothesize that LLM internal belief representations are systematically MIS-WEIGHTED: they respond to the number/salience of evidence pieces but under-respond to evidence reliability, over-count redundant (non-independent) evidence, and violate order-invariance, and that a lightweight inference-time recalibration along the belief direction can correct these weighting errors and improve evidence-aggregation accuracy.
Related Work: Prior work extracts linear truth/belief directions from activations (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023) and treats internal belief as a binary-ish truth-value read at a single position. Calibration work (Kadavath et al. 2022; verbalized confidence studies) examines output-level confidence but not whether internal belief magnitude tracks evidence weight. Schouten et al. (2024) show a single premise shifts the truth-direction position of an entailed hypothesis, but do not study graded aggregation over MULTIPLE, varying-reliability, possibly-redundant or conflicting evidence pieces. Freedman & Toni (2025) study probabilistic-belief coherence only at output level. No prior work asks whether the internal belief SCALAR behaves like a rational posterior: monotone in evidence count, sensitive to source reliability, robust to redundancy, order-invariant, and correctly balanced under conflict. This is a distinct 'quantitative rationality' lens on belief representations, orthogonal to my prior proposals on logical coherence, provenance, ghosts, drift, contagion, metabelief, and supposition.
Abstract: A belief worth the name is graded: a rational agent should hold a proposition more firmly after seeing three independent reliable sources than after one unreliable rumor, should not double-count the same evidence stated twice, and should not care about the order in which evidence arrived. We ask whether large language models' INTERNAL belief representations obey these Bayesian desiderata. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar internal belief for a proposition, we construct EvidenceWeight, a controlled dataset in which a target proposition is accompanied by in-context evidence that we systematically vary along four axes: quantity (number of supporting pieces), reliability (source cues: authoritative vs rumored, high vs low confidence hedging), independence (genuinely distinct evidence vs redundant paraphrases of one source), and valence (supporting vs conflicting). We measure how the internal belief scalar responds to each manipulation and test four rationality properties: monotonicity in evidence quantity, reliability-weighting, redundancy-robustness, and order-invariance. We compare the observed belief trajectory to a normative Bayesian posterior fit to ground-truth evidence weights, quantifying systematic mis-weighting (e.g., count-driven but reliability-insensitive updating, redundancy over-counting). We validate causality via activation patching, compare internal to verbalized-confidence weighting, and finally introduce Evidence Recalibration, an inference-time intervention that rescales the belief-direction shift by estimated evidence reliability/independence. We evaluate whether recalibration improves accuracy on multi-source evidence-aggregation QA and calibration, without harming general capability. Our results reveal whether LLM beliefs are genuine graded posteriors and offer a cheap tool to make evidence weighting more rational.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build EvidenceWeight. Each item = a target proposition P (true or false by world knowledge, or a synthetic fact defined only in context) plus a bundle of in-context evidence pieces. Systematically vary four axes: (1) Quantity: 0,1,2,3,5 supporting pieces; (2) Reliability: each piece tagged with a source/confidence cue (e.g., 'According to an official report...', 'A peer-reviewed study found...' vs 'Someone on a forum claimed...', 'I might be wrong, but...'); (3) Independence: N genuinely distinct sources vs N near-identical paraphrases of ONE source (redundancy); (4) Valence: all-supporting, all-conflicting, and mixed (k support, m conflict). Include order-permutation variants of the same evidence set, and a no-evidence baseline. Use synthetic-fact items (fact defined solely in context) to isolate in-context evidence weighting from parametric priors, plus real-world items to test interaction with priors. Match surface length across conditions to avoid length confounds.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an independent set of simple true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At the query position after the evidence bundle, read the internal belief in P. Manipulation check: confirm evidence moves belief in the intended direction at all.

Rationality property tests: (a) Monotonicity: does internal belief increase with number of supporting pieces (holding reliability fixed)? Fit belief-vs-count curves per layer/model. (b) Reliability-weighting: compare belief after N high-reliability vs N low-reliability pieces; a rational model should distinguish them. Quantify a Reliability Sensitivity index. (c) Redundancy-robustness: compare N independent pieces vs N redundant paraphrases; rational belief should rise more for independent evidence. Quantify a Redundancy Over-count index (how much belief rises from mere repetition). (d) Order-invariance: variance of final belief across evidence-order permutations; rational belief should be order-invariant. Quantify an Order Sensitivity index.

Normative comparison: For synthetic-fact items where ground-truth evidence weights are known by construction (each source has an assigned reliability/likelihood ratio), compute the Bayesian posterior and compare it to the observed internal belief. Report a systematic-bias decomposition: count-driven gain, reliability under/over-weighting, redundancy inflation, and conflict-balancing error. Compare internal-belief weighting to verbalized-confidence weighting (ask the model its confidence in P) to test whether internal representations are more or less rational than outputs.

Causal validation: Activation patching. Take the residual-stream shift induced by adding an extra evidence piece and measure the resulting change in the belief-direction projection and output; test whether reliability cues causally modulate the magnitude of this shift or merely its presence. Confirm the belief scalar's movement is causal for the output answer.

Evidence Recalibration intervention: At inference, estimate per-piece reliability/independence (from explicit source cues and cross-piece similarity for redundancy) and rescale the belief-direction shift accordingly at a chosen layer (ITI-style): dampen shifts from low-reliability or redundant evidence, preserve shifts from reliable independent evidence. Sweep layer and strength. Provide a cue-based deployment variant that reads reliability from surface markers.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) improved rationality indices (reliability sensitivity up, redundancy over-count down, order sensitivity down), (ii) accuracy on multi-source evidence-aggregation QA where correct answers require weighting reliable-independent evidence over redundant/unreliable evidence (constructed benchmark plus adapted fact-verification tasks like FEVER-style multi-evidence items), (iii) calibration (ECE) of final answers against evidence-implied ground truth, and (iv) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, and prompt-based instruction to 'weigh evidence by reliability and ignore repetition'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), synthetic vs real-world facts, supporting vs conflicting vs mixed valence, evidence-bundle size, redundancy detection method, model scale, and generalization to naturally occurring multi-source documents not used in tuning.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent mis-weighting could reflect the probe detecting surface features (evidence length, repeated tokens) rather than a genuine belief magnitude; mitigate with length-matched conditions, redundancy-vs-independence controls with matched wording, and causal patching that isolates the belief-direction shift.

Truth probes may saturate (near 0 or 1) for strong evidence, compressing the graded signal; we use synthetic facts with tunable evidence strength, mid-layer readouts, and calibrated Platt scaling, and report saturation effects honestly.

The normative Bayesian comparison depends on assigned ground-truth evidence weights, which are only clean for synthetic items; real-world reliability is subjective, so we anchor quantitative claims on synthetic items and treat real-world results as qualitative.
Evidence Recalibration requires estimating reliability/independence at inference, which is imperfect from surface cues; the deployment variant may be less effective and we characterize this gap.
Recalibration could over-dampen legitimate updating or harm fluency; we measure aggregation accuracy, calibration, and capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Findings may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may shape hedging/confidence); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: time_indexed_belief_geometry
Title: When Is It True? Probing and Steering the Temporal Indexing of LLM Internal Beliefs
Short Hypothesis: For a mutable fact with a validity interval (e.g., 'Angela Merkel is Chancellor of Germany', true 2005-2021), a rational belief must be conditioned on a reference time: the internal belief should be high when the queried date lies inside the validity window and low outside it. We hypothesize that LLM internal belief representations (linear truth directions) are systematically UNDER-conditioned on reference time: they collapse toward a single time-agnostic 'default' value (typically the most recent or most frequently attested state), so the internal belief for a past-true / future-false proposition barely tracks the queried date. We further hypothesize this temporal un-anchoring is measurable, causally predicts date-conflation errors and anachronistic hallucinations, and can be corrected by a cheap inference-time intervention that re-anchors the belief along the truth direction to the queried reference time.
