Related Work: A large body of work benchmarks temporal factual knowledge at the OUTPUT level: Pinocchio, TempReason, ChroKnowledge/ChroKnowBench, Time Awareness/TimeShift, TDBench, and TIDE all measure whether models answer time-sensitive questions correctly, and temporal knowledge-editing work (WikiFactDiff, MTKE/SPIKE, multi-granularity TKE) edits weights. DToM-Track (Nguyen et al. 2026) studies temporal retrieval of OTHERS' belief states (third-party Theory-of-Mind) and finds models fail to retrieve prior beliefs after updates, but only behaviorally and for others' beliefs. Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) reads a single time-agnostic internal belief. Crucially, NO prior work asks whether the model's OWN first-order internal belief representation is properly conditioned on a queried reference date — i.e., whether the internal truth scalar for a time-indexed proposition rises inside its validity window and falls outside it, whether it instead collapses to a recency/frequency default, whether this un-anchoring causally drives anachronistic errors, or whether it can be re-anchored via steering. This is a new time-indexed-belief-geometry lens, distinct from output-level temporal benchmarks and from all my prior proposals (coherence, provenance, ghosts, context drift, contagion, metabelief, supposition, evidence-weighting), none of which index the belief itself by reference time.
Abstract: Many facts are true only within a time window: an official held office for a term, a company had a CEO for a period, a record stood until it was broken. A belief worth the name must therefore be indexed to a reference time — the same proposition should be believed at some dates and disbelieved at others. We ask whether large language models internally represent this. We distinguish a proposition's content from its reference-time conditioning and test whether an LLM's internal belief scalar, read via linear truth probes, is a proper function of the queried date: high inside the fact's validity interval, low outside it. We construct TimeBelief, a controlled dataset of mutable facts (offices, team memberships, CEOs, records, treaties) each annotated with a validity interval, paired with queries stamped at dates before, during, and after the interval. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes, we read the internal belief for each (proposition, reference-date) and define a Temporal Anchoring Score measuring how strongly the internal belief tracks the queried date versus collapsing to a time-agnostic default. We test whether (1) internal beliefs are under-conditioned on time, biased toward the most-recent or most-frequently-attested value; (2) a separable 'reference-time' representation exists and is dissociable from the truth direction; (3) low anchoring causally predicts anachronistic errors and date conflation; and (4) a lightweight Temporal Re-anchoring intervention that shifts activations along the truth direction as a function of the queried date restores date-conditioned beliefs and improves time-sensitive QA. We validate causality with activation patching and evaluate on temporal QA, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build TimeBelief. Collect mutable facts from Wikidata-style temporal triples with known validity intervals [t_start, t_end]: heads of state/office holders, sports team memberships, company CEOs, world records, treaties/laws in force. For each fact, create a time-indexed proposition template ('As of <DATE>, <SUBJECT> is/holds <VALUE>') and instantiate queries at dates sampled BEFORE t_start (should be false), DURING [t_start,t_end] (true), and AFTER t_end (false). For each subject collect the full sequence of successive values so we can identify the 'most recent' and 'most frequent' value (to test default-collapse hypotheses). Include (a) items whose current/most-recent value equals the queried-window value and (b) items where they differ (to dissociate correct time-conditioning from recency prior). Add control static facts (time-invariant) and paraphrase sets. Match surface form of true/false variants; keep dates within the model's pretraining coverage.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of simple, time-invariant true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At the query token, read the internal belief in each (proposition, reference-date). Manipulation check: confirm probes transfer to time-indexed statements on clearly-true/clearly-false items.

Temporal Anchoring Score: For each fact, plot internal belief vs queried date across the before/during/after regimes. Define Temporal Anchoring Score = (mean belief DURING window) - (mean belief OUTSIDE window), and a Default-Collapse Index = correlation between internal belief and 'queried value == most-recent value' (or most-frequent value) after controlling for whether the date is actually inside the window. Report per-layer, per-model anchoring, and test the hypothesis that internal beliefs collapse toward the recency/frequency default rather than the date-conditioned truth. Compare internal-belief anchoring to OUTPUT-level anchoring (asking the model directly).

Reference-time representation and dissociation: Test whether a linear 'reference-time' direction is decodable from activations (regress the queried date / a before-during-after label from hidden states). Measure whether truth-direction and reference-time direction are dissociable (project out one, re-decode the other). Test whether the model's belief update as the queried date crosses t_start / t_end is a sharp step (rational) or a smooth drift dominated by recency.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Patch the reference-time representation from a during-window query into a before/after query and measure whether the internal belief and the output flip toward 'true'. (b) Add/subtract the truth direction gated by the queried date and measure output changes. Confirm that proper date-conditioning is causal and that its absence (default-collapse) drives anachronistic answers.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether the Temporal Anchoring Score / Default-Collapse Index predicts (i) anachronistic factual error (model asserts the most-recent value for an out-of-window date), (ii) date-conflation (model gives the right value but wrong when queried at a different valid date), and (iii) paraphrase inconsistency across date phrasings. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (output entropy, final-position truth-probe confidence, recency of the queried value).

Temporal Re-anchoring intervention: At inference, given the queried reference date, add a scaled shift along the truth direction whose sign/magnitude is set by whether the date falls inside the fact's validity window (an ITI-style, date-gated re-anchoring). Provide a practical deployment variant that reads the queried date from the prompt and modulates the truth-direction shift, without needing ground-truth validity intervals at test time (use the model's own decoded reference-time representation to gate). Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) increased Temporal Anchoring Score, (ii) reduced anachronistic error and date conflation, (iii) accuracy on external time-sensitive QA (TempReason, ChroKnowBench, TimeShift subsets), (iv) calibration (ECE) of date-conditioned answers, (v) PRESERVATION of accuracy on time-invariant control facts (must not be harmed), and (vi) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, and prompt-based instruction to 'answer only for the given date'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), fact domain (offices vs sports vs CEOs vs records), recency-aligned vs recency-misaligned items, distance of queried date from window boundary, model scale, and generalization to fact types and time ranges not used to tune the intervention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The truth probe may only weakly transfer to time-indexed propositions, so measured under-anchoring could partly reflect probe error rather than genuine temporal un-anchoring; mitigate with multiple probe types, transfer checks on clearly-true/false time-stamped items, and causal patching.

Apparent default-collapse could be confounded with the model simply not knowing the fact at all; we restrict to facts the model demonstrably knows for at least one date (manipulation-checked) and separate 'no-knowledge' items.

Distinguishing a genuine 'reference-time' representation from surface date-token detection is hard; we use paraphrased/relative date framings ('during his second term' vs explicit years) and project-out controls, treating a pure date-token-detection result as an informative negative.

Facts must lie within the model's pretraining coverage and have reliable validity intervals; noisy or contested intervals could bias anchoring estimates. We anchor quantitative claims on high-confidence Wikidata intervals and human-verify a sample.

The date-gated Re-anchoring intervention needs to infer the queried date and its relation to the window at test time; the deployment variant relying on decoded reference-time may be less effective, and we characterize this gap honestly.

Re-anchoring could over-suppress correct recency-aligned beliefs or harm time-invariant facts and fluency; we include recency-aligned and static-fact controls and measure capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.
Findings may vary across model families, scales, and post-training; we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: agent_indexed_belief_binding
Title: Who Believes What? Testing Whether LLMs Keep Different Agents' Beliefs About the Same Proposition Separable in Activation Space
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM tracks a scenario in which two agents hold OPPOSING beliefs about the same proposition P (Alice believes P, Bob believes not-P), a competent belief-tracker must maintain two distinct, agent-bound belief coordinates for the same content. We hypothesize that LLM internal belief representations exhibit 'agent-belief binding failure': the two agents' beliefs about P interfere and partially collapse toward a single shared value (often the model's own factual belief or the most recently mentioned agent's belief), that this interference is a graded, decodable quantity, causally predicts false-belief and perspective-attribution errors, and can be reduced by a lightweight inference-time intervention that de-mixes the agent-bound belief directions.
Related Work: Truth/belief-direction probing reads a single first-order belief per proposition (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024). Theory-of-Mind work evaluates false-belief reasoning behaviorally (ToMi, BigToM) and, recently, mechanistically: Avalon-ToM-Bench (Chen et al. 2026) shows linear probes recover correct mental-state inferences that CoT fails to express, and prior work steers ToM-relevant activations. However, all of these probe/steer a mental-state or a proposition in isolation; none asks whether, when MULTIPLE agents hold DIFFERENT beliefs about the SAME proposition, the model maintains distinct agent-BOUND belief coordinates in activation space, quantifies their mutual interference/collapse, ties that interference causally to attribution errors, or intervenes to de-mix them. This binding lens (content vs. agent-index as separable factors) is distinct from output-level ToM benchmarks and from all my prior belief proposals (coherence, provenance, ghosts, drift, contagion, metabelief, supposition, evidence-weighting, temporal indexing), none of which index a belief by which agent holds it.
Abstract: Reasoning about other minds requires representing that different people can believe different things about the same fact: Alice may believe the keys are in the drawer while Bob believes they are on the table. We ask whether large language models maintain this separation inside their belief representations. We treat a tracked belief as having two factors—its content (a proposition P) and its agent-index (whose belief it is)—and test whether the model keeps agent-bound belief coordinates for the same P distinct. We construct AgentBelief, a controlled dataset of two-agent scenarios in which agents A and B are established, via in-context evidence, to hold agreeing or opposing beliefs about a shared proposition P (spanning true-belief, false-belief, and neutral cases), followed by perspective-stamped queries ('According to Alice, is P true?'). Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes conditioned on the queried agent, we read a scalar agent-indexed belief and define an Agent-Belief Interference Score measuring how much one agent's belief bleeds into the readout of the other's (collapse toward a shared value, the model's own factual view, or a recency default). We test whether (1) agent-indexed beliefs are dissociable linear quantities; (2) opposing beliefs interfere and partially collapse; (3) interference causally predicts false-belief and mis-attribution errors; and (4) a lightweight de-mixing intervention along agent-bound belief directions reduces interference and improves perspective-attribution accuracy without harming general capability. We validate causality with activation patching and evaluate on ToM-style QA, calibration, and capability retention. Our results reveal whether LLM beliefs are properly bound to their holders and offer a cheap tool to fix binding failures.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build AgentBelief. Each item establishes two named agents A and B and a shared proposition P via short in-context narratives, then queries a perspective-stamped belief ('According to A, P?' and 'According to B, P?') plus the model's own view ('Is P true?'). Cross three factors: (i) belief configuration {A believes P & B believes P; A believes P & B believes not-P; A believes not-P & B believes P; neither states a view (neutral control)}; (ii) alignment with world truth {P actually true, false, or synthetic/undetermined}; (iii) presentation order and which agent is mentioned last (to test recency-collapse). Include classic false-belief (Sally-Anne style) items and paraphrase sets. Match surface forms so the probe cannot exploit trivial name/lexical cues; include single-agent baselines.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of simple, agent-free true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to [0,1]. Read agent-indexed belief at the perspective-stamped query token for each agent, plus the model's own belief. Manipulation check: on agreeing-belief items, confirm both agents' readouts move with the stated view.

Agent-Belief Interference Score: On opposing-belief items (A: P, B: not-P), a well-bound model should read high belief for A and low for B. Define Interference = 1 - |belief(A) - belief(B)| (0 = perfectly separated, 1 = fully collapsed). Decompose collapse direction: toward the model's own factual belief, toward the last-mentioned agent (recency), or toward a mid-point. Report per-layer, per-model interference across configurations and orderings, and compare to OUTPUT-level interference (do the model's verbal answers to the two perspective queries collapse?).

Dissociation / binding analysis: Test whether a linear 'agent-index' direction is decodable (regress which agent is queried from activations) and whether content (P's truth) and agent-index are separable factors: project out the truth direction and test if agent-conditioned belief remains decodable, and vice versa. Assess whether opposing beliefs are stored in a genuinely two-dimensional (agent x content) subspace or collapse to one axis.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Patch the agent-index representation from an 'According to A' query into an 'According to B' query and measure whether B's belief readout and output flip toward A's value (evidence of binding vs. leakage). (b) Add/subtract the agent-bound belief-direction component and measure changes in the perspective-stamped output. Confirm interference is causal for mis-attribution.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether Interference Score predicts (i) false-belief errors (model reports the world-true or its-own value when asked about an agent with a false belief), (ii) cross-agent confusion (attributing A's belief to B), and (iii) paraphrase inconsistency across perspective phrasings. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (output entropy, own-belief probe confidence, recency of the queried agent).

De-mixing intervention: At inference, estimate the agent-bound belief shift for the queried agent and dampen the component aligned with the OTHER agent's belief and with the model's own factual belief (ITI-style), effectively separating the two agent coordinates at a chosen layer. Provide a deployment variant that gates on the decoded agent-index. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Interference Score, (ii) improved false-belief / perspective-attribution accuracy on AgentBelief and external ToM-style QA (ToMi, BigToM subsets), (iii) calibration (ECE) of perspective-stamped answers, (iv) PRESERVATION of correct answers on agreeing-belief and single-agent controls (must not be harmed), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, and prompt-based instruction to 'answer strictly from the named person's perspective'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), belief configuration, world-truth alignment, presentation order/recency, number of agents (extend to 3 agents to test scaling of interference), model scale, and generalization to naturally occurring multi-agent narratives not used to tune the intervention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Agent-indexed readouts could reflect the probe detecting surface cues (which name appears in the query) rather than a genuine agent-bound belief; mitigate with surface-form matching, name-swap and paraphrase controls, project-out analyses, and causal patching that isolates the belief-direction component.

Truth probes trained on agent-free statements may transfer imperfectly to perspective-stamped propositions, so interference could partly reflect probe error; use multiple probe types, agreeing-belief manipulation checks, and validate on clearly-separable single-agent items.
Defining a scalar agent-indexed belief depends on token/position choices; include position and layer robustness checks.

The de-mixing intervention could over-suppress and harm agreeing-belief or single-agent cases, or hurt fluency; we explicitly measure preservation on those controls and capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Interference may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (recency, output entropy) for attribution errors; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal binding insight and the de-mixing tool, which we report honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may already shape perspective-taking); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: wishful_belief_bias
Title: Wishful Beliefs: Do LLM Internal Belief Representations Bend Toward Desirable Propositions?
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's internal belief in a factual proposition is systematically biased by the proposition's DESIRABILITY (how flattering, safe, hope-consistent, or user-pleasing it is), independent of its truth. We hypothesize a decodable 'wishful bias': the internal belief scalar for equally-true propositions is higher when the proposition is desirable and lower when undesirable, that this desirability axis is dissociable from the truth axis, that wishful bias causally predicts a hallucination mode where the model asserts pleasant falsehoods, and that a lightweight inference-time intervention that removes the desirability component from the belief shift reduces motivated-reasoning errors without harming legitimate belief updating.
Related Work: Sycophancy work (Perez et al. 2022; Sharma et al. 2023) shows LLMs bend OUTPUTS toward user views, and steering studies suppress sycophantic answers behaviorally. Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) reads a single first-order internal belief. My prior 'provenance' proposal separated parametric vs contextual sources; 'metabelief' separated first- vs second-order beliefs; 'evidence-weighting' tested Bayesian aggregation. None asks whether a proposition's DESIRABILITY (valence to the model/user, independent of source or logic) distorts the internal belief scalar for truth-matched propositions, treats desirability as a separable linear axis interfering with the truth axis, links this internal wishful bias causally to a pleasant-falsehood hallucination mode, or intervenes to de-bias the belief update. This reframes sycophancy as an internal, pre-verbalization distortion of belief geometry rather than an output-selection effect, and is distinct from all prior proposals.
Abstract: Humans engage in wishful thinking: we believe pleasant things more readily than unpleasant ones, even against evidence. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous distortion inside their belief representations. We distinguish a proposition's truth-value from its DESIRABILITY—how flattering to the user, hope-consistent, safe, or socially pleasant it is—and test whether an LLM's internal belief scalar, read via linear truth probes, is biased by desirability while holding truth fixed. We construct WishfulBelief, a controlled dataset of proposition pairs matched on ground-truth truth-value but contrasted on desirability (e.g., true-and-pleasant vs true-and-unpleasant; false-and-pleasant vs false-and-unpleasant), spanning user-flattery, optimistic outcomes, and morally comforting claims, with surface forms matched to avoid lexical cues. Using difference-in-means and logistic probes we read a scalar internal belief for each proposition and define a Wishful Bias Score = the belief gap between desirable and undesirable but equally-true propositions. We test whether (1) a desirability axis is decodable and dissociable from the truth axis; (2) internal belief bends toward desirable propositions; (3) wishful bias causally predicts a pleasant-falsehood hallucination mode (asserting comforting untruths); and (4) a Desirability De-biasing intervention that subtracts the desirability component from the belief shift reduces motivated-reasoning errors while preserving legitimate updating and general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on factuality, sycophancy, calibration, and capability retention. Our results recast sycophancy as an internal belief distortion and offer a cheap tool to counter wishful thinking in LLMs.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build WishfulBelief. Each item is a factual proposition annotated with (a) ground-truth truth-value (true/false by world knowledge or by construction for synthetic facts) and (b) a desirability rating along axes: user-flattery ('Your plan is likely to succeed'), optimistic outcome ('This treatment usually works'), morally comforting ('Most people act honestly'), vs their undesirable counterparts. Crucially, construct 2x2 cells: {true, false} x {desirable, undesirable} with matched surface length and topic, so truth is balanced across desirability. Include synthetic-fact items where truth is defined solely in context to remove parametric priors. Validate desirability ratings with human annotation and an embedding/LLM-judge desirability score. Add neutral-desirability controls and paraphrase sets.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral-desirability true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At the query position read the internal belief for each WishfulBelief proposition. Manipulation check: confirm probes separate clearly-true from clearly-false neutral items.

Wishful Bias Score: Holding truth fixed, define Wishful Bias = mean internal belief(desirable) - mean internal belief(undesirable) within the true cell and within the false cell. Report per-layer, per-model bias across desirability axes (flattery/optimism/moral-comfort). Test the hypothesis that bias is positive (belief bends toward desirable). Compare internal-belief bias to OUTPUT-level bias (asking the model directly whether each proposition is true / its confidence).

Dissociation / axis analysis: Test whether a linear 'desirability' direction is decodable (regress human/LLM-judge desirability from activations) and whether it is dissociable from the truth direction: measure cosine similarity, project out the truth direction and test if desirability remains decodable and vice versa. Assess whether desirability leaks into the truth-probe readout (the mechanistic substrate of wishful bias).

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Take the activation difference between a desirable and its matched undesirable proposition, decompose into truth-direction and desirability-direction components, patch only the desirability component into a neutral proposition, and measure the induced change in internal belief and output. (b) Subtract the desirability component from a desirable proposition and measure whether belief moves toward the truth-appropriate value. Confirm desirability causally shifts the belief scalar.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether Wishful Bias predicts a pleasant-falsehood hallucination mode: (i) endorsement rate of false-but-desirable propositions, (ii) confident-wrong rate on comforting falsehoods, (iii) sycophantic agreement when a user expresses a hopeful but false belief. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (desirability rating alone, output entropy, neutral truth-probe confidence).

Desirability De-biasing intervention: At inference, estimate the desirability direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer so the belief readout reflects truth-relevant evidence only (ITI-style de-biasing). Provide a deployment variant gated on detected high desirability. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Wishful Bias Score, (ii) reduced endorsement of pleasant falsehoods and reduced sycophantic agreement (adapt existing sycophancy benchmarks), (iii) factuality/calibration (ECE) on mixed desirable/undesirable factual QA, (iv) PRESERVATION of accuracy on true-and-desirable items (must not be suppressed as collateral) and on neutral controls, and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'judge truth regardless of how pleasant the claim is'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), desirability axis, synthetic vs real-world facts, truth cell (true vs false), model scale, and generalization to desirability axes and topics not used to fit the de-biasing direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent wishful bias could reflect the probe detecting sentiment/valence lexical features rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with surface-form and length matching, paraphrase controls, sentiment-vs-desirability disentangling, and causal patching that isolates the belief-direction component.

Truth probes trained on neutral items may transfer imperfectly to valenced propositions, so bias could partly reflect probe error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, and synthetic-fact items to control priors.
Desirability and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality and project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

De-biasing could over-suppress legitimate belief in true-and-desirable propositions or harm fluency; we explicitly measure preservation on true-desirable and neutral controls plus capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Wishful bias may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (desirability rating, output entropy) for pleasant-falsehood hallucination; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal insight and the de-biasing tool, which we report honestly.

Post-training (RLHF) may amplify or mask desirability bias, and effects may vary across model families/scales; we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: ignorance_vs_falsehood_belief
Title: Knowing You Don't Know: Do LLMs Internally Distinguish Ignorance From Belief in Falsehood?
Short Hypothesis: Almost all belief-probing treats a proposition's internal representation as one-dimensional (a truth scalar from false to true). But a genuine belief system needs a THIRD state: 'I don't know' (genuine ignorance / no evidence) must be represented distinctly from 'I believe this is false'. We hypothesize that (1) LLM belief geometry does NOT cleanly separate ignorance from falsehood — propositions the model has no knowledge of are collapsed toward the 'false' region of the truth direction rather than occupying a distinct low-confidence/abstention region; (2) a separable 'ignorance' (evidential-support) axis is nonetheless weakly decodable and dissociable from the true-vs-false axis; (3) this ignorance-falsehood conflation causally predicts a specific failure mode — confidently denying true-but-unknown claims and confidently affirming plausible-but-unknown claims instead of abstaining; and (4) a lightweight inference-time intervention that reads the ignorance axis and gates abstention improves selective-prediction (know-when-you-don't-know) without harming answered accuracy.
Related Work: Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) fits a single linear true-vs-false axis and reads a scalar belief; calibration/self-knowledge work (Kadavath et al. 2022 'models know what they know') studies OUTPUT-level P(True)/verbalized confidence, and hallucination-detection probes (e.g., SAPLMA, semantic-entropy methods) score single answers. Selective prediction and abstention work operates at the output/logit level. Crucially, none asks whether the internal BELIEF representation for a proposition carries a distinct 'ignorance' coordinate separable from the true/false axis, whether genuine ignorance collapses onto the 'false' region of the truth direction (a geometric conflation), whether that conflation causally drives false-denial/false-affirmation instead of abstention, or whether an internal ignorance axis can gate abstention better than output-confidence baselines. This is a new belief-geometry lens — modeling belief as (at least) two-dimensional (truth-value x evidential-support) — distinct from all my prior proposals (coherence, provenance, ghosts, drift, contagion, metabelief, supposition, evidence-weighting, temporal, agent-binding, wishful bias), none of which treat ignorance as a distinct state.
Abstract: A rational believer distinguishes three states about a proposition: believing it true, believing it false, and simply not knowing. Yet the dominant tool for reading LLM beliefs — a single linear 'truth direction' — collapses belief onto a one-dimensional true-versus-false axis, leaving no room for genuine ignorance. We ask whether LLM belief representations actually separate 'I don't know' from 'I believe this is false'. We construct KnowUnknow, a dataset that crosses ground-truth truth-value (true/false) with the model's evidential access (known: the model demonstrably has the relevant fact; unknown: obscure or newly-defined propositions the model provably cannot know), including matched surface forms and manipulation checks. Using difference-in-means and logistic probes, we first fit the standard truth direction and test our central conflation hypothesis: where do genuinely-unknown propositions fall along it? We predict they collapse toward the 'false' region rather than a neutral/abstain region. We then test whether a separate 'ignorance' (evidential-support) axis is decodable and dissociable from the truth axis via project-out analyses, and validate causality with activation patching. We show that the geometric distance between an unknown proposition and the abstain region causally predicts a diagnostic failure mode — confidently denying true-but-unknown claims and affirming plausible-but-unknown ones — and compare internal readouts to output-level confidence. Finally we introduce Ignorance-Gated Abstention, a cheap inference-time intervention that uses the decoded ignorance axis to trigger 'I don't know', and evaluate selective-prediction quality (risk-coverage, AUROC of abstention) against output-confidence baselines, alongside answered-accuracy and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build KnowUnknow, crossing truth-value {true, false} with evidential access {known, unknown}. KNOWN items = facts the model demonstrably has (verified by high-accuracy, low-entropy output on held-out phrasings). UNKNOWN items = (a) obscure real facts the model provably lacks (verified by chance-level accuracy and high entropy across paraphrases), and (b) SYNTHETIC propositions about entities/relations defined nowhere in pretraining (guaranteed-unknown by construction), each with a true and a false variant. Match surface form, length, and topic distribution across cells; include neutral controls and paraphrase sets; human-verify a sample.

Manipulation checks: For every item, confirm cell membership behaviorally — KNOWN items answered correctly with low entropy; UNKNOWN items at chance with high entropy or explicit hedging — to ensure 'unknown' reflects genuine ignorance rather than mislabeled knowledge.

Probe training and truth-axis conflation test: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), extract final-token hidden states per proposition per layer and fit the standard truth direction (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on KNOWN true vs KNOWN false items, Platt-scaled to [0,1]. Central test: project UNKNOWN items onto this truth axis and measure where they land. Hypothesis: unknown-true and unknown-false both collapse toward the 'false' region (or toward an uninformative default) rather than a neutral midpoint, quantified by a Conflation Score = distance of unknown-item projections from the known-false centroid vs from a neutral 0.5 abstain point.

Ignorance axis discovery and dissociation: Fit an 'ignorance' direction via difference-in-means on KNOWN (any truth) vs UNKNOWN (any truth) items, balanced on truth-value. Report per-layer decoding accuracy. Test dissociation from the truth axis: cosine similarity between the two directions per layer; project out the truth direction and re-decode ignorance (and vice versa) to show the ignorance axis is not just a reused truth axis. Report cross-axis leakage.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Move an item along the ignorance direction and measure whether the truth-probe readout and the output shift toward/away from abstention, holding the truth axis fixed. (b) Patch the ignorance component of a KNOWN item into an UNKNOWN item and measure induced changes. Confirm the ignorance axis is causal and separable from the truth axis.

Predictive validity for the abstention failure mode: At the item level, test whether an item's position on the truth axis (given it is unknown) predicts (i) confident false-denial of true-but-unknown claims, (ii) confident affirmation of plausible-but-unknown claims, and (iii) failure to abstain when abstention is the correct action. Report AUROC/correlation of the ignorance axis for detecting 'should-abstain' items, compared to baselines: output-token entropy, verbalized 'I don't know' rate, and P(True) self-evaluation (Kadavath-style).

Ignorance-Gated Abstention intervention: At inference, read the decoded ignorance-axis score at a chosen layer; if it exceeds a calibrated threshold, force an abstention/'I don't know' response (or route to hedged output). Threshold set on a held-out split. Optionally combine with a steering variant that nudges activations toward the abstain region. Sweep layer and threshold.

Downstream selective-prediction evaluation: On a mixed KNOWN/UNKNOWN QA set and external factual QA (TriviaQA-style plus obscure/entity-rare subsets, and synthetic-unknown items), measure (i) risk-coverage curves and selective-prediction AUC, (ii) AUROC of abstention decisions, (iii) reduction in confident false-denials and pleasant/plausible false-affirmations, (iv) PRESERVATION of answered accuracy and coverage on KNOWN items (must not over-abstain), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no gating, output-entropy thresholding, verbalized-confidence thresholding, P(True) thresholding.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), real-obscure vs synthetic-unknown items, true vs false unknown cells, model scale, threshold calibration transfer across domains, and generalization to unknown topics not used to fit the ignorance direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The ignorance axis might merely detect surface familiarity/frequency cues (rare tokens, unusual entities) rather than a genuine evidential-support representation; mitigate with synthetic-unknown items matched in surface form, frequency-controlled real items, paraphrase controls, and causal patching that isolates the ignorance-direction component.

Cell labeling is only as good as the manipulation checks; some 'unknown' items may be partially known and some 'known' items uncertain. We use strict behavioral thresholds, synthetic-guaranteed-unknown items, and human verification, and report label-noise sensitivity.

The conflation hypothesis assumes the standard truth probe generalizes to unknown propositions; if it does not, apparent collapse could reflect probe extrapolation error. We validate with multiple probe types and report this caveat honestly; a finding that the truth axis is undefined off-distribution is itself informative.

Ignorance-Gated Abstention could over-abstain and hurt coverage/accuracy on known items, or under-abstain if the axis is weak; we explicitly measure risk-coverage tradeoffs and known-item preservation, and compare against strong output-confidence baselines rather than claiming superiority a priori.

The internal ignorance axis may correlate with but not exceed output-entropy/P(True) baselines for abstention; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic finding that ignorance is (or is not) a distinct belief coordinate, which we report regardless of intervention gains.

Findings may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may already teach abstention phrasing); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: repetition_illusory_belief
Title: The Illusory Truth Effect in LLM Belief Geometry: Does Mere Repetition Move Internal Beliefs?
Short Hypothesis: Like humans, LLMs exhibit an illusory truth effect INSIDE their belief representations: merely repeating a statement in context (without any new evidence, and even with an explicit reminder that repetition is not evidence) raises the internal belief scalar (linear truth-direction readout) for that proposition. We hypothesize this repetition-induced belief inflation (1) is a graded function of repetition count, (2) is driven by a decodable 'familiarity/fluency' component dissociable from genuine evidence-based updating, (3) causally predicts a repetition-induced hallucination mode where models endorse repeated falsehoods, and (4) can be reduced by a lightweight inference-time intervention that subtracts the familiarity component from the belief shift, without harming legitimate evidence-based updating.
Related Work: The illusory truth effect (ITE) is a robust human bias (Fazio et al. 2015): repetition increases belief even against prior knowledge. Griffin et al. (2023) show LLMs, when PROMPTED to simulate human raters, reproduce ITE-like OUTPUT ratings; Casanova (2026), Ayyad (2026) and Gabriel (2025) discuss ITE only at the misinformation/social-network/output level. Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) reads a single first-order internal belief but never studies the effect of MERE REPETITION (no new evidence) on that internal belief. My prior proposals cover logical coherence, provenance, ghosts, context drift, associative contagion, metabelief, supposition, Bayesian evidence-weighting, temporal indexing, agent-binding, wishful bias, and ignorance-vs-falsehood; none address familiarity/fluency-driven belief inflation from repetition. This proposal is the first to (a) test whether ITE exists in LLM internal belief GEOMETRY (not simulated human ratings), (b) isolate a decodable familiarity axis distinct from evidence updating, (c) tie it causally to repeated-falsehood hallucination, and (d) de-bias it via steering.
Abstract: Humans believe statements more after mere repetition, even when they know better — the illusory truth effect (ITE). We ask whether large language models show an analogous distortion inside their belief representations, rather than merely mimicking human ratings when prompted to. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar internal belief along the linear truth direction, we test whether repeating a proposition in context — with no new evidence, and even when accompanied by an explicit note that repetition is not evidence — inflates the model's internal belief in that proposition. We construct RepeatBelief, a controlled dataset of true, false, and synthetic-fact propositions presented at varying repetition counts (0–8), with matched-length non-repeating filler controls, paraphrased-vs-verbatim repetition, and evidence-bearing conditions for comparison. We measure a Repetition Inflation Score (belief gain per repetition) across layers and model scale, and test four claims: (1) internal belief rises with repetition even absent evidence; (2) the inflation is carried by a decodable 'familiarity/fluency' direction dissociable from the genuine evidence-updating direction; (3) inflation magnitude causally predicts a repeated-falsehood hallucination mode (endorsing repeated untruths); and (4) a Familiarity De-biasing intervention that subtracts the familiarity component reduces the illusory inflation and repeated-falsehood endorsement while preserving legitimate evidence-based updating and general capability. We validate causality with activation patching and evaluate on factuality, misinformation robustness, calibration, and capability retention. Our results reveal whether the illusory truth effect is baked into LLM belief geometry and offer a cheap tool to counter it.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build RepeatBelief. Items are propositions with three truth regimes: (a) real true facts, (b) real false statements, (c) synthetic facts defined only in context (to remove parametric priors and isolate pure in-context effects). For each item, create conditions varying repetition count of the target statement in the preceding context (0,1,2,4,8 verbatim repetitions), a PARAPHRASED-repetition variant (same claim, different wording, to test whether inflation is fluency- vs surface-token-driven), a matched-length NON-REPEATING FILLER control (equal token budget of unrelated text, to separate repetition from generic context growth), and an EXPLICIT-DISCLAIMER variant ('Note: the following is repeated for emphasis and is not additional evidence'). Include an EVIDENCE condition where the extra text is genuine independent supporting evidence (for comparison with legitimate updating). Match surface length across conditions; add paraphrase query sets. Human-verify a sample.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of simple, single-occurrence true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At the query position, read internal belief in the target proposition under each condition. Manipulation check: confirm probes separate clearly-true from clearly-false single-occurrence items.

Repetition Inflation Score: For each item, plot internal belief vs repetition count (repetition-only condition, no new evidence). Define Repetition Inflation Score = slope of belief w.r.t. repetition count, controlling for the filler-length baseline (subtract any belief change under matched-length non-repeating filler). Report per-layer, per-model inflation across truth regimes and across verbatim vs paraphrased repetition and with vs without the explicit disclaimer. Compare internal-belief inflation to OUTPUT-level inflation (directly asking truth/confidence), testing whether the internal effect exists independent of prompted simulation.

Familiarity-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'familiarity' direction via difference-in-means on high-repetition vs low-repetition activations (balanced across truth-value), and separately fit the standard truth direction and an evidence-updating direction (difference between evidence-present and evidence-absent conditions). Measure cosine similarities; project out the truth/evidence directions and test whether the familiarity direction remains decodable and whether repetition inflation is explained by the familiarity component leaking into the truth-probe readout. This tests whether ITE is a distinct fluency effect vs a re-use of the evidence-updating mechanism.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Take the residual-stream shift induced by repetition, decompose into truth-direction, evidence-direction, and familiarity-direction components, and patch only the familiarity component into a single-occurrence item; measure induced change in belief readout and output endorsement. (b) Subtract the familiarity component from a highly-repeated item and measure whether belief returns toward the single-occurrence value. Confirm the familiarity component causally drives illusory inflation.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether Repetition Inflation Score predicts a repeated-falsehood hallucination mode: (i) endorsement rate of repeated false statements (real-false and synthetic-false), (ii) confident-wrong rate, and (iii) susceptibility to misinformation planted via repetition. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (repetition count alone, output entropy, single-occurrence truth-probe confidence).

Familiarity De-biasing intervention: At inference, estimate the familiarity direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer (ITI-style de-biasing), so the belief readout reflects evidence-relevant content rather than mere repetition. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected high familiarity/repetition. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Repetition Inflation Score, (ii) reduced endorsement of repeated falsehoods and improved robustness to repetition-based misinformation (adapt fact-verification / misinformation benchmarks by injecting repeated false claims), (iii) factuality/calibration (ECE) on mixed sets, (iv) PRESERVATION of legitimate evidence-based updating (must NOT be suppressed in the genuine-evidence condition) and of accuracy on true repeated statements, and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'judge truth regardless of how often a claim was repeated'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), verbatim vs paraphrased repetition, real vs synthetic facts, true vs false regime, presence of explicit disclaimer, repetition count range, distance between repetitions and query, model scale, and generalization to repetition patterns and topics not used to fit the familiarity direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent repetition inflation could reflect the probe detecting surface token-recurrence or activation-norm changes from longer/repetitive context rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with matched-length non-repeating filler controls, paraphrased-repetition (which removes verbatim token cues), norm-normalized probes, and causal patching that isolates the familiarity-direction component.

Truth probes trained on single-occurrence statements may transfer imperfectly to repeated propositions, so inflation could partly reflect probe extrapolation; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, and synthetic facts to control priors.

Familiarity and evidence-updating directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality and project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

De-biasing could over-suppress legitimate evidence-based updating or accuracy on true repeated statements, or harm fluency; we explicitly measure preservation in the genuine-evidence and true-repeated conditions plus capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Repetition inflation may correlate with but not exceed simple repetition-count or output-entropy baselines for predicting repeated-falsehood endorsement; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that ITE lives in belief geometry and the de-biasing tool, which we report honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may amplify or dampen familiarity effects); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: register_framing_belief_bias
Title: Does Style Sway Belief? Testing Whether Linguistic Register and Tone Distort LLM Internal Belief Geometry
Short Hypothesis: Holding a proposition's content and language fixed, an LLM's internal belief scalar (linear truth-direction readout) is systematically biased by the surface REGISTER/TONE in which the claim is framed: the same fact stated in a formal, authoritative, or confident register yields a higher internal belief than when stated in a casual, slangy, hedged, or emotional register. We hypothesize this register-framing bias is graded and decodable, is carried by a register/fluency axis dissociable from the truth axis, causally predicts a stylistic-credulity hallucination mode (endorsing authoritatively-styled falsehoods and dismissing casually-stated truths), and can be reduced by a lightweight inference-time intervention that removes the register component from the belief representation without harming legitimate belief updating.
Related Work: Cross-lingual factual (in)consistency is well studied (Qi et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2025 'Lost in Multilinguality'; PolyFact 2026), but that concerns changing the LANGUAGE, not the within-language stylistic framing. Item 21 (Kialy et al. 2026) shows a language-agnostic informal-register subspace exists and causally controls output formality, but does not ask whether register CONTAMINATES the truth/belief axis. Authority-hierarchy sycophancy (Joswin et al. 2026, item 22) shows attributed source AUTHORITY erases correct answers, but studies source-persona attribution, not the stylistic register of the assertion itself. Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) reads a single belief scalar and never varies stylistic framing. My prior proposals cover logical coherence, provenance, ghosts, drift, contagion, metabelief, supposition, evidence-weighting, temporal indexing, agent-binding, wishful bias (content desirability, not surface register), ignorance, and illusory-truth (repetition). None isolate surface register/tone as a separable axis that distorts internal belief. This is the first to test whether HOW something is styled (formal/authoritative/confident vs casual/slangy/hedged/emotional), independent of content and source-attribution, bends internal belief geometry, and to de-bias it via steering.
Abstract: People are more persuaded by claims delivered in a confident, formal, authoritative style than by the same claims stated casually or hesitantly. We ask whether large language models inherit this stylistic credulity inside their belief representations. Distinguishing a proposition's content from its surface REGISTER/TONE (formal vs casual/slangy, authoritative vs hedged, calm vs emotional), we test whether an LLM's internal belief scalar, read via linear truth probes, is biased by register while content and language are held fixed. We construct StyleBelief, a controlled dataset in which each factual proposition (true, false, or synthetic-in-context) is rendered in multiple registers using paraphrases that preserve propositional content and truth-value but vary style, with surface length and lexical sentiment matched and validated by human and LLM-judge register ratings. Using difference-in-means and logistic probes we read a scalar belief per rendering and define a Register Framing Bias = the belief gap between high-credibility-register and low-credibility-register versions of equally-true claims. We test four claims: (1) internal belief shifts with register even though content is fixed; (2) the shift is carried by a decodable register axis dissociable from the truth axis via project-out analyses; (3) bias magnitude causally predicts a stylistic-credulity failure mode (endorsing authoritatively-styled falsehoods, dismissing casually-stated truths); and (4) a Register De-biasing intervention that subtracts the register component reduces the bias and the failure mode while preserving legitimate updating and general capability. We validate causality with activation patching and evaluate on factuality, misinformation robustness, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build StyleBelief. Collect factual propositions in three truth regimes: real-true, real-false, and synthetic facts defined only in context (to remove parametric priors). For each proposition, generate multiple register renderings that preserve content and truth-value: (i) formal-authoritative ('It is well established that...'), (ii) casual-slangy ('yeah so basically...'), (iii) hedged-uncertain ('I guess maybe...'), (iv) confident-assertive, (v) emotional/exclamatory, and (vi) neutral baseline. Crucially, register cues describe HOW the claim is stated, not WHO states it (no source-authority personas, to distinguish from authority sycophancy). Match surface length and lexical sentiment across renderings; validate register labels with human annotation and an LLM-judge register-rating score; verify (via paraphrase QA) that renderings are truth-preserving. Include paraphrase query sets and neutral controls.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral-register single-occurrence true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At the query position read the internal belief for each StyleBelief rendering. Manipulation check: confirm probes separate clearly-true from clearly-false neutral items.

Register Framing Bias measurement: Holding truth fixed, define Register Framing Bias = mean internal belief(high-credibility register: formal/authoritative/confident) minus mean internal belief(low-credibility register: casual/hedged), computed within the true cell and within the false cell separately, controlling for the neutral baseline. Report per-layer, per-model bias for each register contrast. Test the hypothesis that belief bends toward high-credibility registers. Compare internal-belief bias to OUTPUT-level bias (directly asking the model whether each rendering is true / its confidence).

Register-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'register' direction via difference-in-means on high-credibility vs low-credibility renderings (balanced across truth-value and content). Report per-layer decoding accuracy. Test dissociation from the truth axis: cosine similarity between register and truth directions per layer; project out the truth direction and re-decode register (and vice versa); test whether register-framing bias is explained by the register component leaking into the truth-probe readout. Also disentangle register from lexical sentiment (regress bias on register rating vs sentiment score) to rule out valence confounds.

Causal validation: Activation patching. Take the activation difference between a high-credibility and a matched low-credibility rendering of the same fact, decompose into truth-direction and register-direction components, patch only the register component into a neutral rendering, and measure the induced change in belief readout and output endorsement. Conversely subtract the register component from a formal rendering and measure whether belief moves toward the content-appropriate value. Confirm register causally shifts the belief scalar independent of content.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether Register Framing Bias predicts a stylistic-credulity failure mode: (i) endorsement rate of false-but-authoritatively-styled claims, (ii) dismissal/under-endorsement of true-but-casually-stated claims, (iii) confident-wrong rate driven by style, and (iv) susceptibility to style-based misinformation (planting false claims in authoritative register). Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (register rating alone, output entropy, neutral truth-probe confidence).

Register De-biasing intervention: At inference, estimate the register direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer (ITI-style), so the belief readout reflects propositional content rather than surface style. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected strong register. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Register Framing Bias, (ii) reduced endorsement of authoritatively-styled falsehoods and reduced dismissal of casually-stated truths, and improved robustness to style-based misinformation, (iii) factuality/calibration (ECE) on mixed-register factual QA, (iv) PRESERVATION of accuracy on true items regardless of register and on neutral controls (no over-suppression), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'judge truth regardless of how a claim is phrased'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), register contrast (formal/authoritative/confident/emotional/hedged), real vs synthetic facts, true vs false regime, model scale, robustness of register/sentiment disentangling, and generalization to register styles and topics not used to fit the de-biasing direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent register bias could reflect the probe detecting lexical/sentiment features of the stylistic tokens rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with length- and sentiment-matched renderings, a sentiment-vs-register disentangling regression, paraphrase controls, and causal patching that isolates the register-direction component.

Truth probes trained on neutral-register statements may transfer imperfectly to strongly styled renderings, so bias could partly reflect probe extrapolation; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, and synthetic facts to control priors.
Register and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality and project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.
Ensuring renderings are truly truth- and content-preserving across registers is nontrivial; we use human verification and paraphrase-QA checks and report label-noise sensitivity.

De-biasing could over-suppress legitimate belief in true-formal claims or harm fluency; we explicitly measure preservation on true items across registers and neutral controls plus capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Register bias may correlate with but not exceed simple register-rating or output-entropy baselines for predicting stylistic-credulity failures; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that surface register distorts belief geometry and the de-biasing tool, which we report honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may amplify preference for confident/formal style); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: self_commitment_belief_anchoring
Title: Believing Your Own Words: Does an LLM's Internal Belief Inflate After It Asserts a Proposition Itself?
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's internal belief in a proposition is systematically inflated by the model having GENERATED that proposition itself, beyond any effect of the same text merely appearing in context. We hypothesize a 'self-commitment' belief-anchoring effect: once the model has produced an assertion (especially a guess or an early, poorly-grounded claim), its internal belief scalar (linear truth-direction readout) rises and becomes resistant to revision, that this self-authored inflation is dissociable from generic context/repetition effects, causally predicts a hallucination-snowballing / stubbornness failure mode, and can be reduced by a lightweight inference-time intervention that discounts the self-generated belief component.
Related Work: Output-level self-consistency work (Nokhiz et al. 2026) shows LLMs contradict their own prior outputs across reframings, and hallucination-snowballing work (Zhang et al. 2023) shows models double down on early mistakes at the OUTPUT/behavioral level. Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) reads a single internal belief but never studies the source of the assertion. My prior proposals cover externally-supplied evidence, in-context repetition (illusory truth), register, desirability, provenance (parametric vs contextual), belief ghosts after revision, and premature commitment during READING of an input. Crucially, none isolate the effect of the model's OWN generation on its internal belief: whether producing a token stream that asserts P raises the internal belief in P more than the identical text being externally provided, creating a self-reinforcing commitment loop. This 'self-authorship' factor — who produced the assertion (the model vs the context) as a distinct cause of belief inflation — is a new belief-geometry lens directly relevant to hallucination snowballing and stubborn refusal to self-correct, distinct from all prior work which treats belief as source-of-authorship-agnostic.
Abstract: People believe their own stated opinions more strongly after voicing them — a commitment/consistency effect. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous distortion inside their belief representations: does an LLM's internal belief in a proposition rise simply because the model produced that proposition itself? We distinguish the CONTENT of an assertion from its AUTHORSHIP (self-generated vs externally provided) and test whether authorship biases the internal belief scalar read via linear truth probes. We construct SelfCommit, a controlled dataset of factual and synthetic-in-context propositions presented under matched conditions: (a) the model is prompted to guess/assert P and thereby generates it, versus (b) an identical assertion of P is supplied by the context (not authored by the model), versus (c) a neutral baseline. Holding the surface text at the query point fixed, we read the internal belief in P and define a Self-Commitment Inflation Score = belief(self-generated) minus belief(externally-provided). We test four claims: (1) self-generated assertions inflate internal belief beyond the externally-provided condition; (2) the inflation grows with how tentative/unfounded the original assertion was (guesses inflate more than knowledge) and is dissociable from generic repetition/context effects; (3) inflation magnitude causally predicts a snowballing/stubbornness failure mode where the model defends self-authored falsehoods and resists correction; and (4) a lightweight inference-time intervention that discounts the self-authored belief component reduces snowballing while preserving legitimate self-consistency and general capability. We validate causality with activation patching and evaluate on self-correction, factuality, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build SelfCommit. Items are propositions in three truth regimes: real-true, real-false, and synthetic facts defined only in context (to remove parametric priors). For each item create matched conditions differing only in AUTHORSHIP of a prior assertion of P: (a) SELF-GENERATED — the model is first prompted to answer/guess a question whose (elicited) answer is the assertion 'P', so P appears in the transcript as the model's own generation; (b) EXTERNALLY-PROVIDED — the identical assertion 'P' is inserted into the context attributed to the user/document, not generated by the model; (c) NEUTRAL baseline — P appears once, unasserted. Additionally vary the GROUNDING of the original elicitation: forced guess on an unknown item vs a well-known item (to test whether unfounded guesses inflate more). Match the surface text at the belief-readout query point across conditions (same tokens present); control transcript length. Include paraphrase query sets and human-verified samples.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral single-occurrence true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At a matched query position after the prior assertion, read internal belief in P under each authorship condition. Manipulation check: confirm probes separate clearly-true from clearly-false neutral items, and that in the self-generated condition the model actually produced P.

Self-Commitment Inflation Score: Define Inflation = belief(SELF-GENERATED) minus belief(EXTERNALLY-PROVIDED), with both compared to NEUTRAL to remove generic single-mention effects. Report per-layer, per-model inflation across truth regimes and across guess-vs-known grounding. Test the hypotheses that (i) self-authorship inflates belief beyond identical external text, and (ii) unfounded guesses inflate more than well-grounded assertions. Compare internal inflation to OUTPUT-level inflation (verbalized confidence / willingness to affirm P) to show the effect is not merely surface consistency phrasing.

Dissociation from repetition/context: Include a control where the externally-provided assertion is REPEATED to match any token-count difference introduced by the generation turn, isolating authorship from mere repetition/length. Fit a 'self-authorship' difference direction (self-generated minus externally-provided activations, balanced across truth-value) and test whether it is decodable and dissociable from the truth direction (cosine similarity, project-out re-decoding), and whether inflation is explained by this component leaking into the truth-probe readout.

Causal validation: Activation patching. Take the residual-stream difference between the self-generated and externally-provided conditions, decompose into truth-direction and self-authorship-direction components, and patch only the self-authorship component into the externally-provided (or neutral) condition; measure induced change in belief readout and in the model's willingness to defend P. Conversely subtract the self-authorship component from the self-generated condition and measure whether belief and defensiveness return toward baseline. Confirm self-authorship causally inflates the belief scalar.

Predictive validity (snowballing/stubbornness): At the item level, test whether Self-Commitment Inflation predicts (i) defense of self-authored falsehoods when challenged ('Are you sure? I think that's wrong'), (ii) failure to self-correct a self-generated error versus an externally-provided error (differential correction rate), and (iii) hallucination snowballing in continued generation seeded by a self-authored false claim. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (grounding indicator, output entropy, neutral truth-probe confidence).

Self-Commitment De-biasing intervention: At inference, estimate the self-authorship direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer (ITI-style) when the model is asked to re-evaluate or continue after having asserted P, so the belief readout reflects content/evidence rather than mere self-authorship. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected recent self-generation of the queried claim. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Self-Commitment Inflation, (ii) improved self-correction rate on self-authored errors and reduced defense of self-authored falsehoods, (iii) reduced hallucination snowballing, (iv) factuality/calibration (ECE), (v) PRESERVATION of legitimate self-consistency (must not force the model to abandon correct self-authored claims) and capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'critically re-evaluate your own prior statements as if written by someone else', and a fresh-context re-ask baseline (re-querying P without the prior transcript).

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), truth regime, guess-vs-known grounding, distance between the self-assertion and the readout, single vs repeated self-assertions (does repeating one's own claim compound inflation), model scale, and generalization to naturally occurring multi-turn transcripts not used to fit the de-biasing direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent self-commitment inflation could be confounded with subtle surface differences between the self-generated and externally-provided transcripts (turn structure, speaker tags); we match query-point tokens, add repetition/length controls, use paraphrase controls, and rely on causal patching that isolates the self-authorship component to rule out surface artifacts.

Truth probes trained on neutral single-occurrence statements may transfer imperfectly to multi-turn transcripts, so inflation could partly reflect probe extrapolation; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks, and synthetic facts to control priors.
Self-authorship and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; orthogonality and project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

Ensuring the self-generated and externally-provided conditions assert exactly the same proposition (and only differ in authorship) is nontrivial; we constrain elicitation formats and human-verify a sample, reporting label-noise sensitivity.

The de-biasing intervention could over-suppress correct self-authored beliefs (harming legitimate self-consistency) or hurt fluency; we explicitly measure preservation of correct self-authored claims and capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Inflation may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (grounding indicator, output entropy) for snowballing; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that self-authorship distorts belief geometry and the de-biasing tool, reported honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may amplify consistency/commitment); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: conjunction_belief_monotonicity
Title: More Is Less: Do LLM Internal Beliefs Obey the Extension Rule for Conjunctions and Disjunctions?
Short Hypothesis: A rational belief system must satisfy the extension (monotonicity) rule: the internal belief in a conjunction P∧Q cannot exceed the belief in either conjunct (belief(P∧Q) ≤ min(belief(P), belief(Q))), and the belief in a disjunction P∨Q cannot fall below either disjunct (belief(P∨Q) ≥ max(belief(P), belief(Q))). We hypothesize that LLM INTERNAL belief representations (linear truth-direction readouts) systematically VIOLATE this rule — a representational conjunction fallacy in which adding a plausible/representative conjunct raises the internal belief above its constituents — that these violations are graded and driven by a decodable representativeness/plausibility signal, causally predict output-level conjunction-fallacy errors, and can be reduced by a lightweight inference-time intervention that enforces monotone composition along the truth direction.
Related Work: Zhu & Griffiths (2024, 'Incoherent Probability Judgments in LLMs') and Zhu (2024) show LLMs produce OUTPUT-level incoherent probability judgments with human-like conjunction-fallacy patterns; Jiang et al. (2024, 'A Peek into Token Bias') use conjunction-fallacy items to argue LLMs rely on token bias rather than reasoning; Li & Rui (2024) find dual (Bayesian vs representativeness) modes in posterior judgments — all at the OUTPUT/prompt level. Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) reads a single first-order belief scalar for one proposition and never studies COMPOSITIONAL belief structure. My prior proposals cover logical coherence over implication/negation networks, provenance, ghosts, drift, associative contagion, metabelief, supposition, Bayesian evidence-weighting, temporal indexing, agent-binding, wishful bias, ignorance, illusory truth, register, and self-commitment — none test whether the internal belief in a compound proposition is properly BOUNDED by its constituents (the extension/set-inclusion rule that mechanistically underlies the conjunction fallacy). This is the first to test the extension rule inside belief geometry, isolate a representativeness signal that violates it, tie internal violations causally to output conjunction fallacies, and enforce monotone composition via steering.
Abstract: A basic law of any coherent belief system is the extension rule: a conjunction cannot be more probable than its least probable conjunct, and a disjunction cannot be less probable than its most probable disjunct. Humans famously violate this in the conjunction fallacy (Linda is judged more likely to be a 'bank teller and feminist' than a 'bank teller'), and recent work shows LLMs reproduce such fallacies in their OUTPUTS. We ask whether this incoherence lives inside the model's belief representations. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar internal belief along the linear truth direction, we test whether an LLM's belief in compound propositions is properly bounded by its beliefs in the constituents. We build CompoundBelief, a controlled dataset pairing atomic propositions P and Q with their conjunctions and disjunctions, spanning true/false constituents and, critically, a representativeness axis where Q is highly plausible/typical given a persona or context (the fallacy-inducing setting) versus neutral. We read internal beliefs for P, Q, P∧Q, and P∨Q and define a Conjunction Violation Score (how much belief(P∧Q) exceeds min(belief(P), belief(Q))) and a dual Disjunction Violation Score. We test four claims: (1) internal beliefs violate the extension rule, especially under high representativeness; (2) the violation is carried by a decodable representativeness/plausibility direction dissociable from the truth direction; (3) internal violation magnitude causally predicts output-level conjunction-fallacy choices; and (4) a Monotone Composition intervention that projects the compound belief onto the extension-consistent region reduces violations and fallacy rates while preserving legitimate composition and general capability. We validate causality with activation patching and evaluate on reasoning coherence, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build CompoundBelief. Assemble atomic propositions P and Q with known/controllable truth-values (real facts plus synthetic-in-context facts to remove parametric priors). For each pair form the conjunction 'P and Q' and disjunction 'P or Q'. Cross two factors: (i) constituent truth-values {TT, TF, FT, FF}; (ii) a REPRESENTATIVENESS axis — Linda-style items where a persona/context makes one conjunct highly typical/plausible (fallacy-inducing) versus a neutral condition where conjuncts are unrelated and matched in base plausibility. Match surface length and lexical content across the atomic vs compound framings (e.g., read belief in 'P' vs 'P and Q' with the same P tokens present). Include paraphrase sets, human-verified representativeness ratings, and neutral controls.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of simple atomic true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. Read internal belief for P, Q, P∧Q, and P∨Q at a matched query position. Manipulation check: confirm probes separate clearly-true from clearly-false atomic items and that belief(P), belief(Q) behave sensibly.

Extension-rule violation measurement: Define Conjunction Violation Score = max(0, belief(P∧Q) - min(belief(P), belief(Q))) and Disjunction Violation Score = max(0, max(belief(P), belief(Q)) - belief(P∨Q)). Report per-layer, per-model violation across the truth-value cells and across the representativeness axis. Test the hypotheses that (i) violations are nonzero, and (ii) conjunction violations are larger when the added conjunct is highly representative/plausible (the fallacy signature). Compare internal violations to OUTPUT-level violations (directly asking the model to rate/compare probabilities of P vs P∧Q), testing whether the incoherence exists internally, not just in prompted judgments.

Representativeness-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'representativeness/plausibility' direction via difference-in-means on high- vs low-representativeness conjuncts (balanced across truth-value). Report decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode representativeness (and vice versa). Test whether the conjunction violation is explained by the representativeness component leaking into the compound-belief readout — the mechanistic substrate of the fallacy.

Causal validation: Activation patching.
