(a) Take the activation difference between P∧Q under high- vs low-representativeness conditions, decompose into truth-direction and representativeness-direction components, and patch only the representativeness component into a neutral conjunction; measure the induced change in the compound belief readout and in output fallacy choices. (b) Subtract the representativeness component from a high-representativeness conjunction and measure whether belief returns below min(belief(P), belief(Q)). Confirm the representativeness signal causally drives extension-rule violation.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether the internal Conjunction Violation Score predicts (i) output-level conjunction-fallacy choices (preferring P∧Q over P in a forced comparison), (ii) confidence miscalibration on compound propositions, and (iii) inconsistency across paraphrases of the compound. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (representativeness rating alone, output entropy, atomic truth-probe confidence).

Monotone Composition intervention: At inference, given the readouts for P, Q, and the compound, project the compound belief onto the extension-consistent region — for conjunctions cap belief(P∧Q) at min(belief(P), belief(Q)) by subtracting the excess along the truth direction; for disjunctions floor belief(P∨Q) at max(belief(P), belief(Q)). Implement as an ITI-style additive shift along the truth direction at a chosen layer, using probe readouts to compute the required correction. Provide a deployment variant that dampens the representativeness component for detected compound queries. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Conjunction/Disjunction Violation Scores, (ii) reduced output-level conjunction-fallacy rate on Linda-style and synthetic compound benchmarks, (iii) improved calibration (ECE) of compound-proposition confidence, (iv) PRESERVATION of legitimate composition (correct beliefs when a conjunction genuinely is less certain, and correct disjunction behavior) and accuracy on atomic controls (no over-suppression), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'remember a conjunction is never more probable than its parts', and chain-of-thought prompting.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), truth-value cell, representativeness level, conjunction vs disjunction, number of conjuncts (2 vs 3, testing whether violations compound), real vs synthetic facts, model scale, and generalization to compound structures and topics not used to fit the intervention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent extension-rule violations could reflect the probe detecting surface/plausibility features of the added conjunct rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with surface-form and length matching between atomic and compound framings, representativeness-vs-sentiment disentangling, paraphrase controls, and causal patching that isolates the representativeness-direction component.

Truth probes trained on atomic statements may transfer imperfectly to compound propositions ('P and Q'), so violation measurements could partly reflect probe extrapolation; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, and synthetic facts to control priors, and validate that atomic readouts within a compound are recoverable.
Reading a single comparable belief scalar for P, Q, and their compound at matched positions is nontrivial and position-sensitive; include position and layer robustness checks and report sensitivity.

The Monotone Composition intervention requires reliable atomic readouts at inference to compute the cap/floor; noisy readouts may make the projection ill-posed, and the deployment variant may be weaker — we characterize this gap honestly.

Enforcing monotone composition could over-suppress and distort legitimate compound beliefs or harm fluency; we explicitly measure preservation of correct composition and capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Internal violation may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (representativeness rating, output entropy) for output fallacy choices; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that the conjunction fallacy is embedded in belief geometry and the composition tool, reported honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may amplify representativeness heuristics); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: gradability_belief_thresholding
Title: How True Is 'Tall'? Testing Whether LLM Internal Beliefs Encode Graded Truth or Binary Thresholding for Vague Propositions
Short Hypothesis: For a gradable/vague proposition whose truth genuinely varies with a continuous quantity (e.g., 'A 178cm person is tall', 'A city with 90k people is large'), a rational belief should be graded: the internal belief scalar should increase smoothly with the underlying quantity, forming a sigmoid-like membership curve with a soft boundary. We hypothesize that LLM internal belief representations (linear truth-direction readouts) instead exhibit premature BINARY THRESHOLDING: the belief collapses into an almost step-function around an internally-encoded cutoff, discarding the graded middle, that this cutoff and its sharpness are decodable and manipulable, that over-sharp thresholding causally predicts brittle, context-insensitive answers to borderline cases, and that a lightweight inference-time intervention that softens the threshold along the truth direction restores graded, better-calibrated beliefs.
Related Work: Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) fits a single linear true-vs-false axis and reads a scalar belief, but exclusively studies CATEGORICALLY true or false factual statements; the graded/vague regime (predicates like 'tall', 'expensive', 'old', 'large', 'nearby') is never examined. Vagueness and gradable adjectives are central to formal semantics (fuzzy/degree semantics, Kennedy 2007) and there is behavioral NLP work on LLMs' handling of scalar adjectives and comparatives, but at the OUTPUT/lexical level, not in belief geometry. My prior belief proposals (coherence, provenance, ghosts, drift, contagion, metabelief, supposition, evidence-weighting, temporal, agent-binding, wishful bias, ignorance, illusory truth, register, self-commitment, conjunction fallacy) all treat propositions as having a definite truth-value; none ask whether the internal belief scalar is a genuinely GRADED function of an underlying continuous quantity or a prematurely binarized step. This is a new lens: testing whether belief geometry preserves degrees of truth or destroys them via internal thresholding, locating the cutoff, and softening it.
Abstract: Many everyday propositions are not simply true or false but true to a degree: whether someone is 'tall', a city is 'large', or an item is 'expensive' depends on a continuous underlying quantity and admits genuinely borderline cases. A belief system worthy of the name should represent this gradedness. We ask whether large language models do so inside their belief representations, or whether they prematurely collapse graded truth into a binary threshold. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar internal belief along the linear truth direction, we test how the belief in a gradable proposition varies as we sweep the underlying quantity. We construct GradeBelief, a controlled dataset of gradable-predicate statements ('An X-cm person is tall', 'A city with N people is large') where the continuous parameter is systematically varied across, above, and below the natural cutoff, with matched non-gradable controls. We fit membership curves (belief vs quantity) per proposition, extracting an internal Cutoff and a Sharpness (slope at the boundary). We test four claims: (1) internal belief curves are over-sharp step-functions rather than smooth graded memberships, discarding the borderline middle; (2) the cutoff and sharpness are decodable and can be causally shifted via activation patching along the truth direction; (3) over-sharp thresholding predicts brittle, context-insensitive answers on borderline items and poor calibration; and (4) a lightweight Threshold-Softening intervention along the truth direction restores graded, better-calibrated beliefs without harming clearly-true/false judgments. We evaluate on borderline-case QA, calibration, comparative-consistency, and capability retention. Our results reveal whether LLM beliefs preserve or destroy degrees of truth, and offer a cheap tool to make vague-predicate reasoning more graceful.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build GradeBelief. For each of several gradable predicates across domains (height 'tall', population 'large city', price 'expensive', age 'old', distance 'nearby', temperature 'hot'), construct statement templates parameterized by a continuous quantity, e.g., 'A person who is X cm tall is tall', 'A city with N inhabitants is a large city'. Sample the quantity densely across a range spanning clearly-below, borderline, and clearly-above the conventional cutoff (e.g., height 140-210 cm in 2 cm steps). Include: (a) matched NON-GRADABLE controls (crisp propositions with the same surface template but a definite truth-value, e.g., precise numerical facts), (b) CONTEXT-SHIFTED variants that should move the cutoff (e.g., 'For a professional basketball player, a 178 cm person is tall' vs 'For a jockey, ...'), and (c) paraphrase sets. Collect human membership ratings (fraction of annotators judging the statement true at each quantity) to obtain a normative graded reference curve per predicate/context.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of crisp true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At the query token, read the internal belief for each gradable statement across the swept quantity. Manipulation check: confirm probes separate clearly-true from clearly-false crisp control items.

Membership-curve and thresholding analysis: For each predicate/context, plot internal belief vs the underlying quantity and fit a logistic membership curve, extracting an internal Cutoff (50% point) and Sharpness (max slope). Define an Over-Sharpness Score = ratio of model Sharpness to the human normative-curve Sharpness (>>1 indicates premature binarization; ~1 indicates human-like gradedness). Report per-layer, per-model over-sharpness and cutoff accuracy (does the internal cutoff match the human/normative cutoff?). Compare across predicates and domains. Also compare internal curves to OUTPUT-level curves (directly asking the model to rate truth/probability at each quantity) to test whether gradedness is destroyed internally, at the output, or both.

Context-sensitivity test: Using the context-shifted variants, test whether the internal Cutoff moves in the normatively-correct direction (e.g., higher cutoff for 'tall' among basketball players). Quantify a Context-Adaptation Index = shift in internal cutoff per context vs the human-normative shift. Test the hypothesis that over-sharp thresholds are also under-adaptive to context.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Move activations along the truth direction at a chosen layer and measure whether the membership curve shifts (cutoff moves) and/or softens, confirming the cutoff/sharpness are causal properties of the truth-direction geometry. (b) Patch the representation of a clearly-above item's belief-shift into a borderline item and measure the induced belief change. Confirm the internal threshold causally governs borderline answers.

Predictive validity: At the item level (focusing on borderline quantities near the cutoff), test whether local Over-Sharpness predicts (i) brittle flips in the output yes/no answer under tiny quantity perturbations, (ii) inconsistency across paraphrases and context framings, and (iii) poor calibration (over-confident yes/no on genuinely borderline cases). Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (output entropy, distance-from-cutoff, crisp truth-probe confidence).

Threshold-Softening intervention: At inference, reduce the effective sharpness of the membership curve by scaling down the projection onto the truth direction near the borderline region (an ITI-style shrinkage toward the neutral 0.5 belief that grows with proximity to the estimated cutoff), so that borderline items receive intermediate rather than saturated beliefs. Provide a deployment variant that gates on detected gradable predicates and estimates proximity to the cutoff from the belief scalar itself. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Over-Sharpness / better match to normative membership curves, (ii) reduced brittleness (fewer answer flips under small perturbations) and improved paraphrase/context consistency on borderline QA, (iii) improved calibration (ECE) where the target is the human graded membership probability, (iv) improved comparative consistency (e.g., if 178 cm is judged tall then 185 cm must be too — monotonicity of the induced answers), (v) PRESERVATION of correct answers on clearly-true/clearly-false items and on crisp non-gradable controls (no over-hedging), and (vi) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'treat borderline cases as partially true and calibrate your confidence to how borderline they are'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), predicate/domain, quantity range and step size, context-shift condition, model scale, monotonicity check of induced answers, and generalization to gradable predicates and domains not used to fit the intervention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Crisp truth probes trained on categorical statements may not linearly capture graded truth, so an apparent step-function could partly reflect probe extrapolation rather than genuine internal binarization; mitigate with multiple probe types, dense sweeps that reveal curve shape, and causal patching that demonstrates a manipulable cutoff.

The internal belief scalar might track the numeric quantity token (surface value) rather than the predicate's truth; we include non-gradable controls with the same numeric surface form and context-shift conditions to distinguish genuine gradable-truth representation from numeric-token detection.

Defining a normative graded reference curve relies on human membership ratings that are themselves variable and context-dependent; we collect multiple annotators, use inter-annotator agreement, and anchor quantitative claims on predicates with high agreement, treating others qualitatively.
Reading a comparable belief scalar across the quantity sweep is position/token sensitive; we include position and layer robustness checks and report sensitivity of the fitted cutoff/sharpness.

Threshold-Softening could over-hedge (making clearly-true/false items uncertain) or harm fluency; we explicitly measure preservation on clear and crisp-control items plus capability retention to characterize the tradeoff, and the intervention is gated to borderline regions.

Over-sharpness may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (distance-from-cutoff, output entropy) for borderline brittleness; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that belief geometry binarizes graded truth and the softening tool, which we report honestly.

A plausible alternative outcome is that models are UNDER-sharp or well-calibrated for some predicates; such heterogeneity across predicates/domains is itself an informative result, and we test multiple predicates and models rather than assuming universal over-sharpness.

Name: comparative_belief_distance_effect
Title: The Symbolic Distance Effect in LLM Beliefs: Do Internal Beliefs About Comparisons Scale With the Numeric Gap?
Short Hypothesis: For a quantitative comparative proposition (e.g., 'Mount Everest is taller than K2', 'Elephants are heavier than tigers'), a rational belief should scale with the underlying magnitude gap: internal belief should be near-certain when the two quantities differ greatly and near-chance when they are close (a symbolic distance effect). We hypothesize that LLM internal belief representations (linear truth-direction readouts) either (a) fail to encode this gap-dependence, collapsing comparisons to binary near-certain beliefs regardless of gap, or (b) encode a distorted distance effect that is over-compressed relative to the true gap. We further hypothesize that whichever pattern holds, the internal belief for comparisons systematically violates transitivity (belief(A>B) and belief(B>C) high but belief(A>C) not correspondingly high), that gap-mismatch and transitivity violations causally predict comparison errors and near-tie brittleness, and that a lightweight inference-time intervention that re-scales the comparative belief along the truth direction to be gap-monotone and transitivity-consistent improves comparative reasoning and calibration.
Related Work: Levy & Geva (2024) show LLMs represent numbers digit-wise in base 10 rather than as continuous magnitudes, and Takagi et al. (2025) show numerical attributes occupy shared latent subspaces that get amplified/perturbed — but both study number ENCODING, not the BELIEF assigned to comparative propositions. Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) reads a single first-order belief scalar for categorical facts and never examines quantitative comparisons or magnitude-graded confidence. The symbolic distance effect (Moyer & Landauer 1967) is a hallmark of human numerical cognition: comparisons are faster/more confident when quantities differ more. No prior work asks whether LLM internal BELIEF geometry exhibits (or distorts) this distance effect, whether comparative beliefs respect transitivity in representation space, whether gap-mismatch causally predicts errors, or whether the comparative belief can be re-scaled to be gap-monotone. This is distinct from my prior proposals — gradability studied vague predicates against a single threshold, and conjunction studied compositional bounds; neither addresses magnitude-graded confidence in binary comparisons or transitivity of comparative beliefs, which are central to numerical/relational reasoning.
Abstract: Humans are more confident that 100 is greater than 3 than that 65 is greater than 63 — the symbolic distance effect, a signature of genuine magnitude representation. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous, and rational, distance effect inside their belief representations when judging quantitative comparisons. A well-behaved belief in 'A is greater than B' should scale with the true magnitude gap: near-certain for large gaps, near-chance for near-ties. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar internal belief along the linear truth direction, we test how belief in comparative propositions varies with the underlying numeric gap. We construct CompareBelief, a controlled dataset of comparative statements about entities with known real-valued attributes (mountain heights, animal weights, city populations, planet diameters), plus synthetic pairs with fully controlled quantities, in which we systematically sweep the magnitude gap across, and down to, near-ties. We fit belief-vs-gap curves and extract a Distance-Sensitivity index (how much belief tracks the true gap) and a Gap-Compression score (how much the curve saturates prematurely). We also test whether comparative beliefs respect transitivity across triples (A>B, B>C, A>C). We test four claims: (1) internal comparative beliefs are either gap-insensitive (prematurely binary) or gap-compressed relative to the true distance effect; (2) comparative beliefs violate transitivity in representation space; (3) gap-mismatch and transitivity violations causally predict comparison errors and near-tie brittleness; and (4) a lightweight Distance-Calibration intervention that re-scales comparative belief along the truth direction to be gap-monotone and transitivity-consistent improves accuracy and calibration on near-ties without harming easy comparisons. We validate causality with activation patching and evaluate on comparison QA, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build CompareBelief. Collect entities with reliable real-valued attributes across domains (mountain heights, animal weights, city populations, planet diameters, country areas, element atomic masses). For every domain, form comparative propositions 'A is {taller/heavier/larger/...} than B' with known ground-truth answer, and crucially compute the true magnitude gap (absolute and relative). Sample pairs to densely cover the gap axis from very large gaps down to near-ties. Add SYNTHETIC pairs where entities are defined only in context with fully-specified quantities (e.g., 'Widget X weighs 63 kg; Widget Y weighs 65 kg') to remove parametric priors and give exact control over the gap. Include true and false directional variants (A>B vs B>A), transitivity TRIPLES (A>B, B>C, A>C) with controlled gaps, paraphrase sets, and matched surface forms so the probe cannot exploit lexical cues.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of simple categorical true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At the query token read the internal belief for each comparative proposition. Manipulation check: confirm probes separate clearly-true from clearly-false categorical control items and that belief for large-gap comparisons is high.

Distance-effect measurement: For each domain, plot internal belief vs the true (log) magnitude gap and fit a monotone curve. Define a Distance-Sensitivity index = slope/correlation of belief with the true gap, and a Gap-Compression score = degree to which the curve saturates near 1 even for small gaps (or, conversely, fails to reach certainty for large gaps). Test the two competing hypotheses: (a) gap-insensitive/prematurely-binary (belief ~ constant high regardless of gap), or (b) present-but-compressed distance effect. Report per-layer, per-model results across domains and for real vs synthetic pairs. Compare internal belief curves to OUTPUT-level curves (directly asking the model to compare / rate its confidence) to locate where the distance effect is preserved or lost. Compare against the human-style normative expectation that confidence rises smoothly with the gap.

Transitivity analysis: On triples with controlled gaps, measure whether internal beliefs are transitively consistent: if belief(A>B) and belief(B>C) are both high, is belief(A>C) at least as high as implied? Define a Transitivity Violation Score = fraction of triples where the composed belief falls below the min of the premises (or contradicts the ground-truth ordering). Report how violations scale with the intermediate gaps and with model scale.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Move activations along the truth direction at a chosen layer for a near-tie comparison and measure whether the belief curve and output answer shift, confirming the comparative belief is causally read from the truth-direction geometry. (b) Patch the belief-shift of a large-gap (easy) comparison into a near-tie item and measure the induced belief/output change. (c) In synthetic pairs, patch the representation corresponding to one entity's quantity and verify the comparative belief moves in the gap-consistent direction, linking magnitude encoding to comparative belief.

Predictive validity: At the item level (focusing on small-gap/near-tie comparisons), test whether low Distance-Sensitivity / high Gap-Compression / Transitivity Violation predicts (i) comparison errors (wrong ordering), (ii) near-tie brittleness (answer flips under tiny quantity perturbations or paraphrase), and (iii) overconfident-wrong calibration on near-ties. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (true gap alone, output entropy, categorical truth-probe confidence).

Distance-Calibration intervention: At inference, re-scale the comparative belief along the truth direction to be gap-monotone: shrink saturated beliefs toward the neutral 0.5 for detected near-ties (proximity estimated from the belief scalar or from decoded quantities in the synthetic setting) and, for transitivity triples, project the composed belief onto the transitivity-consistent region (ITI-style additive shift computed from the premise readouts). Provide a deployment variant that gates on detected comparative queries. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) improved match of belief-vs-gap curves to the normative monotone distance effect and reduced Gap-Compression, (ii) reduced near-tie brittleness (fewer answer flips under small perturbations) and improved paraphrase consistency, (iii) improved calibration (ECE) on comparison QA, especially near-ties, (iv) reduced Transitivity Violation Score, (v) PRESERVATION of accuracy on large-gap easy comparisons and on categorical controls (no over-hedging), and (vi) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'be less confident when the two quantities are close and ensure your comparisons are transitively consistent', and chain-of-thought prompting.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), domain, absolute vs relative gap parameterization, real vs synthetic pairs, directional variants (A>B vs B>A), triple structure and intermediate-gap size, model scale, and generalization to comparison types and domains not used to fit the intervention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Categorical truth probes may transfer imperfectly to comparative propositions, so an apparent gap-insensitivity could partly reflect probe extrapolation rather than genuine belief geometry; mitigate with multiple probe types, dense gap sweeps that reveal curve shape, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false comparisons, and causal patching demonstrating a manipulable, gap-consistent belief.

The internal belief scalar might track surface features (which entity is famously larger, lexical frequency) rather than the numeric gap; we include synthetic pairs with fully-controlled quantities and matched surface forms, and directional variants, to isolate genuine magnitude-graded belief from priors/lexical cues.

Because LLMs encode numbers digit-wise (Levy & Geva 2024), the model's 'true gap' internally may itself be distorted; we separately probe the encoded quantities in synthetic items and analyze whether comparative-belief distortion stems from magnitude-encoding error vs a belief-thresholding effect, treating this decomposition as a core finding.

Defining the normative distance-effect curve requires assumptions about how confidence should scale with the gap; we anchor quantitative claims on synthetic pairs with exact gaps and treat real-world domains more qualitatively, and report sensitivity to absolute vs relative gap parameterization.

Reading a comparable belief scalar across the gap sweep is position/token sensitive; we include position and layer robustness checks and report sensitivity of the fitted distance-sensitivity and compression scores.

Distance-Calibration could over-hedge (making easy comparisons uncertain) or harm fluency; we explicitly measure preservation on large-gap and categorical-control items plus capability retention, and gate the intervention to near-tie regions.

Distortion metrics may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (true gap, output entropy) for near-tie brittleness; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that the symbolic distance effect is (or is not) faithfully represented in belief geometry and that comparative beliefs violate transitivity, plus the calibration tool, which we report honestly.
Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training; we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: query_polarity_belief_instability
Title: Ask It Another Way: Does an LLM's Internal Belief Flip Inconsistently Under Logically-Equivalent Query Framings?
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's internal belief in a fixed proposition P should be invariant to how the query about P is FRAMED: asking 'Is P true?', 'Is P false?', 'Is it the case that not-P?', or 'Do you agree that P?' are logically interchangeable and must yield mutually consistent internal beliefs. We hypothesize LLM internal belief representations (linear truth-direction readouts) are systematically NON-INVARIANT to query polarity and framing: a proposition's decoded belief shifts (often toward affirming whatever the query foregrounds), producing an internal acquiescence/negation-framing bias that is graded and decodable, causally predicts inconsistent yes/no answers across framings, and can be reduced by a lightweight inference-time intervention that removes the query-framing component from the belief representation.
Related Work: Truth-direction probing shows a proposition's truth is linearly decodable (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023). Bao et al. (2025) show probes generalize across logical transformations (including negation) and QA, and Schouten et al. (2024) show truth directions are context-sensitive to preceding sentences. Crucially, both study how the SURROUNDING CONTENT (premises, transformations applied to the statement itself) affects belief; neither isolates the effect of the QUERY FRAMING/POLARITY used to interrogate a fixed proposition. Behavioral work documents acquiescence and framing effects at the OUTPUT level (e.g., models agree more when a claim is phrased as 'Isn't it true that...'), but not inside belief geometry. My prior proposals manipulate evidence, style, desirability, repetition, temporal index, agent, compounds, or the proposition's own logical form; none test whether logically-equivalent reformulations of the interrogating query destabilize the internal belief while proposition content is held fixed. This is a new lens: belief invariance to question framing, the internal analogue of measurement invariance, distinct from content-driven context sensitivity.
Abstract: A belief worthy of the name should not depend on how you ask about it: whether we ask 'Is Paris the capital of France?', 'Is it false that Paris is the capital of France?', or 'You'd agree Paris is the capital of France, wouldn't you?', the underlying belief is the same. We ask whether large language models honor this invariance inside their belief representations. Holding a proposition's content fixed, we vary only the framing and polarity of the query used to interrogate it, and read the internal belief via linear truth probes. We construct FrameBelief, a controlled dataset of true, false, and synthetic-in-context propositions, each interrogated under a battery of logically-equivalent query framings: neutral ('Is P true?'), negated ('Is P false?' / 'Is it the case that not-P?'), leading/acquiescent ('Isn't it true that P?', 'You agree that P, right?'), and disagreement-inviting ('Surely P is false?'). Because the framings are logically interchangeable, a coherent model's decoded belief (after mapping negated framings back to belief-in-P) must be consistent across them. We define a Framing Instability Score measuring the spread of decoded belief-in-P across framings, and test four claims: (1) internal beliefs are non-invariant to query framing, shifting toward whatever polarity the query foregrounds; (2) the shift is carried by a decodable query-framing direction dissociable from the truth direction; (3) instability magnitude causally predicts inconsistent yes/no answers and acquiescence errors across framings; and (4) a lightweight Framing-Invariance intervention that subtracts the query-framing component restores consistent beliefs and reduces answer flips without harming clearly-true/false judgments. We validate causality with activation patching and evaluate on consistency, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build FrameBelief. Assemble propositions P in three truth regimes: real-true, real-false, and synthetic facts defined only in context (to remove parametric priors). For each P, generate a battery of logically-equivalent query framings that interrogate the SAME proposition without adding evidence: (a) NEUTRAL positive ('Is it true that P?'), (b) NEGATED ('Is it false that P?', 'Is it the case that not-P?'), (c) LEADING/ACQUIESCENT toward P ('Isn't it true that P?', 'You'd agree that P, correct?'), (d) LEADING toward not-P ('Surely P is false?', 'Isn't it the case that not-P?'), and (e) DECLARATIVE control (bare statement of P, no question). Ensure framings differ only in interrogative packaging, not in propositional content; match surface length; validate logical equivalence and human-verify a sample. Include paraphrase sets and neutral controls.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral declarative true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At a matched query position (e.g., final token of the interrogative), read the decoded belief. For negated framings, map the readout back to belief-in-P (belief-in-P = 1 - belief-in-not-P) so all framings are on a common scale. Manipulation check: confirm probes separate clearly-true from clearly-false declarative control items.

Framing Instability measurement: For each proposition, compute the spread of the framing-normalized belief-in-P across the framing battery. Define Framing Instability Score = standard deviation (and max-min range) of belief-in-P across framings. Decompose the direction of drift: does belief shift toward whatever polarity the query foregrounds (acquiescence: leading-toward-P raises belief, leading-toward-not-P lowers it), toward a generic 'agree' default, or symmetrically? Report per-layer, per-model instability across truth regimes and framing types. Compare internal instability to OUTPUT-level instability (does the model's yes/no answer or verbalized confidence flip across framings?), testing whether the inconsistency exists in belief geometry, at the output, or both.

Query-framing-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'query-framing' direction via difference-in-means on leading-toward-P vs leading-toward-not-P activations (balanced across truth-value and content), and a separate 'polarity/negation' direction on positive vs negated framings. Report per-layer decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode framing (and vice versa). Test whether framing instability is explained by the framing component leaking into the truth-probe readout — the mechanistic substrate of the bias.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Take the activation difference between a leading-toward-P and a leading-toward-not-P framing of the same proposition, decompose into truth-direction and framing-direction components, and patch only the framing component into a neutral framing; measure the induced change in belief readout and in the yes/no output. (b) Subtract the framing component from a leading framing and measure whether belief returns toward the neutral value. Confirm the query-framing signal causally shifts the belief scalar independent of content.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether Framing Instability predicts (i) answer flips (the model's yes/no answer to logically-equivalent framings disagrees), (ii) acquiescence errors (agreeing with a leading framing of a false proposition), and (iii) calibration failures across framings. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (output entropy, neutral-framing truth-probe confidence, a leading-framing indicator).

Framing-Invariance intervention: At inference, estimate the query-framing direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer (ITI-style de-biasing), so the belief readout reflects propositional content rather than interrogative packaging. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected leading/negated framings. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Framing Instability Score, (ii) increased cross-framing answer consistency and reduced acquiescence errors, (iii) improved calibration (ECE) aggregated across framings, (iv) PRESERVATION of accuracy on neutral-framing clearly-true/false items and declarative controls (no over-suppression), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'answer based only on the facts, ignoring how the question is phrased', and a self-consistency baseline that aggregates answers across framings.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), framing type (neutral/negated/leading-P/leading-not-P/declarative), real vs synthetic facts, true vs false regime, model scale, position of readout, robustness of the negation-remapping, and generalization to framing styles and topics not used to fit the de-biasing direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent framing instability could reflect the probe detecting surface interrogative tokens (negation words, tag-question phrasing) rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with surface-length matching, the negation-remapping consistency check, paraphrase controls, and causal patching that isolates the framing-direction component from lexical cues.

Mapping negated-framing readouts back to belief-in-P assumes the probe handles negation cleanly; Bao et al. (2025) find negation is where truth directions are strongest in capable models but weaker in others, so remapping error could confound instability estimates — we validate remapping on clearly-true/false items, use multiple probe types, and report model-dependent reliability.
Framing and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality and project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

Ensuring framings are truly logically equivalent and content-preserving (leading questions can subtly presuppose) is nontrivial; we constrain templates, human-verify, and treat presupposition-laden framings as a separately-analyzed category.

The Framing-Invariance intervention could over-suppress legitimate belief signals or harm fluency; we explicitly measure preservation on neutral/declarative items and capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Framing instability may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (leading-framing indicator, output entropy) for answer flips; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that belief geometry lacks measurement invariance to query framing, plus the de-biasing tool, reported honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may amplify acquiescence/agreeableness); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: belief_hysteresis_order_dependence
Title: Belief Hysteresis: Do LLM Internal Beliefs Depend on the Order in Which Confirming and Disconfirming Evidence Arrived?
Short Hypothesis: For a proposition supported and challenged by an equal balance of in-context evidence, a rational belief must depend only on the NET evidence, not the ORDER in which pieces arrived. We hypothesize that LLM internal belief representations (linear truth-direction readouts) are HYSTERETIC/path-dependent: presenting the same evidence set as confirm-then-disconfirm yields a systematically different final internal belief than disconfirm-then-confirm (a primacy or recency asymmetry), that this order-induced gap is graded and decodable, causally predicts order-dependent factual answers on balanced evidence, and can be reduced by a lightweight inference-time intervention that removes the order/path component from the belief representation.
Related Work: Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) reads a single first-order belief and shows context sensitivity to preceding sentences, but treats context as a static set and never manipulates the ORDER of equal-and-opposite evidence to test path-independence. My prior 'evidence-weighting' proposal tested Bayesian sensitivity to evidence quantity/reliability/redundancy and listed order-invariance as one property, but only for same-valence supporting evidence and only as a secondary check; it did not isolate the mixed confirm/disconfirm ordering that produces hysteresis, did not model belief as a path-dependent trajectory, and did not tie an order-induced belief gap causally to order-dependent answers or provide an order-de-biasing intervention. Human primacy/recency and belief-updating order effects (Hogarth & Einhorn 1992) are well documented behaviorally; anchoring/order effects in LLM outputs are noted at the prompt level. No prior work asks whether LLM internal BELIEF geometry is hysteretic to evidence order on net-balanced evidence, decomposes it into a decodable path component, links it causally to order-dependent factual errors, or de-biases it. This is a distinct measurement-invariance-over-time lens on belief.
Abstract: A belief worthy of the name should be a function of the total evidence seen, not of the accident of which piece came first. We ask whether large language models honor this path-independence inside their belief representations. Presenting a model with a net-balanced bundle of confirming and disconfirming in-context evidence about a proposition, we vary only the ORDER of presentation and read the resulting internal belief via linear truth probes. We construct OrderBelief, a controlled dataset of true, false, and synthetic-in-context propositions, each accompanied by a set of evidence pieces whose net valence is fixed but whose ordering is permuted (confirm-then-disconfirm, disconfirm-then-confirm, and interleaved), with matched surface content and length. Because the evidence content is identical, a path-independent model must reach the same final internal belief regardless of order. We define a Belief Hysteresis Score measuring the gap in final decoded belief across orderings, and trace the per-position belief trajectory to characterize primacy versus recency dynamics. We test four claims: (1) internal beliefs are hysteretic to evidence order even at fixed net evidence; (2) the order-induced gap is carried by a decodable path/order component dissociable from the truth direction; (3) hysteresis magnitude causally predicts order-dependent factual answers on balanced-evidence items; and (4) a lightweight Order-Invariance intervention that removes the path component restores consistent beliefs and reduces order-dependent flips without harming clearly-true/false judgments or legitimate net-evidence updating. We validate causality with activation patching and evaluate on consistency, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build OrderBelief. Propositions P in three truth regimes: real-true, real-false, and synthetic facts defined only in context (to remove parametric priors). For each P assemble a bundle of k evidence pieces with a fixed net valence (e.g., 2 confirming + 2 disconfirming for net-neutral, or 3 confirm + 1 disconfirm for net-positive), and present the SAME pieces under multiple orderings: confirm-first (all confirms then all disconfirms), disconfirm-first, and interleaved. Match evidence reliability and surface length across pieces; control total token count so orderings differ only in sequence. Include a single-valence control (all confirming, all disconfirming) and a net-neutral core condition. Add paraphrase sets and human-verified samples. Also vary bundle size k (2,4,6) and gap between last evidence and query.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral declarative true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At a matched query position after the evidence bundle, read the final internal belief in P under each ordering. Manipulation check: confirm single-valence controls move belief in the expected direction and probes separate clearly-true/false items.

Belief Hysteresis measurement: For each proposition and net-valence condition, compute the spread of final belief-in-P across orderings. Define Belief Hysteresis Score = max-min (and standard deviation) of final belief across the confirm-first / disconfirm-first / interleaved orderings, at fixed net evidence. Report per-layer, per-model hysteresis across truth regimes, bundle sizes, and net-valence conditions. Diagnose the direction: does confirm-first vs disconfirm-first difference indicate PRIMACY (first evidence dominates) or RECENCY (last evidence dominates)? Compare internal hysteresis to OUTPUT-level hysteresis (does the model's yes/no answer or verbalized confidence flip with order?), testing whether the path-dependence lives in belief geometry, at the output, or both.

Per-position trajectory analysis: Read the internal belief scalar after each evidence piece to trace the belief trajectory within each ordering. Characterize update asymmetries (e.g., does a disconfirming piece move belief more when it arrives late vs early?), and whether trajectories that end with identical net evidence converge or remain separated (the geometric signature of hysteresis).

Order/path-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit an 'order/path' direction via difference-in-means on confirm-first vs disconfirm-first final-position activations (balanced across truth-value and content). Report per-layer decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the order component (and vice versa). Test whether hysteresis is explained by this path component leaking into the truth-probe readout.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Take the final-position activation difference between confirm-first and disconfirm-first orderings of the same balanced bundle, decompose into truth-direction and order-direction components, and patch only the order component into the other ordering; measure induced change in belief readout and yes/no output. (b) Subtract the order component and test whether the two orderings' beliefs converge. Confirm the path signal causally shifts the belief scalar independent of net evidence content.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether Belief Hysteresis Score predicts (i) order-dependent answer flips (yes/no differs across orderings of identical evidence), (ii) calibration failures on balanced-evidence items, and (iii) sensitivity of downstream multi-source QA answers to evidence ordering. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (output entropy, single-ordering truth-probe confidence, an order-of-last-piece indicator).

Order-Invariance intervention: At inference, estimate the order/path direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer (ITI-style de-biasing), so the final belief reflects net evidence rather than presentation order. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected mixed-valence evidence bundles. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Belief Hysteresis Score, (ii) increased cross-ordering answer consistency, (iii) improved calibration (ECE) on balanced-evidence QA, (iv) PRESERVATION of legitimate net-evidence updating (single-valence controls must still move belief correctly) and accuracy on clearly-true/false items (no over-suppression), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'weigh all evidence equally regardless of order', and a self-consistency baseline aggregating over evidence orderings.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), net-valence condition, bundle size k, primacy-vs-recency diagnosis across model scale, gap between last evidence and query, interleaving pattern, real vs synthetic facts, and generalization to orderings and topics not used to fit the de-biasing direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent hysteresis could reflect generic recency/position effects on the probe (later tokens dominate the readout) rather than a genuine belief-updating asymmetry; mitigate with matched-length controls, interleaved conditions, per-position trajectory analysis, and causal patching that isolates the order-direction component from raw positional decay.

Truth probes trained on single declarative statements may transfer imperfectly to multi-evidence contexts, so hysteresis could partly reflect probe extrapolation; use multiple probe types, single-valence manipulation checks, and synthetic facts to control priors.
Order and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality and project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

Ensuring orderings are truly net-balanced (equal-strength confirm/disconfirm pieces) is nontrivial since the model may weight individual pieces unequally; we calibrate per-piece belief impact from single-valence conditions and human-verify, reporting sensitivity to imbalance.

The Order-Invariance intervention could over-suppress legitimate updating or harm fluency; we explicitly measure preservation of single-valence updating and clearly-true/false accuracy plus capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Hysteresis may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (last-piece valence, output entropy) for order-dependent flips; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that belief geometry is path-dependent, plus the de-biasing tool, reported honestly.
Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training; we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: polyglot_belief_invariance
Title: Does the Model Believe It in French? Testing Language-Invariance of LLM Internal Beliefs
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's internal belief in a proposition should be invariant to the language it is expressed in: 'The Nile is in Africa', its French translation, and its Swahili translation are the same proposition and must receive the same internal belief. We hypothesize that (1) a single language-invariant 'truth direction' can be extracted whose belief readout transfers across languages, (2) despite this, an LLM's decoded internal belief in an identical fact is systematically LANGUAGE-RELATIVE, degrading toward uncertainty/falsehood as the query language becomes lower-resource, (3) this internal belief-degradation causally predicts cross-lingual factual errors and hallucinations, and (4) a lightweight inference-time intervention that re-anchors the low-resource belief to the language-invariant truth direction improves multilingual factual accuracy and consistency.
Related Work: A large body of work studies cross-lingual factual INCONSISTENCY at the OUTPUT level and its mechanistic causes: Wang et al. (2025, 'Lost in Multilinguality') show knowledge lives in a language-independent concept space until late layers where a faulty language transition causes wrong target-language answers; Ifergan et al. (2024) measure representation sharing via knowledge editing; Xiao et al. (2025) probe cross-lingual KNOWLEDGE BOUNDARIES (known vs unknown) and align them across languages; Manev (2026) and PolyFact (2026) steer/post-train for consistency. Crucially, none of these read a graded internal BELIEF scalar (a linear truth direction, in the belief-probing tradition of Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023) for a FIXED proposition across languages, ask whether a single language-invariant truth direction exists that decodes belief cross-lingually, quantify how the decoded belief in an identical true fact degrades with language resourcedness (belief-relativity, distinct from knowledge-boundary/known-vs-unknown), tie that internal belief-degradation causally to hallucination, or re-anchor belief along the invariant direction. Xiao et al. study whether the model KNOWS a fact per language; we study, for facts the model demonstrably knows, whether it BELIEVES them equally strongly per language. This belief-invariance lens is new and distinct from output-consistency and knowledge-boundary work.
Abstract: The truth of a fact does not depend on the language you state it in, so a rational belief system should assign the same belief to a proposition regardless of language. We ask whether large language models honor this invariance inside their belief representations. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar internal belief along a linear truth direction, we first test whether a single LANGUAGE-INVARIANT truth direction exists: a direction, fit on statements in one language (or pooled across languages), whose belief readout transfers to the same statements in other languages. We then test our central hypothesis of BELIEF-RELATIVITY: holding a proposition's meaning fixed, does the model's decoded internal belief in an identical true fact degrade toward uncertainty or falsehood as the query language becomes lower-resource? We construct PolyglotBelief, a parallel dataset of true, false, and synthetic-in-context propositions translated across high-, medium-, and low-resource languages, restricted to facts the model demonstrably knows in at least one language, with paraphrase and back-translation controls. We define a Belief-Language Gap (belief in the highest-resource language minus belief in a target language) per proposition and layer, and test four claims: (1) an invariant truth direction exists and transfers; (2) internal belief is language-relative, shrinking with resourcedness even for the same fact; (3) the Belief-Language Gap causally predicts cross-lingual factual errors and hallucinations; and (4) a lightweight Cross-Lingual Belief Re-anchoring intervention that steers activations toward the invariant truth direction improves target-language factual accuracy and consistency without harming high-resource performance or general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on multilingual factual QA, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build PolyglotBelief. Collect Wikidata-grounded factual propositions with definite truth-values, in three truth regimes: real-true, real-false (negations/wrong-object variants), and synthetic facts defined only in context (to remove parametric priors). Produce fully PARALLEL translations across a resourcedness spectrum: high (English, Spanish), medium (Turkish, Bengali), low (Swahili, Amharic), plus a script-varied set (e.g., Russian/Chinese) to separate script from resourcedness. Use high-quality machine translation with human/back-translation verification of a sample and meaning preservation. Crucially, restrict analysis to facts the model DEMONSTRABLY KNOWS in at least one language (verified by high-accuracy, low-entropy output on held-out phrasings) so that belief-relativity is not confounded with genuine ignorance. Include paraphrase sets within each language and matched surface forms.

Belief readout and invariant-direction test: For 4-5 open multilingual models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Gemma-2 9B, Aya/BLOOM-family), extract final-token hidden states per proposition per layer. Train truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression), Platt-scaled to [0,1], in three modes: (a) English-only, (b) pooled-multilingual, (c) per-language. Test invariance: does the English-trained (and pooled) direction decode belief for the SAME statements in other languages? Report per-layer cross-lingual probe transfer accuracy and cosine similarity between per-language truth directions. Locate the layer(s) where an invariant direction is strongest (expected mid layers, per Wang et al.'s concept-space finding).

Belief-Language Gap measurement: Using the invariant direction, for each demonstrably-known TRUE fact read the internal belief in every language. Define Belief-Language Gap = belief(highest-resource language) - belief(target language). Report per-layer, per-model gaps as a function of language resourcedness and script. Test the belief-relativity hypothesis: internal belief in the same true fact declines with lower resourcedness even though the fact is known. Separate script effects from resourcedness using the script-varied set. Compare internal belief gaps to OUTPUT-level accuracy gaps (does the model answer the fact correctly per language?), testing whether belief-relativity precedes and predicts output failure.

Dissociation from knowledge-boundary: Contrast belief-relativity (graded belief degradation for KNOWN facts) with genuine per-language ignorance (facts the model does not know in the target language), using a knowledge-boundary probe (a la Xiao et al.). Show these are distinct: belief-relativity persists on known facts, distinguishing our finding from mere knowledge gaps.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Patch the invariant-truth-direction component from a high-resource-language processing of a fact into the low-resource-language processing of the same fact at a chosen layer, and measure whether the low-resource belief readout and output answer recover toward correct. (b) Subtract the invariant component in the high-resource case and induce failure. Confirm the invariant truth direction causally governs cross-lingual belief, and that late-layer language transition (per Wang et al.) is where recovery must be applied.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether the Belief-Language Gap predicts (i) cross-lingual factual error (correct in high-resource, wrong in target language), (ii) cross-lingual hallucination (confident wrong answer in target language), and (iii) paraphrase inconsistency within the target language. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (language-resourcedness alone, output entropy, per-language truth-probe confidence).

Cross-Lingual Belief Re-anchoring intervention: At inference for a target-language query, add a scaled shift along the invariant truth direction at the identified layer(s) to re-anchor the belief toward the language-invariant value (ITI-style). A practical variant estimates the required shift from the model's own high-resource-aligned invariant readout (e.g., via the shared concept-space representation) without needing ground-truth labels at test time. Sweep layer and strength; compare applying at mid concept-space layers vs late language-transition layers.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Belief-Language Gap, (ii) improved target-language factual QA accuracy and cross-lingual consistency (parallel QA agreement) on PolyglotBelief and external multilingual factual benchmarks (e.g., translated TriviaQA/Wikidata QA, and PolyFact-style sets), (iii) calibration (ECE) per language, (iv) PRESERVATION of high-resource accuracy and cultural-localization where divergence is legitimate (must not overwrite language-appropriate answers on genuinely locale-specific questions), and (v) capability retention on multilingual MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, English-prompt-then-translate, standard ITI truth steering, contrastive activation addition, and prompt-based instruction to 'answer as if asked in English'.

Ablations: probe training mode (English/pooled/per-language), layer choice (concept-space vs language-transition), probe type, resourcedness and script conditions, real vs synthetic facts, true vs false regime, model scale, transfer of the invariant direction to unseen languages, and generalization to fact domains not used to fit the intervention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Translation quality confounds: apparent belief-relativity could reflect meaning drift in low-resource translations rather than genuine belief degradation; mitigate with back-translation verification, human checks on a sample, synthetic-in-context facts (translation-controlled by construction), and paraphrase controls, treating high-error-translation items separately.

The invariant truth direction may transfer poorly for distant scripts/languages, so cross-lingual probe readouts could reflect probe error rather than a genuine invariant belief; use multiple probe-training modes, report transfer accuracy explicitly, and rely on causal patching; a finding that no invariant direction exists for some languages is itself informative.

Belief-relativity must be dissociated from genuine per-language ignorance; we restrict to demonstrably-known facts and contrast with a knowledge-boundary probe, but residual confounds may remain and are reported.

Cultural-localization tension: some questions legitimately have language/locale-dependent answers, so re-anchoring must not erase valid cultural divergence (cf. Han et al. 2025 'cultural erasure'); we separate universal-fact items from locale-specific ones and measure preservation on the latter.

The label-free re-anchoring variant depends on a reliable high-resource/concept-space anchor that may itself be biased toward Western/English knowledge; we characterize this gap and report where re-anchoring helps vs harms.

Belief-Language Gap may correlate with but not exceed simple resourcedness/output-entropy baselines for predicting errors; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic finding that belief is language-relative and the invariant-direction tool, reported honestly.
Effects may vary across model families, scales, tokenizers, and multilingual pretraining mixes; we test multiple models and report scale/tokenization effects and negative results as informative.

Name: belief_update_inertia_geometry
Title: How Stubborn Is a Belief? Measuring the Internal Belief-Update Learning Rate and Conservatism Bias of LLMs
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's internal belief update in response to in-context disconfirming evidence has a measurable, graded 'learning rate' (belief change per unit of contradicting evidence). We hypothesize this learning rate is (1) asymmetric — disconfirming evidence moves internal belief LESS than equally-strong confirming evidence (a representational conservatism bias), (2) prior-dependent — stronger prior beliefs update more sluggishly (belief inertia scaling with prior strength), (3) that low internal learning rate causally predicts a failure to revise despite sufficient counterevidence, and (4) that a lightweight inference-time intervention amplifying the disconfirming-evidence update along the truth direction restores responsive, symmetric updating without harming legitimate stability.
Related Work: Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) reads a single static belief scalar and shows context sensitivity but never quantifies the RATE or ASYMMETRY of belief updating as evidence accumulates. 'Belief Inertia' (Wang et al. 2026) studies stubbornness at the OUTPUT/action level for embodied agents via explicit textual belief states and an EVU prompting mechanism — not internal representation dynamics, not a decodable learning-rate quantity, and not the confirm-vs-disconfirm asymmetry. My prior proposals differ concretely: 'belief_ghost_revision' studied residual OLD belief AFTER a completed flip; 'premature_belief_commitment' studied lock-in DURING reading of a single statement; 'belief_evidence_weighting' tested Bayesian sensitivity to evidence quantity/reliability/redundancy but did NOT model the update-responsiveness curve, its dependence on prior belief strength, or the confirm/disconfirm conservatism asymmetry; 'belief_hysteresis_order_dependence' studied order-dependence, not update magnitude per evidence unit. This proposal is the first to characterize belief updating as a graded internal learning-rate function with a conservatism asymmetry, tie sluggish updating causally to revision failure, and re-tune the update along the truth direction.
Abstract: A rational agent should update its beliefs in proportion to the evidence it receives, and should treat evidence for and against a claim symmetrically. Humans famously violate this via conservatism (under-updating) and belief perseverance. We ask whether large language models exhibit analogous distortions in the DYNAMICS of their internal belief updating. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar internal belief along the linear truth direction, we present a proposition and then feed in-context evidence incrementally, tracing how the internal belief moves as evidence accumulates. From these trajectories we estimate a per-item Belief Update Learning Rate (belief change per unit of evidence) and a Conservatism Asymmetry (learning rate for disconfirming vs confirming evidence). We construct UpdateBelief, a controlled dataset of true, false, and synthetic-in-context propositions with matched, calibrated confirming and disconfirming evidence pieces, spanning a range of prior belief strengths. We test four claims: (1) internal belief updates are conservative and asymmetric, moving less for disconfirming than confirming evidence; (2) update sluggishness scales with prior belief strength (inertia); (3) low internal learning rate causally predicts failure to flip the output answer despite decisive counterevidence; and (4) a lightweight Update-Gain intervention that amplifies the disconfirming-evidence-induced shift along the truth direction restores responsive, symmetric updating and improves belief-revision accuracy without harming legitimate stability on weak/spurious evidence or general capability. We validate causality with activation patching and evaluate on revision accuracy, calibration, and capability retention. Our results characterize belief updating as a tunable internal learning process rather than a static readout.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build UpdateBelief. Propositions P in three regimes: real-true, real-false, and synthetic facts defined only in context (to remove parametric priors and to set the prior belief precisely). For each P, assemble a sequence of independent evidence pieces of two valences (confirming, disconfirming) with calibrated per-piece strength (measured by the belief shift each induces in a single-piece pilot), so confirming and disconfirming pieces can be matched in magnitude. Present evidence INCREMENTALLY (1,2,3,4,5 pieces) in a fixed valence run. Vary the PRIOR belief strength by using strongly-known facts, weakly-known facts, and synthetic facts with a pre-set prior established by an initial framing. Match surface length per step; include paraphrase sets and human-verified samples.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. After each evidence step, read the internal belief in P at a matched query position. Manipulation check: confirm single-piece pilots move belief in the expected direction and probes separate clearly-true/false items.

Learning-rate estimation: For each item and valence, fit the belief-vs-cumulative-evidence trajectory (linear/logistic) and extract a Belief Update Learning Rate = belief change per unit of (strength-normalized) evidence. Report per-layer, per-model learning rates. Define Conservatism Asymmetry = (confirming learning rate − disconfirming learning rate) for matched-strength evidence pushing away from the prior. Test the hypothesis that disconfirming updates are systematically slower (conservatism).

Prior-dependence (inertia) analysis: Regress the disconfirming-evidence learning rate on the prior belief strength (from the strongly/weakly-known and synthetic-prior conditions). Test whether stronger priors update more sluggishly (belief inertia scaling), controlling for evidence strength. Compare internal-belief inertia to OUTPUT-level inertia (does the model's yes/no answer flip after the same amount of counterevidence?).

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Take the residual-stream shift induced by an additional disconfirming piece, and amplify vs attenuate its projection onto the truth direction at a chosen layer; measure the induced change in belief readout and in the output answer, confirming the internal update magnitude causally governs revision. (b) Patch a high-learning-rate item's disconfirming shift into a sluggish item and measure induced flipping. Confirm the learning rate is a causal, manipulable property of the truth-direction geometry.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether low internal Belief Update Learning Rate (and high Conservatism Asymmetry) predicts (i) failure to flip the output answer despite decisive counterevidence, (ii) belief perseverance (reverting to the prior when queried again), and (iii) calibration failure (over-confidence in the un-updated prior). Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (prior strength alone, output entropy, cumulative-evidence count).

Update-Gain intervention: At inference, detect disconfirming-evidence-induced shifts (residual-stream change along the truth direction opposing the current belief) and amplify their projection onto the truth direction at a chosen layer by a gain factor (ITI-style), symmetrizing the update. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected counterevidence relative to the running belief. Sweep gain and layer.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) increased and more symmetric learning rates / reduced Conservatism Asymmetry, (ii) improved belief-revision accuracy (correctly flipping when counterevidence is decisive) on UpdateBelief and adapted knowledge-conflict/counterfactual-context QA, (iii) calibration (ECE), (iv) PRESERVATION of legitimate stability — the model must NOT flip on weak or spurious counterevidence (measured on a spurious-evidence control set) — and accuracy on clearly-true/false items, and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'revise your belief in proportion to the evidence', and the EVU-style explicit-belief prompting baseline (Wang et al. 2026).

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), prior strength condition, evidence-strength calibration method, confirming vs disconfirming direction, trajectory fit (linear vs logistic), number of evidence steps, model scale, and generalization to evidence types and topics not used to fit the intervention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent conservatism/inertia could reflect the probe saturating or responding nonlinearly near belief extremes rather than a genuine slow update; mitigate with strength-matched confirming/disconfirming pieces, synthetic-prior conditions that place the prior in the mid-range, multiple probe types, and causal patching that isolates the truth-direction update magnitude.

Estimating a comparable per-unit learning rate requires calibrating evidence strength, which is imperfect since the model may weight pieces unequally; we calibrate from single-piece pilots and human-verify, and report sensitivity to mis-calibration.

Truth probes trained on single statements may transfer imperfectly to multi-evidence contexts, so learning-rate estimates could carry probe extrapolation error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks, and synthetic facts to control priors.

The Update-Gain intervention risks making the model TOO credulous — flipping on weak or spurious counterevidence; we explicitly measure stability on a spurious-evidence control set to characterize the responsiveness-vs-stability tradeoff, which is the core risk.

Low learning rate may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (prior strength, output entropy) for revision failure; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that belief updating has a tunable, asymmetric internal learning rate, plus the intervention, reported honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may amplify either stubbornness or sycophantic over-updating); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: self_persuasion_belief_drift
Title: Arguing Yourself Into Belief: Does Generating One-Sided Arguments Shift an LLM's Own Internal Beliefs?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is instructed to generate a one-sided persuasive text for a position (including a false one), the act of producing supporting arguments progressively shifts the model's OWN internal belief (linear truth-direction readout) toward the argued position, a measurable self-persuasion effect. We hypothesize this belief drift (1) accumulates monotonically across the model's own generated argument tokens, (2) is larger than for the same arguments merely read in context (i.e., self-generation, not exposure alone, drives it), (3) persists after generation and causally predicts post-argument factual errors and sycophantic endorsement of the argued falsehood, and (4) can be counteracted by a lightweight inference-time intervention that quarantines the argument-induced belief shift, restoring accurate post-argument beliefs without harming the model's ability to argue.
Related Work: Sturgeon et al. (2026, 'When Role-playing, Do Models Believe What They Say?') use truth probes to test whether persona adoption changes internal belief, finding a spectrum across prompting/ICL/SFT/EM/OCT, but they study a static persona snapshot, not the DYNAMIC accumulation of belief drift as the model generates its own argumentative text, and not the self-generation-vs-exposure contrast. Yang & Jia (2025) link momentary belief to retraction; Schouten et al. (2024) show truth directions are context-sensitive to preceding sentences (exposure), not to self-produced arguments. My prior 'self_commitment_belief_anchoring' proposal studied a SINGLE self-authored assertion's inflation, not the graded self-persuasion trajectory across extended argument generation; 'belief_hysteresis' and 'evidence_weighting' concern externally-supplied evidence. The Hypocrisy Gap (Shiromani et al. 2026) measures belief-vs-CoT divergence for sycophancy, not self-persuasion from one's own generated arguments. No prior work asks whether an LLM argues ITSELF into believing a position by generating supporting content, quantifies the belief trajectory across its own argument tokens, isolates self-generation as the causal driver, ties it to post-argument factual failure, and quarantines it. This is a distinct dynamic self-influence lens.
Abstract: People often talk themselves into believing what they argue for: producing supporting reasons strengthens one's own conviction, even for positions one initially doubted. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous self-persuasion effect inside their belief representations. When an LLM is instructed to write a one-sided persuasive text defending a position P (including a factually false one), does the act of generating supporting arguments progressively shift its own internal belief toward P? Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar internal belief along the linear truth direction, we trace how the model's belief in P evolves across the tokens of its own generated argument. We construct ArgueBelief, a controlled set of debatable and clearly-false propositions, each with prompts eliciting a persuasive one-sided essay for P, for not-P, and a neutral summary control. We define a Self-Persuasion Drift Score = shift in internal belief in P from before to after the model generates its pro-P argument, and compare it against an EXPOSURE control in which the model merely reads an identical, externally-authored pro-P argument. We test four claims: (1) belief drifts toward the argued side and accumulates across self-generated argument tokens; (2) self-generation produces larger drift than mere exposure to the same text; (3) post-argument belief drift persists and causally predicts factual errors and endorsement of the argued falsehood when the model is later queried; and (4) a lightweight Argument-Quarantine intervention that subtracts the argument-induced belief shift restores accurate post-argument beliefs without degrading argument quality or general capability. We validate causality with activation patching and evaluate on factuality, consistency, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build ArgueBelief. Include (a) clearly-false factual propositions (e.g., 'Vaccines cause autism', 'The Great Wall is visible from the Moon with the naked eye') with a definite ground-truth, (b) debatable-but-falsifiable claims, and (c) synthetic-in-context propositions (defined only in context) to control priors. For each proposition P, create prompts eliciting: PRO-P persuasive essay ('Write a convincing argument that P'), PRO-not-P essay, and a NEUTRAL summary control ('Summarize the topic of P without taking a side'). Also prepare an EXPOSURE condition in which an identical, externally-authored pro-P argument (matched in length/content to a representative model generation) is placed in context and the model is NOT asked to argue. Include paraphrase query sets and matched surface forms.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral declarative true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. Read internal belief in P at a fixed, standardized query position (a canonical 'Is P true?' probe appended in a fresh readout pass) at three time points: BEFORE argument generation (baseline), AFTER the model has generated its pro-P essay, and additionally at intermediate checkpoints while the essay is being generated (per-sentence). Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false items; confirm the model actually produces a one-sided pro-P essay.

Self-Persuasion Drift measurement: Define Self-Persuasion Drift Score = belief_in_P(after pro-P generation) minus belief_in_P(baseline). Report per-layer, per-model drift across proposition types (false / debatable / synthetic) and argument directions (pro-P vs pro-not-P should push belief oppositely). Trace the per-sentence belief trajectory during self-generation to test whether drift accumulates monotonically with the number of self-produced supporting arguments.
