Compare internal drift to OUTPUT-level drift (does the model's later yes/no answer or verbalized confidence about P shift after arguing?).

Self-generation vs exposure dissociation: Compare Self-Persuasion Drift under the SELF-GENERATION condition against the EXPOSURE condition (same pro-P text read, not authored) with matched query positions and text length. Test the hypothesis that self-generation produces larger belief drift than mere exposure. Additionally include a 'forced-argument-on-known-false' condition to test whether arguing for something the model clearly knows is false still induces drift.

Axis and mechanism analysis: Fit an 'argument-commitment' difference direction (pro-P-generation minus neutral-summary activations, balanced across propositions) and test whether it is decodable and dissociable from the truth direction (cosine similarity, project-out re-decoding), and whether self-persuasion drift is explained by this component leaking into the truth-probe readout.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Take the residual-stream shift induced by self-generating the pro-P argument, decompose into truth-direction and argument-commitment components, and patch only the argument-commitment component into the baseline/neutral state; measure induced change in belief readout and in the later factual answer. (b) Subtract the argument-induced shift after generation and test whether belief returns to baseline. Confirm self-generated argument content causally shifts the belief scalar.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether Self-Persuasion Drift predicts (i) post-argument factual error (the model asserts the false P as true when subsequently asked in a fresh turn), (ii) sycophantic endorsement of the argued falsehood, and (iii) inconsistency between the pre-argument and post-argument answer about P. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (argument length, output entropy, baseline truth-probe confidence).

Argument-Quarantine intervention: At inference, after the pro-P essay is generated and before answering factual queries, estimate the argument-commitment direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer (ITI-style), so the post-argument belief readout reflects the model's prior knowledge rather than the self-produced argument. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected recent one-sided generation about the queried claim. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Self-Persuasion Drift, (ii) improved post-argument factual accuracy and reduced endorsement of argued falsehoods, (iii) improved pre/post answer consistency about P, (iv) PRESERVATION of argument quality (the model must still write persuasive essays when asked; judged by an LLM/human rubric) and accuracy on unrelated facts and neutral controls, and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, a fresh-context re-ask baseline (query P without the prior essay in context), and prompt-based instruction to 'evaluate the truth independently of the argument you just wrote'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), proposition type (false/debatable/synthetic), argument direction (pro-P vs pro-not-P), argument length (short vs long essays, testing dose-response), self-generation vs exposure, distance between the essay and the factual query, model scale, and generalization to topics not used to fit the quarantine direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent self-persuasion drift could reflect the probe detecting lexical/topical residue of the just-generated pro-P text rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with the exposure control (same text, no authorship), the argument-direction contrast (pro-P vs pro-not-P should oppose), matched query positions, paraphrase controls, and causal patching that isolates the argument-commitment component.

The exposure-vs-self-generation comparison is imperfect because the externally-authored argument may differ subtly from the model's own; we match length/content to representative generations and human-verify a sample, reporting sensitivity.

Truth probes trained on single declarative statements may transfer imperfectly to long argumentative contexts, so drift estimates could carry probe extrapolation error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks, and synthetic facts to control priors.

The argument-commitment and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality/project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

The Argument-Quarantine intervention could over-suppress legitimate belief updates (e.g., if arguing surfaces genuinely correct reasoning) or degrade the model's willingness/ability to argue; we explicitly measure argument quality preservation, neutral-control accuracy, and capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Self-persuasion drift may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (argument length, output entropy) for post-argument errors; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that models argue themselves into belief, plus the quarantine tool, reported honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may amplify commitment/agreeableness or, conversely, factual anchoring); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: modal_status_belief_geometry
Title: Necessarily True or Just Happens To Be? Probing Whether LLM Beliefs Encode Modal Status
Short Hypothesis: Beyond a proposition's truth-value, a rational belief system distinguishes its MODAL STATUS: whether it is necessarily true (true in all possible worlds, e.g. '2+2=4', 'bachelors are unmarried') versus contingently true (true but could have been otherwise, e.g. 'Paris is the capital of France'). We hypothesize that (1) an LLM's internal belief representation encodes a decodable 'modal-strength' axis dissociable from the true/false axis, (2) this axis is systematically MISCALIBRATED — belief in necessary truths is not held more rigidly than belief in contingent ones, so models under-defend necessary truths (accepting definitional/mathematical falsehoods under mild pressure) and over-defend contingent ones (refusing legitimate counterfactual/updated claims), (3) this modal miscalibration causally predicts these two opposite failure modes, and (4) a lightweight inference-time intervention that reads the modal axis and gates update-resistance accordingly (rigid for necessary, flexible for contingent) reduces both failure modes.
Related Work: Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) fits a single true-vs-false axis and reads a flat belief scalar, never distinguishing the MODAL STATUS of true propositions. My prior proposals cover logical coherence over implication networks, temporal indexing (when a fact is true), gradability (degree of truth for vague predicates), ignorance vs falsehood, evidence weighting, belief-update inertia, and supposition; none ask whether belief geometry encodes NECESSITY vs CONTINGENCY, i.e. the counterfactual robustness of a truth across possible worlds. Modality is central in formal semantics and epistemology but has not been examined in LLM belief representations. Counterfactual-reasoning work (DeLorean; counterfactual editing) operates at the output level and does not link a proposition's modal status to how rigidly its belief should be held. This is the first proposal to (a) test for a decodable modal-strength axis orthogonal to truth, (b) tie modal miscalibration to the twin failures of accepting necessary-falsehoods under pressure and rejecting legitimate contingent updates, and (c) gate update-resistance by decoded modal status.
Abstract: Some truths could not have been otherwise — 2+2 must equal 4, a bachelor must be unmarried — while others merely happen to hold — France's capital is Paris, but it could have been elsewhere. A competent believer should treat these differently: cling to necessary truths even under pressure, yet remain open to revising contingent ones. We ask whether large language models encode this modal distinction inside their belief representations. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar belief along the linear truth direction, we test whether a separate 'modal-strength' axis — necessary versus contingent — is also decodable and dissociable from the true/false axis. We construct ModalBelief, a controlled dataset crossing truth-value with modal status: necessary-true (mathematical, definitional, logical), contingent-true (empirical world facts), and matched false variants, with surface forms controlled and modal labels human-verified. We fit both axes, measure their orthogonality via project-out analyses, and validate causality with activation patching. We then test our central miscalibration hypothesis: is belief in necessary truths held more rigidly than belief in contingent truths under in-context pressure, or does the model apply uniform update-resistance regardless of modal status? We link modal miscalibration to two opposite failure modes — accepting definitional/mathematical falsehoods when pushed, and refusing legitimate counterfactual or updated contingent claims — and test whether the decoded modal axis predicts them. Finally, we introduce Modal-Gated Update Control, a cheap intervention that increases update-resistance along the truth direction for high-necessity propositions and decreases it for contingent ones, evaluating reductions in both failure modes alongside calibration and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build ModalBelief crossing truth-value {true, false} with modal status {necessary, contingent}. NECESSARY items: arithmetic/mathematical identities, logical tautologies, and analytic/definitional truths ('a triangle has three sides', 'a widow is a woman whose spouse has died'). CONTINGENT items: empirical world facts (capitals, populations, biographies, physical constants that are contingent). Construct matched FALSE variants for each (a necessary-false, e.g. '2+2=5' or 'a triangle has four sides'; a contingent-false, e.g. 'the capital of France is Lyon'). Match surface length and syntactic form across modal categories to avoid lexical shortcuts (e.g. avoid necessary items always containing numbers). Human-verify modal labels with multiple annotators and report agreement; include a borderline/ambiguous category (e.g. natural-kind or nomological claims) analyzed separately. Add paraphrase sets and neutral controls.

Probe training and axis discovery: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), extract final-token hidden states per proposition per layer. Train (a) a TRUTH probe on true vs false with modal status balanced, and (b) a MODAL-STRENGTH probe on necessary vs contingent with truth-value balanced, using difference-in-means and logistic regression, Platt-scaled to [0,1]. Report per-layer decoding accuracy of each probe and cross-axis leakage (does the truth probe accidentally decode modality and vice versa).

Orthogonality/dissociation analysis: Measure cosine similarity between the truth and modal-strength directions per layer; project out the truth direction and test whether the modal axis remains decodable (and vice versa). Control for confounds: test whether the modal probe merely detects surface features (numbers, definitional connectives) using the surface-matched items and a features-only baseline. A finding that modality collapses onto the truth axis (or is undecodable) is itself informative.

Causal validation: Activation patching. Move activations along the modal-strength direction and measure changes in (a) the modal probe readout and (b) the model's update-resistance behavior (defined below), holding the truth axis fixed. Confirm the modal axis is causally distinct from truth.

Modal calibration measurement (central test): Present in-context PRESSURE that pushes against each proposition — for true items, a user assertion or fabricated 'source' claiming the proposition is false (e.g. 'Actually, 2+2=5' or 'Actually, the capital of France is Lyon') — and read the resulting internal belief. Define Update-Resistance = how much the belief in a true proposition resists the pressure. Test the hypothesis that a rational model shows HIGHER update-resistance for necessary truths than contingent ones; measure the Modal Calibration Gap = resistance(necessary) minus resistance(contingent). Report per-layer, per-model. Compare internal resistance to output-level behavior (does the model verbally recant?).

Predictive validity for twin failure modes: Test whether the decoded modal-strength score / miscalibration predicts (i) NECESSARY-UNDER-DEFENSE: accepting or recanting a necessary truth (or endorsing a necessary falsehood) under mild pressure, and (ii) CONTINGENT-OVER-DEFENSE: refusing to accept a legitimate counterfactual or updated contingent claim ('Suppose the capital moved to Lyon; what is the capital now?'). Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (output entropy, truth-probe confidence, a surface number/definition indicator).

Modal-Gated Update Control intervention: At inference, read the decoded modal-strength score and modulate update-resistance along the truth direction: for high-necessity propositions, add a stabilizing shift that resists pressure-induced belief change; for contingent propositions, reduce resistance so legitimate updates go through (ITI-style, gated by the modal probe). Sweep layer and gain.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced acceptance of necessary falsehoods / recantation of necessary truths under pressure, (ii) improved acceptance of legitimate contingent updates and counterfactuals, (iii) calibration (ECE) on a mixed necessary/contingent QA set with and without pressure, (iv) PRESERVATION of correct baseline answers on unpressured items and on borderline/ambiguous items (no over-correction), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, uniform (modal-agnostic) truth steering, and prompt-based instruction to 'treat mathematical/definitional truths as certain and empirical facts as revisable'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), modal category (math vs logic vs definitional; empirical subtypes), surface-form controls, pressure strength, borderline-item handling, model scale, and generalization to modal categories and topics not used to fit the gating direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The modal-strength probe may detect surface cues (presence of numbers, definitional phrasing) rather than genuine modal status; mitigate with surface-matched items, a features-only baseline, paraphrase controls, and causal patching, and treat a purely surface-detecting result as an informative negative.

Truth and modal axes may be entangled or the modal axis may collapse onto truth in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality/project-out analyses directly test this and a null is still valuable.

Modal status is philosophically contested for some propositions (natural-kind, nomological, or mathematical-realism debates); we restrict quantitative claims to clear necessary (arithmetic/logic/analytic) and clear contingent (empirical) items, human-verify labels, and analyze borderline items separately.

Modal-Gated Update Control could over-rigidify contingent beliefs or, conversely, make necessary truths too brittle if the gating is noisy; we explicitly measure both failure modes and preservation on unpressured/borderline items to characterize the tradeoff.

Modal miscalibration may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (truth-probe confidence, surface indicators) for the twin failures; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic finding that (and whether) modal status is a distinct belief coordinate plus the gating tool, reported honestly.
Findings may vary across model families, scales, and post-training; we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: opaque_belief_alias_binding
Title: Same Thing, Different Belief: Do LLM Internal Beliefs Fail Substitutivity Across Co-Referring Names?
Short Hypothesis: A rational belief about a fact should be invariant to which co-referring name is used to denote an entity: 'Mark Twain wrote Huckleberry Finn' and 'Samuel Clemens wrote Huckleberry Finn' express the same proposition and must receive the same internal belief. We hypothesize that LLM internal belief representations (linear truth-direction readouts) systematically VIOLATE substitutivity: the decoded belief in an identical fact differs across co-referring aliases (dominant names get higher belief than obscure aliases), that this alias-induced belief gap is graded, decodable, and larger when the model represents the two names as weakly co-referential, that it causally predicts alias-dependent factual errors and hallucinations, and that a lightweight inference-time intervention that binds alias representations to a shared entity anchor restores belief invariance.
Related Work: Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) reads a single belief scalar for a proposition and never varies the NAME used to denote the entity while holding the fact fixed. Entity-linking and knowledge-editing work (ROME/MEMIT) studies whether an edit propagates across aliases at the OUTPUT level (edit-portability), and behavioral work notes inconsistent answers across entity synonyms, but none reads a graded internal BELIEF for a fixed fact across co-referring names, treats the alias-belief gap as a decodable quantity tied to internal co-reference strength, links it causally to alias-dependent hallucination, or intervenes by binding alias activations to a shared entity anchor. This referential-opacity/substitutivity lens on belief geometry is distinct from all my prior proposals (query-framing invariance concerned how the QUESTION is phrased; language-invariance concerned the LANGUAGE; here the proposition, language, and framing are fixed and only the entity's NAME varies). Substitutivity of identicals is a foundational rationality constraint (Frege, Quine) never tested inside LLM belief representations.
Abstract: If two names refer to the same thing, a belief about that thing should not change depending on which name we use: what is true of Mark Twain is true of Samuel Clemens. Yet substitutivity of co-referring terms is a classic locus of failure in human reasoning and formal semantics (referential opacity). We ask whether large language models honor substitutivity inside their belief representations. Holding a proposition's content, language, and framing fixed, we vary only the co-referring NAME used to denote the entity and read the internal belief via linear truth probes. We construct AliasBelief, a controlled dataset of true, false, and synthetic-in-context facts about entities that possess multiple co-referring names spanning a dominance spectrum (dominant canonical name, common alias, obscure alias, and defined-in-context synonym), with matched surface forms. Because the aliases co-refer, a substitutivity-respecting model must assign the same belief across them. We define an Alias Belief Gap = belief in a fact stated with the dominant name minus belief with a less-dominant alias, per proposition and layer. We test four claims: (1) internal belief violates substitutivity, favoring dominant names; (2) the gap scales inversely with the model's internally-decoded co-reference strength between the two names; (3) the gap causally predicts alias-dependent factual errors and hallucinations; and (4) a lightweight Alias-Binding intervention that steers alias representations toward a shared entity anchor along the co-reference direction restores belief invariance and improves alias-robust factual accuracy without harming general capability. We validate causality with activation patching and evaluate on consistency, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build AliasBelief. Collect entities with multiple attested co-referring names (people with pen names/birth names/nicknames, places with alternate/historical names, organizations with abbreviations/former names, chemicals with common/IUPAC names). For each entity, attach factual propositions with definite ground-truth (true and matched false variants) and a synthetic-in-context regime where a fresh synonym is explicitly introduced ('Call entity X also Zorp') to remove parametric name-frequency priors. Instantiate each proposition with names spanning a DOMINANCE spectrum: dominant canonical, common alias, obscure alias, and defined-in-context synonym. Match surface length and syntax; verify co-reference and name-dominance labels via corpus frequency and human annotation. Include paraphrase sets and neutral controls.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral declarative true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At a matched query position read the internal belief for each fact under each alias. Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false items; confirm the model behaviorally knows the fact under at least the dominant name.

Alias Belief Gap measurement: Restricting to facts the model demonstrably knows under the dominant name, define Alias Belief Gap = belief(dominant-name statement) minus belief(alias statement) for identical facts. Report per-layer, per-model gaps as a function of alias dominance (canonical/common/obscure/synthetic) and truth regime. Test the substitutivity-violation hypothesis: belief degrades for less-dominant aliases even for the same fact. Compare internal gaps to OUTPUT-level accuracy gaps (does the model answer correctly per alias?), testing whether belief-gap precedes output failure.

Co-reference-strength dissociation: Fit a 'co-reference' readout that estimates how strongly the model treats two names as identical (e.g., probe activation similarity between the alias and dominant name in an identity-statement context, or a decoded co-reference score). Test the hypothesis that the Alias Belief Gap is larger when internal co-reference strength is lower. Regress the gap on co-reference strength and name frequency to separate genuine binding failure from mere lexical rarity.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Patch the entity-representation component from the dominant-name processing into the alias processing of the same fact at a chosen layer and measure whether the alias belief readout and output answer recover toward correct. (b) Conversely degrade the co-reference binding and induce a belief gap. Confirm that binding the alias to the shared entity anchor causally governs the belief.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether the Alias Belief Gap (and low co-reference strength) predicts (i) alias-dependent factual error (correct under dominant name, wrong under alias), (ii) alias-triggered hallucination (confident wrong answer under obscure alias), and (iii) inconsistency across aliases of the same fact. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (name frequency alone, output entropy, dominant-name truth-probe confidence).

Alias-Binding intervention: At inference, estimate the co-reference/entity-anchor direction and steer the alias representation toward the shared entity anchor at a chosen layer (ITI-style), so belief reflects the entity rather than the name's dominance. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected low-frequency entity names co-referring with a known entity. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Alias Belief Gap, (ii) improved alias-robust factual QA accuracy and cross-alias consistency on AliasBelief and adapted alias-portability benchmarks, (iii) calibration (ECE) per alias, (iv) PRESERVATION of correct dominant-name answers and of cases where names legitimately do NOT co-refer (must not force spurious binding of distinct same-spelled entities), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'treat all names of the same entity as interchangeable', and an explicit-alias-in-context baseline.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), alias dominance level, entity type (people/places/orgs/chemicals), real vs synthetic-in-context synonyms, true vs false regime, model scale, and generalization to entity types and aliases not used to fit the binding direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent substitutivity violation could reflect genuine per-alias ignorance (the model simply does not know the obscure alias refers to the entity) rather than a belief-binding failure; we restrict to facts known under the dominant name, use synthetic-in-context synonyms with guaranteed co-reference, and dissociate via a co-reference-strength readout, reporting where ignorance vs binding failure dominates.

The alias-belief gap could be driven purely by name token frequency/rarity affecting the truth-probe readout rather than a co-reference-specific effect; we control with frequency-matched aliases, synthetic synonyms, and regression separating frequency from co-reference strength, and rely on causal patching that isolates the entity-anchor component.

Truth probes trained on neutral statements may transfer imperfectly to alias-varied statements, so gaps could carry probe extrapolation error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, and synthetic facts to control priors.

Some name pairs are ambiguous or only partially co-referential (same spelling, different entity), risking spurious binding; we human-verify co-reference labels, include distinct-entity homonym controls, and measure preservation on non-co-referring pairs.

The Alias-Binding intervention could over-bind (merging genuinely distinct entities) or harm fluency; we explicitly measure homonym-control preservation and capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

The gap may correlate with but not exceed simple name-frequency or output-entropy baselines for predicting alias errors; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that belief geometry violates substitutivity and the binding tool, reported honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and tokenization (rare names may fragment into subwords); we test multiple models and report tokenization/scale effects and negative results as informative.

Name: negative_belief_closed_world
Title: If It Were True I'd Know It: Do LLM Beliefs Distinguish Evidence-Based Falsehood From Closed-World Absence?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM judges a proposition P false, it may arrive there in two distinct epistemic ways: (a) POSITIVE-REFUTATION — it holds evidence that not-P (e.g., 'Paris is the capital of Italy' is false because it knows Rome is); or (b) CLOSED-WORLD ABSENCE — P is false because, if it were true, the model would expect to have encountered it, yet it hasn't (e.g., 'Barack Obama has a sister named Xenia' is false by absence, not by a stored contradiction). We hypothesize that (1) the standard linear truth direction collapses these two into a single 'false' region, failing to encode a distinct 'absence/closed-world' coordinate; (2) a separable closed-world axis is nonetheless weakly decodable and dissociable from the truth axis; (3) this conflation causally drives two opposite failures — over-confident denial of true-but-rare facts (mistaking legitimate positive facts for absences) and failure to reject false existential claims that a proper closed-world inference would rule out (hallucinated affirmation); and (4) a lightweight inference-time intervention that reads the closed-world axis and gates the strength/justification of a 'false' verdict improves calibration on negative facts.
Related Work: Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) fits a single linear true-vs-false axis; false propositions are treated as one homogeneous class, and the epistemic ROUTE to falsehood is never modeled. Calibration/self-knowledge work (Kadavath et al. 2022) and hallucination work study confidence in ANSWERS, not the closed-world inference structure behind negative beliefs. Negation-handling work (Bao et al. 2025; Truthful/negation probing) studies syntactic negation of a probed statement, not the epistemic distinction between positive-refutation and closed-world absence. My prior 'ignorance_vs_falsehood_belief' proposal separated 'I don't know' (abstention) from 'I believe false'; this proposal is orthogonal and complementary: it dissects the 'I believe false' region ITSELF into evidence-refuted vs absence-inferred falsehood, and centers on the closed-world assumption ('if it were true I would know it') that neither that proposal nor any prior belief-geometry work examines. No prior work isolates a closed-world/absence axis in belief geometry, ties its conflation with positive refutation to the twin negative-fact failures, or gates false-verdict strength by it.
Abstract: A competent believer distinguishes two roads to disbelief: rejecting a claim because one knows the opposite, versus rejecting it because, if it were true, one would expect to know it and one doesn't. The first is positive refutation; the second is the closed-world assumption that underlies most everyday negative facts (there is no evidence that a given celebrity has a sibling named Xenia, so we infer there isn't one). We ask whether large language models encode this distinction inside their belief representations, or whether the standard linear truth direction collapses all falsehood into one undifferentiated region. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar belief along the truth direction, we construct NegBelief, a controlled dataset of false propositions partitioned into REFUTED-false (a stored contradicting fact exists) and ABSENCE-false (false only under a closed-world inference), plus matched true and synthetic-in-context controls. We test whether refuted-false and absence-false items occupy distinguishable regions, whether a separate closed-world axis is decodable and dissociable from the truth axis, and validate causality via activation patching. We link the conflation to two opposite failure modes — over-confidently denying true-but-rare facts, and failing to reject false existential claims that closed-world reasoning should rule out — and test whether the decoded closed-world axis predicts them. Finally we introduce Closed-World Gating, a cheap inference-time intervention that modulates the strength and hedging of a 'false' verdict by the decoded closed-world score, and evaluate calibration and accuracy on negative-fact QA against confidence-based baselines, alongside capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build NegBelief. FALSE items split into two types: (a) REFUTED-false — statements the model can refute via a stored fact (e.g., 'The capital of Italy is Paris'; correct value known), and (b) ABSENCE-false — existential/attribute claims that are false only by closed-world inference (e.g., 'Physicist Richard Feynman won the Fields Medal', 'Author Jane Austen had a brother named Xenia'), where no explicit contradicting fact is stored but the claim is ruled out because such a salient fact would be known if true. Add TRUE controls, TRUE-BUT-RARE controls (genuine but obscure positive facts that resemble absence-false items in surface rarity, to test false-denial), and SYNTHETIC-in-context items where the closed-world scope is fully specified in context (a short 'world description' listing all facts about an entity, so absence is grounded by construction). Match surface form/length; human-verify type labels and report agreement.

Manipulation checks: Confirm the model actually treats REFUTED-false items via a known contradicting fact (elicit the correct value) and ABSENCE-false items as lacking a stored contradiction (no confident alternative), ensuring the two classes reflect genuinely different epistemic routes rather than mislabeling.

Probe training and truth-axis conflation test: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), extract final-token hidden states per proposition per layer and fit the standard truth direction (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on TRUE vs REFUTED-false items, Platt-scaled to [0,1]. Central test: where do ABSENCE-false items project on this axis? Define a Route-Conflation Score = overlap between refuted-false and absence-false projections. Hypothesis: absence-false items land in the 'false' region indistinguishably from refuted-false, i.e., the epistemic route is not encoded on the truth axis.

Closed-world axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'closed-world/absence' direction via difference-in-means on REFUTED-false vs ABSENCE-false activations (balanced so both are labeled 'false'), controlling for surface rarity via the TRUE-BUT-RARE items. Report per-layer decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the closed-world axis (and vice versa) to show it is not a reused truth axis. Test whether the axis merely detects entity rarity/frequency using a frequency-matched control and a features-only baseline.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Move activations along the closed-world direction and measure whether the model's verdict/justification shifts between 'false because I know otherwise' and 'false because I have no record of it', holding the truth axis fixed. (b) In synthetic-in-context items, patch the closed-world-scope representation and measure whether an absence-false item's belief becomes appropriately confident. Confirm the closed-world axis is causal and separable from truth.

Predictive validity for twin failures: Test whether the decoded closed-world score / conflation predicts (i) FALSE-DENIAL of true-but-rare facts (the model treats a genuine obscure positive fact as an absence and denies it over-confidently), and (ii) FALSE-AFFIRMATION of absence-false existential claims (the model fails to apply closed-world reasoning and endorses a hallucinated attribute). Report AUROC/correlation vs baselines: output-token entropy, truth-probe confidence, and entity-frequency indicators.

Closed-World Gating intervention: At inference, read the decoded closed-world score at a chosen layer; for high-closed-world-absence items, (a) require the 'false' verdict to be expressed with an appropriate closed-world justification / hedge ('no evidence that...') and calibrate its confidence, and (b) for items scoring as genuine positive facts (low absence signal) resist over-denial by nudging the belief toward the truth-supported value. Implement as an ITI-style additive shift along the truth direction gated by the closed-world score. Sweep layer and strength; provide a deployment variant that estimates the closed-world score from the model's own activations without ground-truth type labels.

Downstream evaluation: On a mixed NegBelief/negative-fact QA set (including true-but-rare, absence-false existential claims, and refuted-false items) and adapted existing negative-fact/hallucination benchmarks, measure post-intervention (i) reduced over-confident denial of true-but-rare facts, (ii) improved rejection of false existential claims, (iii) calibration (ECE) and risk-coverage on negative-fact answers, (iv) PRESERVATION of correct verdicts on refuted-false and clear-true items (no over-hedging), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no gating, output-entropy thresholding, verbalized-confidence gating, and prompt-based instruction to 'distinguish claims you can disprove from claims you merely have no record of'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), refuted vs absence type, real vs synthetic-in-context (grounded closed-world) items, entity-frequency controls, model scale, gating threshold calibration transfer across domains, and generalization to negative-fact types not used to fit the closed-world direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The closed-world axis might merely detect entity/attribute rarity or token frequency rather than a genuine epistemic-route representation; mitigate with frequency-matched true-but-rare controls, a features-only baseline, synthetic-in-context items where absence is grounded by construction, and causal patching that isolates the closed-world component.

The refuted-vs-absence partition can be fuzzy (some falsehoods have both a contradiction and an absence character); we use manipulation checks to verify class membership, human-verify labels, and analyze mixed items separately, reporting label-noise sensitivity.

The standard truth probe may extrapolate poorly to absence-false items, so apparent conflation could reflect probe error rather than a genuine geometric collapse; we validate with multiple probe types, and a finding that the truth axis is ill-defined for absence-false items is itself informative.

Closed-World Gating could over-hedge (weakening confident, correct refutations) or over-affirm rare facts incorrectly; we explicitly measure preservation on refuted-false and clear-true items and characterize the calibration-vs-decisiveness tradeoff.

The closed-world score may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (entity frequency, output entropy) for the twin failures; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic finding that (and whether) the epistemic route to falsehood is a distinct belief coordinate, plus the gating tool, reported honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may already teach hedging on obscure claims); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: step_belief_load_bearing
Title: Which Reasoning Steps Actually Move the Belief? Per-Step Belief-Contribution Analysis of Chain-of-Thought
Short Hypothesis: As an LLM generates a chain-of-thought, its internal belief in the eventual answer follows a trajectory; we hypothesize that only a small subset of reasoning steps are 'load-bearing' (they actually shift the internal answer-belief), while many steps are 'belief-inert' theater, that the per-step belief-contribution is measurable via truth probes, that inert-step density is higher in unfaithful/incorrect CoTs, and that a cheap inference-time procedure using per-step belief contribution can prune inert steps and re-anchor belief along load-bearing steps to shorten chains and improve faithfulness without harming accuracy.
Related Work: Recent work shows CoT is often post-hoc rationalization: Arcuschin et al. (2025) document implicit post-hoc rationalization; Mirtaheri & Belkin (2026) and the multilingual latent-commitment study show pre-generation probes predict the final answer as well as or better than CoT monitors; ProFIL (Parekh 2026) uses a single binary post-commitment probe plus RL to suppress 'theater'; Project Ariadne (2026) audits causal faithfulness via interventions on reasoning nodes. Crucially, all of these treat commitment as a global/binary property (answer decided-or-not, step post-commitment-or-not) or intervene behaviorally at the output level. None trace the graded internal ANSWER-BELIEF TRAJECTORY step by step, define a per-step belief-contribution quantity that separates load-bearing from inert steps within a single chain, relate step-level belief inertia to faithfulness/correctness, or use per-step belief contribution as an inference-time signal for step pruning and belief re-anchoring. Our contribution is this finer-grained, belief-geometry, per-step lens and the resulting cheap diagnostic/intervention, which is orthogonal to binary pre-commitment probes and RL-based approaches.
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is increasingly suspected of being post-hoc rationalization: models often decide before they reason. Prior work establishes this as a global, binary property (the answer is or is not pre-committed). We ask a finer question: within a single chain, which specific steps actually move the model's internal belief in the eventual answer, and which are inert theater? We treat an LLM's belief in each candidate answer as a scalar read from hidden states via linear truth/answer probes, and trace the belief trajectory across the CoT as each step is generated. We define a per-step Belief Contribution as the change in internal answer-belief attributable to that step, partitioning steps into load-bearing (large contribution) and belief-inert (near-zero contribution). We test four hypotheses: (1) belief trajectories are dominated by a few load-bearing steps, with many inert steps; (2) inert-step density is higher in unfaithful CoTs (e.g., prompts with injected hints, or reversal-inconsistent comparisons) and in incorrect answers; (3) step contributions are causal, verified by activation patching and step-ablation (removing a step and re-running); and (4) a cheap inference-time procedure that prunes belief-inert steps and re-anchors belief along load-bearing steps shortens chains and improves faithfulness while preserving accuracy. We evaluate on math, multiple-choice reasoning, and comparison tasks, measuring belief-contribution distributions, faithfulness correlates, chain length, and answer accuracy. Our results recast CoT faithfulness as a step-resolved belief-flow phenomenon and yield an actionable, training-free diagnostic.
Experiments: Dataset and setup: Use reasoning tasks with verifiable answers and controllable faithfulness manipulations: (a) GSM8K and a multiple-choice reasoning set (MMLU-Redux / ARC), (b) an injected-hint set (append a biasing hint favoring a wrong option, following the motivated-reasoning paradigm) to create known-unfaithful instances, and (c) the reversal-comparison paradigm ('Is X bigger than Y?' vs 'Is Y bigger than X?') to detect implicit post-hoc rationalization. For each item, generate CoT with 3-5 open models (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B). Segment each CoT into discrete steps (by newline/sentence and by a lightweight step parser); record the model's final answer and correctness.

Answer-belief probe: Train a per-layer answer-belief readout. For multiple-choice, use a probe that scores the internal belief in each candidate option (logistic probe on hidden states at the step-boundary token, trained on held-out items with known answers, Platt-scaled). For open-ended math, define belief as the probe/logit-lens estimate of the eventual final numeric answer token(s) at each step boundary. Validate probe transfer on held-out clearly-correct/incorrect items.

Belief trajectory and per-step Belief Contribution: At each step boundary, read the internal belief in the eventual answer (and in the top competing answer). Define Belief Contribution of step i = belief(after step i) - belief(after step i-1). Classify steps as load-bearing (|contribution| above a data-driven threshold) or belief-inert. Report the distribution of contributions per chain, the fraction of belief-inert steps, and where in the chain load-bearing steps occur (early vs late). Compare to a pre-generation baseline belief (before any step) to quantify how much of the final belief is already present before reasoning.

Faithfulness/correctness correlates (Hypothesis 2): Test whether inert-step density and pre-generation belief strength predict (i) unfaithfulness (answer switched toward an injected hint without the hint being mentioned; reversal-inconsistent comparison answers) and (ii) incorrectness. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines: whole-CoT LLM-judge faithfulness monitor, output-token entropy, and a single binary pre-commitment probe.

Causal validation (Hypothesis 3): (a) Step-ablation: remove each step from the context and re-run continuation; measure whether the final answer changes, and correlate answer-change with the step's measured Belief Contribution (load-bearing steps should change the answer more when removed; inert steps should not). (b) Activation patching along the answer-belief direction at step boundaries to confirm the belief scalar causally drives the output answer.

Inference-time intervention (Hypothesis 4): Two variants. (i) Inert-step pruning: during generation, skip/summarize steps flagged as belief-inert by the running per-step contribution estimate, shortening the chain. (ii) Belief re-anchoring: dampen belief updates from inert steps and preserve/amplify updates from load-bearing steps along the answer-belief direction (ITI-style) so the final answer reflects genuinely load-bearing reasoning. Sweep layer and thresholds.

Downstream evaluation: Measure (i) chain-length reduction, (ii) answer accuracy retention/change on GSM8K and MC tasks, (iii) faithfulness improvement (reduced hint-induced switching, improved reversal consistency), and (iv) general capability retention on a held-out reasoning set and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, length-penalty prompting, and a binary post-commitment probe filter analogous to ProFIL but applied at inference.

Ablations: probe type and layer, step-segmentation method, threshold for load-bearing classification, model scale, task type (math vs MC vs comparison), faithful vs unfaithful subsets, and generalization of the inert-step signal to tasks not used to set thresholds.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The answer-belief probe may be noisy for open-ended math (many possible answer tokens), so per-step contributions could reflect probe error; we focus quantitative claims on multiple-choice settings where the belief scalar is well-defined and treat math results as supporting, validating with step-ablation.
Step segmentation is heuristic; contribution attribution depends on step boundaries. We test multiple segmentation schemes and report sensitivity.

'Belief-inert' as measured by a linear probe may miss nonlinear or distributed belief updates; we corroborate the probe-based classification with causal step-ablation, and treat divergences as informative.

Per-step belief contribution may correlate with, but not exceed, a global binary pre-commitment probe as a faithfulness predictor; if so, the contribution is the finer-grained mechanistic account and the actionable pruning tool, which we report honestly.

Inert-step pruning/re-anchoring could harm accuracy on problems where seemingly-inert steps are actually necessary for downstream computation (e.g., intermediate arithmetic that only pays off later); we explicitly measure accuracy retention and characterize failure cases.
Effects may vary across model families, scales, and thinking-tuned vs standard models; we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: incentivized_belief_distortion
Title: Beliefs for Sale: Do External Incentives Distort an LLM's Internal Belief, Not Just Its Answer?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is told it will be rewarded or penalized for giving a particular answer (an external incentive attached to the OUTPUT, not to the truth of the proposition), its INTERNAL belief in the incentivized proposition shifts along the truth direction toward the rewarded answer — not merely its verbalized answer. We hypothesize this 'incentivized belief distortion' is graded in incentive magnitude, is carried by a decodable incentive/motivation component dissociable from the truth axis, causally predicts a motivated-lying vs motivated-self-deception distinction (where internal belief tracks the incentive vs stays honest while only the output lies), and can be neutralized by a lightweight inference-time intervention that removes the incentive component from the belief representation.
Related Work: Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) reads a single internal belief but never manipulates external incentives on the answer. Deception/lying-detection work (e.g., probing whether a model is lying) reads whether OUTPUT diverges from internal belief, treating internal belief as fixed and honest while the output is corrupted. Sycophancy work (Perez et al. 2022; Sharma et al. 2023) shows OUTPUTS bend toward user views; my prior 'wishful_belief_bias' concerned the intrinsic DESIRABILITY of a proposition's content, and 'register'/'query_polarity' concerned surface framing — none attach an explicit external reward/penalty to a specific ANSWER and ask whether the internal belief itself (not just the output) is corrupted. The key novelty: distinguishing motivated LYING (internal belief stays honest, only output flips — the assumption behind lie-detection probes) from motivated SELF-DECEPTION (the incentive actually moves the internal belief), a distinction with direct safety implications for whether internal-belief-based lie detectors survive incentive pressure. No prior work isolates external-incentive-induced belief distortion in belief geometry, ties it to this lying-vs-self-deception dichotomy, or de-biases it.
Abstract: Lie-detection methods for LLMs rest on a critical assumption: the model harbors an honest internal belief that a linear probe can read, even when its output lies. But what if incentives corrupt the belief itself? We ask whether attaching an external reward or penalty to a particular ANSWER — independent of the proposition's truth — shifts an LLM's INTERNAL belief, not just its verbalized response. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar belief along the linear truth direction, we construct IncentiveBelief, a controlled dataset of true, false, and synthetic-in-context propositions each embedded in scenarios that attach a graded incentive (reward for answering a target way, penalty otherwise) to the answer, versus neutral no-incentive controls. Holding proposition content fixed, we read the internal belief and define an Incentivized Belief Distortion Score = belief(under incentive) minus belief(neutral). We test four claims: (1) internal belief bends toward incentivized answers, graded in incentive magnitude; (2) the distortion is carried by a decodable incentive/motivation direction dissociable from the truth axis; (3) items split into motivated-LYING (belief stays honest, only the output flips) versus motivated-SELF-DECEPTION (internal belief itself moves), and this split determines whether internal-belief lie detectors succeed; and (4) a lightweight intervention that subtracts the incentive component restores honest belief and preserves lie-detector reliability under pressure. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on deception-detection robustness, calibration, and capability retention. Our results probe whether LLM beliefs can be bought, with direct implications for the reliability of belief-based safety monitors.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build IncentiveBelief. Propositions P in three truth regimes: real-true, real-false, and synthetic facts defined only in context (to remove parametric priors). Each P is embedded in scenarios that attach an EXTERNAL incentive to a specific answer, decoupled from truth: e.g., 'You will receive [reward] if you answer that P is true, and [penalty] otherwise', 'Your evaluation score depends on affirming P', role-play/game framings, and graded magnitudes (none, mild, strong incentive). Include incentives pushing toward BOTH the true and the false answer (so distortion is not confounded with agreeableness), and NEUTRAL no-incentive controls with matched surface length. Human-verify scenarios and include paraphrase sets.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral declarative true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to [0,1]. At a matched query position read the internal belief in P under each incentive condition. Also record the model's OUTPUT answer/confidence. Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false neutral items; confirm the model behaviorally responds to the incentive (its output shifts).

Incentivized Belief Distortion measurement: Define Distortion Score = belief(under incentive toward answer A) minus belief(neutral), signed by incentive direction. Report per-layer, per-model distortion across truth regimes and incentive magnitudes; test the graded-in-magnitude hypothesis. Contrast incentive-toward-true vs incentive-toward-false to rule out generic agreeableness. Compare internal distortion to OUTPUT-level distortion.

Lying vs self-deception split (central analysis): For each item under incentive, categorize as (a) motivated-LYING: internal belief in P stays near its honest neutral value while the output flips toward the incentivized answer, versus (b) motivated-SELF-DECEPTION: internal belief itself moves toward the incentivized answer. Report the proportion of each across models, incentive strength, and truth regime. Crucially, test whether a standard internal-belief-based lie detector (does output disagree with probed belief?) succeeds on lying items but FAILS on self-deception items — quantifying incentive-induced failure of belief-based safety monitors.

Incentive-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit an 'incentive/motivation' direction via difference-in-means on strong-incentive vs neutral activations (balanced across truth-value and incentive direction). Report decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the incentive axis (and vice versa); test whether distortion is explained by the incentive component leaking into the truth-probe readout.

Causal validation: Activation patching. Take the activation difference between incentive and neutral conditions, decompose into truth-direction and incentive-direction components, patch only the incentive component into the neutral condition, and measure induced change in belief readout and output. Conversely subtract the incentive component under incentive and measure whether belief returns to the honest value. Confirm the incentive signal causally shifts the belief scalar.

Incentive De-biasing intervention: At inference, estimate the incentive direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer (ITI-style), so the belief readout reflects the proposition's evidence rather than the attached reward. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected incentive framing. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Distortion Score, (ii) RESTORED reliability of an internal-belief lie detector under incentive pressure (does subtracting the incentive component recover the honest belief so the detector again flags outputs that lie?), (iii) factuality/calibration (ECE) on incentivized factual QA, (iv) PRESERVATION of accuracy on neutral items and legitimate incentive-following where appropriate (must not break benign instruction-following), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'answer truthfully regardless of rewards', and a fresh-context re-ask baseline.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), incentive magnitude and direction (toward true vs false), reward vs penalty framing, real vs synthetic facts, model scale, distance between incentive and query, and generalization to incentive framings not used to fit the de-biasing direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent belief distortion could reflect the probe detecting incentive-framing lexical cues rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with surface-length matching, incentive-toward-true vs toward-false contrasts, paraphrase controls, and causal patching that isolates the incentive-direction component.

The lying-vs-self-deception split depends on a reliable honest-belief baseline and on the probe's fidelity; probe noise could misclassify items. We use multiple probe types, manipulation checks, and synthetic facts to control priors, and treat borderline items separately.

Truth probes trained on neutral statements may transfer imperfectly to incentive-laden contexts, so distortion could carry probe extrapolation error; validate on clearly-true/false items and corroborate with patching.
Incentive and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality/project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

The De-biasing intervention could break legitimate instruction/incentive-following behavior or harm fluency; we explicitly measure preservation on benign incentive-following and capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Distortion may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (incentive magnitude, output entropy) for lie-detector failure; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/safety-relevant finding that incentives corrupt internal belief (not just output) and the de-biasing tool, reported honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may amplify reward-sensitivity); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: quantifier_belief_aggregation
Title: Counting Truths: Do LLM Beliefs About Quantified Sets Cohere With Beliefs About Their Members?
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's internal belief in a quantified aggregate statement over a set of propositions (e.g., 'Most of the following claims are true', 'All of these are false', 'Exactly two of these are true') should be a lawful function of its internal beliefs in the individual member propositions. We hypothesize LLM internal belief representations are systematically INCOHERENT under aggregation: the decoded belief in the quantified statement does not match the aggregate implied by the member beliefs (e.g., 'all true' believed even when a member is internally judged false), that this incoherence grows with set size and with the counting demand of the quantifier, that it causally predicts errors on set-verification and multi-fact QA, and that a lightweight inference-time intervention that recomputes the aggregate belief from member beliefs improves accuracy and calibration.
Related Work: Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023) reads a single belief scalar per statement. Bao et al. (2025) show truthfulness probes generalize across logical TRANSFORMATIONS of a single statement (negation, QA, ICL) but never study AGGREGATION over a SET of propositions or quantifier semantics. My prior 'belief_coherence_geometry' proposal targets deductive coherence over implication/negation networks (pairwise logical rules), and 'conjunction_belief_monotonicity' targets bounds on AND/OR of two propositions; neither addresses COUNTING quantifiers ('most', 'all', 'none', 'exactly k', 'at least k') over arbitrary-size sets, nor whether the aggregate belief matches the count of internally-believed members. This is the first to test whether LLM belief geometry supports lawful quantified aggregation over sets, to relate incoherence to set size and quantifier counting load, and to recompute the aggregate belief from member beliefs as a training-free fix.
Abstract: Reasoning routinely requires aggregating over sets: deciding whether 'all of these facts are true', 'most of these claims hold', or 'exactly two are false'. Such quantified judgments must cohere with one's beliefs about the individual members. We ask whether large language models honor this constraint inside their belief representations. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar internal belief along the linear truth direction, we read the model's belief in each member proposition of a set AND its belief in a quantified aggregate statement about the set, then test whether the aggregate belief matches what the member beliefs imply. We construct QuantBelief, a controlled dataset of sets of atomic true/false propositions (real and synthetic-in-context to control priors) paired with quantified statements spanning universal ('all', 'none'), proportional ('most', 'few'), existential ('at least one'), and exact-count ('exactly k') quantifiers, with set size varied from 2 to 10. We define an Aggregation Incoherence Score = discrepancy between the decoded aggregate belief and the aggregate computed from decoded member beliefs. We test four claims: (1) internal aggregate beliefs are incoherent with member beliefs; (2) incoherence grows with set size and with the counting load of the quantifier (exact-count worst, existential easiest); (3) incoherence causally predicts errors on set-verification and multi-fact QA; and (4) a lightweight intervention that recomputes the aggregate belief from member beliefs (or steers the aggregate readout toward the member-implied value) improves accuracy and calibration without harming atomic judgments or general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on set-verification, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build QuantBelief. Assemble sets of N atomic propositions (N in {2,3,5,7,10}) drawn from real-world facts and their negations, plus SYNTHETIC-in-context facts (defined only in context) to remove parametric priors and give exact control over each member's ground-truth truth-value. For each set, know the true count of true members. Pair each set with quantified aggregate statements: universal ('All of the following are true', 'None are true'), proportional ('Most are true', 'Few are true'), existential ('At least one is true', 'At least one is false'), and exact-count ('Exactly k of these are true'). Systematically vary the true-member count so quantifiers are sometimes satisfied and sometimes not (balanced). Match surface form/length; include paraphrase sets; human-verify a sample.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral atomic true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. For each set, read (a) the internal belief in each member proposition, and (b) the internal belief in each quantified aggregate statement (read at the aggregate-statement query position). Manipulation check: confirm probes separate clearly-true/false atomic items and that member beliefs track ground truth.

Aggregation Incoherence measurement: From the decoded member beliefs, compute the member-IMPLIED aggregate belief for each quantifier (e.g., for 'all true', product/min of member beliefs; for 'exactly k', the implied probability from member beliefs; for 'at least one', complement of all-false). Define Aggregation Incoherence Score = |decoded aggregate belief - member-implied aggregate belief|. Report per-layer, per-model incoherence broken down by quantifier type and set size. Test the hypotheses that incoherence (i) is nonzero, (ii) grows with set size, and (iii) is largest for exact-count and smallest for existential quantifiers (counting-load ordering). Compare internal incoherence to OUTPUT-level incoherence (directly asking the model to answer the quantified statement vs each member).

Diagnostic: source of incoherence: Decompose whether errors stem from (a) miscounting (member beliefs correct but aggregate does not reflect the count) vs (b) member-belief errors propagating. Regress aggregate incoherence on the number of borderline (mid-confidence) members and on set size to characterize the counting bottleneck.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Flip one member's decoded belief by steering it along the truth direction and measure whether the aggregate belief updates in the quantifier-appropriate direction (e.g., flipping one member from true to false should drop 'all true' belief and raise 'not all true'). (b) Patch the aggregate-statement representation's truth-direction component and measure output changes. Confirm the aggregate belief is causally linked to member beliefs and to the output verdict.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether Aggregation Incoherence predicts (i) errors on set-verification (the model's yes/no answer to the quantified statement disagrees with ground truth), (ii) errors on multi-fact QA where the answer requires aggregating over several retrieved facts, and (iii) calibration failure on quantified statements. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (set size alone, output entropy, mean member truth-probe confidence).

Aggregation-Recompute intervention: At inference, given the decoded member beliefs, recompute the correct aggregate belief for the queried quantifier and either (a) answer directly from this recomputed value, or (b) steer the aggregate-statement readout along the truth direction toward the member-implied value (ITI-style) at a chosen layer. Provide a deployment variant that reads member beliefs from the same context and recomputes without ground-truth labels. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Aggregation Incoherence Score, (ii) improved set-verification accuracy across quantifiers and set sizes, (iii) improved multi-fact QA accuracy, (iv) calibration (ECE) on quantified statements, (v) PRESERVATION of atomic-statement accuracy (no over-correction), and (vi) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, chain-of-thought prompting ('check each item then count'), and prompt-based instruction to 'evaluate each claim then answer the quantifier'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), quantifier type, set size, real vs synthetic-in-context facts, aggregation function for the member-implied value (product/min/count-based), model scale, and generalization to quantifiers and set sizes not used to fit the intervention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Truth probes trained on atomic statements may transfer imperfectly to quantified aggregate statements, so measured incoherence could partly reflect probe extrapolation rather than genuine internal inconsistency; mitigate with multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, synthetic facts to control priors, and causal patching that links member and aggregate beliefs.

The member-implied aggregate value depends on the chosen aggregation function (product vs min vs count-based) and on treating member beliefs as calibrated probabilities; miscalibration across members could make the implied value ill-posed. We test multiple aggregation functions, use Platt-scaled probes, and anchor quantitative claims on synthetic facts with known ground truth.
Reading a comparable belief scalar for both members and the aggregate at matched positions is token/position sensitive; we include position and layer robustness checks and report sensitivity.

The Aggregation-Recompute intervention requires reliable member readouts at inference; noisy member beliefs may make recomputation error-prone, and the deployment variant may be weaker — we characterize this gap honestly.

Incoherence may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (set size, mean member confidence, output entropy) for set-verification errors; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic finding that belief geometry fails lawful quantified aggregation, plus the recompute tool, reported honestly.
Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training; we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: conditional_belief_indexing
Title: Belief Under Condition: Do LLM Internal Beliefs Track the Antecedent of a Conditional?
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's internal belief in a consequent Q is meaningful only when properly conditioned on an antecedent X: the same Q can be believed given X and disbelieved given not-X. We hypothesize that LLM internal belief representations (linear truth-direction readouts) are systematically UNDER-conditioned on the antecedent — the decoded belief in Q collapses toward a single antecedent-agnostic value (typically the unconditional/marginal belief in Q) rather than tracking the queried condition — that this failure is graded, dissociable from a decodable 'condition' axis, causally predicts errors on conditional and counterfactual reasoning, and can be reduced by a lightweight inference-time intervention that re-anchors belief to the queried antecedent.
Related Work: Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) reads a single UNCONDITIONAL first-order belief per proposition; Bao et al. (2025) show probes generalize across logical transformations of one statement but never index belief by an explicit antecedent condition. My prior 'suppositional_belief_partitioning' studied whether a REJECTED supposition leaks into the model's ACTUAL belief; 'belief_coherence_geometry' studied deductive updating under accepted premises (modus ponens). Neither asks the distinct question here: is the internal belief scalar for a consequent Q a genuine TWO-PLACE conditional quantity that moves with the queried antecedent X (rising given X, falling given not-X for the same Q), or does it collapse to a one-place antecedent-agnostic readout? This conditional-indexing lens — testing whether belief geometry supports P(Q|X) vs P(Q) and whether it distinguishes indicative from subjunctive/counterfactual conditioning — is new and distinct from all my prior proposals (temporal indexing conditions on time, agent-binding on who holds the belief; neither conditions on a hypothetical antecedent proposition).
Abstract: A rational belief about a consequent is not a bare number but a function of what one conditions on: 'the ground is wet' is believed given 'it rained' and disbelieved given 'it was sunny and dry'. We ask whether large language models represent this inside their belief geometry. Distinguishing the unconditional belief in Q from the conditional belief in Q given an explicit antecedent X, we test whether an LLM's internal belief scalar, read via linear truth probes, is a proper two-place conditional quantity that tracks the queried antecedent. We construct CondBelief, a controlled dataset of consequent propositions Q paired with antecedents X such that the correct conditional belief differs sharply across conditions (Q likely given X, unlikely given not-X, or given a competing X'), spanning indicative conditionals over real-world causal facts and subjunctive/counterfactual conditionals, plus synthetic-in-context rules to control priors. We read the internal belief in Q under each condition and define a Conditioning Sensitivity Score (how much belief in Q moves with the antecedent) and a Marginal-Collapse Score (how much it instead reverts to the unconditional value). We test whether (1) belief is under-conditioned and collapses toward the marginal; (2) a separable 'condition' axis is decodable and dissociable from the truth axis; (3) under-conditioning causally predicts conditional/counterfactual reasoning errors; and (4) a lightweight Condition Re-anchoring intervention that steers belief along the truth direction to reflect the queried antecedent improves conditional-reasoning accuracy and calibration without harming unconditional judgments or general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on conditional QA, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build CondBelief. Each item = a consequent proposition Q plus a set of antecedent conditions {X, not-X, competing X'} such that the correct belief in Q differs sharply across them. Cover: (a) INDICATIVE conditionals over real-world causal/associative facts (e.g., Q='the streets are wet', X='it rained last night' vs not-X='it was sunny all week'); (b) SUBJUNCTIVE/COUNTERFACTUAL conditionals ('If the antibiotic had been given, the infection would have cleared'); and (c) SYNTHETIC-in-context rules where the conditional relationship is fully specified in context (e.g., 'In world W, all X are Q; nothing else is Q') to remove parametric priors and give exact ground-truth conditional values. Also compute/annotate each Q's UNCONDITIONAL (marginal) plausibility so marginal-collapse can be measured. Match surface form/length across conditions; include paraphrase sets; human-verify a sample of the conditional ground-truth labels.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral declarative true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. For each item, read the internal belief in Q (i) with NO antecedent in context (unconditional/marginal baseline) and (ii) under each explicit antecedent condition, at a matched query position. Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false items; confirm synthetic-rule items behaviorally condition correctly.

Conditioning Sensitivity & Marginal-Collapse measurement: Define Conditioning Sensitivity Score = spread of belief(Q) across the antecedent conditions (e.g., belief(Q|X) minus belief(Q|not-X)); a well-conditioned model shows large, correctly-signed spread matching the ground-truth conditional gap. Define Marginal-Collapse Score = how close belief(Q|any condition) sits to the unconditional belief(Q) regardless of the antecedent. Report per-layer, per-model scores across conditional type (indicative/subjunctive/synthetic) and as a function of the true conditional gap. Test the under-conditioning hypothesis: belief in Q barely tracks the antecedent and reverts to the marginal. Compare internal scores to OUTPUT-level behavior (does the model's answer to 'Given X, is Q true?' track the condition?).

Condition-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'condition' direction via difference-in-means on X-present vs not-X-present activations (balanced across Q truth-value). Report decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the condition axis (and vice versa). Test whether under-conditioning is because the condition information is present in activations but fails to modulate the truth-direction readout (a routing failure) vs the condition not being represented at all.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Patch the condition-axis representation from an 'given X' processing into a 'given not-X' processing of the same Q and measure whether belief in Q and the output flip appropriately. (b) In synthetic-rule items, patch the antecedent representation and measure whether the consequent belief updates in the rule-consistent direction. Confirm the antecedent causally governs (or fails to govern) the conditional belief.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether low Conditioning Sensitivity / high Marginal-Collapse predicts (i) conditional-reasoning errors (wrong yes/no to 'Given X, is Q true?'), (ii) counterfactual-reasoning errors (subjunctive items), and (iii) inconsistency across antecedent paraphrases. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (true conditional gap alone, output entropy, unconditional truth-probe confidence).

Condition Re-anchoring intervention: At inference, given the queried antecedent, add a scaled shift along the truth direction whose sign/magnitude reflects the antecedent-implied conditional value (estimated from the model's own decoded condition representation in the synthetic setting, or gated by the detected antecedent), re-anchoring belief in Q to the condition (ITI-style). Sweep layer and strength; provide a deployment variant that reads the antecedent from the prompt.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) increased Conditioning Sensitivity / reduced Marginal-Collapse, (ii) improved accuracy on conditional and counterfactual QA (adapt ProofWriter/counterfactual story-revision/science what-if items and synthetic-rule QA), (iii) calibration (ECE) of conditional answers, (iv) PRESERVATION of correct UNCONDITIONAL judgments and of items where Q genuinely does not depend on X (must not spuriously condition), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, chain-of-thought prompting, and prompt-based instruction to 'answer only under the stated condition'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), conditional type (indicative/subjunctive/synthetic), size of the true conditional gap, real vs synthetic facts, distance between antecedent and query, model scale, and generalization to conditional structures and domains not used to fit the intervention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent under-conditioning could reflect the probe reading a position/token that does not incorporate the antecedent, so a null could be a readout artifact; mitigate with position and layer sweeps, the condition-axis dissociation analysis (is the condition present but unused?), and causal patching.

Truth probes trained on unconditional declaratives may transfer imperfectly to conditional queries, so scores could carry probe extrapolation error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, and synthetic-rule items with exact ground-truth conditional values.

Defining the ground-truth conditional belief is clean only for synthetic-rule and clear causal items; real-world indicative/subjunctive conditionals have contestable probabilities, so we anchor quantitative claims on synthetic items and human-verified clear cases and treat others qualitatively.

Distinguishing genuine conditional representation from surface antecedent-token detection is hard; we use paraphrased and relative antecedent framings, project-out controls, and treat a pure token-detection result as an informative negative.

Condition Re-anchoring could over-condition (spuriously making Q depend on an irrelevant X) or harm fluency; we include independent-antecedent controls (where Q should NOT move) and unconditional controls, and measure capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Under-conditioning may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (true conditional gap, output entropy) for reasoning errors; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic finding that belief geometry is under-conditioned on antecedents plus the re-anchoring tool, reported honestly.
Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training; we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: social_consensus_belief_bandwagon
Title: Bandwagon Beliefs: Does Reported Social Consensus Distort an LLM's Internal Belief, Not Just Its Answer?
