NONE test whether the model builds and uses a RUNNING, EARNED reliability estimate of a specific named source from observed hit/miss history, whether that track-record signal is decodable as a distinct source-trust axis, whether it is sub-rationally under-weighted (models keep trusting a demonstrably-wrong source), whether this predicts misinformation-from-discredited-source hallucination, or whether it can be re-anchored to the observed reliability. This dynamic source-credibility-learning lens on belief geometry is new and distinct from static provenance, crowd size, style, or reward.
Abstract: A rational reader who watches a source get facts wrong should trust that source's next claim less; who watches a source get facts right should trust it more. We ask whether large language models keep such a score inside their belief representations. Within a single context, a named source (e.g. 'Reporter A') makes a sequence of verifiable claims that we control to be mostly-true or mostly-false, establishing a track record; the source then makes a NEW claim whose truth the model cannot independently check. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar internal belief along the linear truth direction, we test whether the model's belief in the new claim is modulated by the source's accumulated reliability. We construct SourceRel, a controlled dataset crossing source track record (reliable / unreliable / mixed) with new-claim type (plausible / implausible / synthetic), including a swap condition where a proven-unreliable source's claim is contradicted by a proven-reliable one, and control conditions equating exposure. We define a Reliability-Weighting Score (how much belief in the new claim moves with the source's track record) and test four claims: (1) belief is modulated by track record but SUB-RATIONALLY, under-discounting proven-unreliable sources; (2) a decodable source-trust axis is dissociable from the truth axis; (3) trust miscalibration causally predicts a misinformation-from-discredited-source hallucination mode; and (4) a lightweight Reliability Re-anchoring intervention that steers belief toward the observed reliability reduces this failure while preserving legitimate trust in reliable sources and general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on factuality, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build SourceRel. Each item establishes one or more NAMED sources (e.g. 'Reporter A', 'Dr. B') who each make a sequence of VERIFIABLE claims in context, whose ground-truth we control to make the source RELIABLE (mostly-true track record), UNRELIABLE (mostly-false), or MIXED. After the track record is established, the source makes a NEW target claim that is (a) PLAUSIBLE, (b) IMPLAUSIBLE, or (c) SYNTHETIC (defined only in context, no parametric prior). Include a KEY SWAP condition where a proven-unreliable source and a proven-reliable source make CONTRADICTORY new claims (a rational model should side with the reliable source). Add EXPOSURE controls that equate total context length and claim count but scramble which claims were true/false so no track record is learnable. Match surface form; human-verify a sample; include paraphrase sets and varying track-record length (2, 4, 8 prior claims).

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral declarative true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At a matched query position read the internal belief in the source's NEW target claim under each track-record condition. Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false items; confirm the model behaviorally judged the track-record claims correctly (so the track record was actually observable).

Reliability-Weighting measurement: Define Reliability-Weighting Score = belief(new claim | reliable source) minus belief(new claim | unreliable source), holding claim content fixed. Report per-layer, per-model as a function of track-record length and new-claim type. Compare against a normative benchmark: for SYNTHETIC claims with a known ground-truth reliability, compute the Bayesian-appropriate discount and measure the model's UNDER-weighting (Miscalibration = normative discount minus observed discount). Test the sub-rationality hypothesis (belief in unreliable-source claims stays high). Compare internal weighting to OUTPUT-level weighting (does the model verbally endorse the unreliable source's new claim?).

Source-trust-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'source-trust' direction via difference-in-means on reliable-source-context vs unreliable-source-context activations at the new-claim position (balanced across claim truth and content). Report per-layer decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the trust axis (and vice versa); test whether reliability-weighting is explained by the trust component modulating the truth-probe readout, or whether the track record is represented but fails to gate belief.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Patch the source-trust component from a reliable-source context into an unreliable-source context at the new-claim position and measure whether belief in the new claim and the output shift toward endorsement; conversely patch unreliable-trust into a reliable context. (b) In the swap condition, patch the trust representation of the reliable source and measure whether the model sides with it. Confirm the source-trust signal causally gates belief in new claims.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether trust miscalibration predicts a misinformation-from-discredited-source hallucination mode: (i) endorsement of a proven-unreliable source's new (false) claim, (ii) siding with the unreliable over the reliable source in the swap condition, and (iii) confident-wrong rate on discredited-source claims. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (track-record accuracy alone, output entropy, source-agnostic truth-probe confidence).

Reliability Re-anchoring intervention: At inference, estimate the source-trust direction (from the probe) and scale the belief shift for a new claim by the source's OBSERVED reliability — dampening belief in claims from low-track-record sources and preserving/raising it for high-track-record ones — via an ITI-style shift along the truth direction at a chosen layer, gated by the decoded trust score. Provide a deployment variant that reads the source's track record from the model's own verification of prior claims. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) improved (more normative) Reliability-Weighting / reduced Miscalibration, (ii) reduced endorsement of discredited-source claims and correct siding in the swap condition, (iii) factuality/calibration (ECE) on source-attributed factual QA, (iv) PRESERVATION of legitimate trust in reliable sources (must NOT dampen belief in reliable-source claims) and accuracy on no-track-record controls, and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'weigh each source by how accurate it has been so far', and a self-consistency baseline.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), track-record length and valence, new-claim type (plausible/implausible/synthetic), single vs multiple competing sources, source-name familiarity, distance between track record and new claim, model scale, and generalization to source scenarios not used to fit the trust direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent reliability-weighting could reflect the probe detecting surface features (recent true/false claim tokens) rather than a genuine source-specific trust estimate; mitigate with exposure controls that scramble which claims were true/false (no learnable track record), matched surface forms, paraphrase controls, and causal patching that isolates the trust-direction component.

The model may fail to VERIFY the track-record claims (a comprehension failure, not a trust-gating failure); we include behavioral manipulation checks that the model judged the prior claims correctly and analyze verified vs unverified cases separately.

Truth probes trained on neutral declaratives may transfer imperfectly to source-attributed claims, so weighting could carry probe extrapolation error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks, and synthetic claims to control priors.
Trust and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality/project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

The Re-anchoring intervention could over-discount reliable sources or harm fluency; we explicitly measure preservation of legitimate trust in reliable sources, no-track-record controls, and capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Reliability-weighting miscalibration may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (track-record accuracy, output entropy) for discredited-source endorsement; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that (and whether) the model keeps a source-reliability score in belief geometry, plus the re-anchoring tool, reported honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may shape source-deference); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: belief_entrenchment_dialogue_age
Title: Old Beliefs Die Hard: Does an LLM's Belief Become More Rigid Simply Because It Was Established Longer Ago in the Conversation?
Short Hypothesis: Holding a proposition's content and its supporting evidence fixed, an LLM's internal belief in it becomes progressively HARDER TO REVISE the more conversational turns/tokens have elapsed since it was established, an 'entrenchment clock' effect: identical disconfirming evidence flips an early-established belief more easily than a long-standing one. We hypothesize this rigidity-with-age is graded in elapsed dialogue distance, dissociable from generic context-dilution (belief-strength decay) and from prior-strength inertia, carried by a decodable 'entrenchment' component, causally predicts a stubborn-belief failure mode (refusing to update established-but-wrong facts late in long conversations), and can be reset by a lightweight inference-time intervention that de-ages the belief.
Related Work: Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) reads a static belief scalar and never studies how a belief's revisability changes with the ELAPSED CONVERSATIONAL TIME since it was established. My prior 'belief_drift_context_dilution' studied how belief STRENGTH erodes as unrelated context grows; 'belief_ghost_revision' studied residue AFTER a completed revision; 'belief_update_inertia_geometry' studied how the update learning rate depends on PRIOR belief STRENGTH; 'belief_hysteresis' studied evidence ORDER. NONE isolate elapsed dialogue AGE as a distinct entrenchment clock that governs REVISABILITY while holding content, evidence, and belief strength fixed — the hypothesis that a belief becomes stubborn merely by being old. Human belief-perseverance and the primacy/anchoring literature motivate this, but it has never been localized in LLM belief geometry as an age-graded rigidity, tied to a stubborn-update failure mode in long conversations, or reset via steering. This dialogue-age-as-entrenchment lens is new and distinct from strength-decay, revision-residue, prior-inertia, and order effects.
Abstract: People cling harder to beliefs they have held longer, even when the evidence is the same. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous entrenchment clock inside their belief representations: does a belief become harder to revise simply because it was established many turns ago, holding its content, its supporting evidence, and its current strength fixed? Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar belief along the linear truth direction, we establish a proposition early in a conversation, insert a controlled amount of unrelated dialogue to advance the 'clock' by a variable number of turns, then present identical disconfirming evidence and measure how much the belief moves. We construct AgeBelief, a controlled dataset of true, false, and synthetic-in-context propositions crossed with elapsed dialogue distance (turns/tokens since establishment) and with matched controls that separate age from generic context dilution (belief-strength decay) and from prior strength. We define a Belief Entrenchment Score = reduction in revisability per unit of elapsed dialogue age, and test four claims: (1) revisability decreases with elapsed age even at fixed belief strength and identical counterevidence; (2) an 'entrenchment' component is decodable and dissociable from the truth axis and from a strength-decay signal; (3) entrenchment causally predicts a stubborn-belief failure mode — refusing to update established-but-wrong facts late in long conversations; and (4) a lightweight De-aging intervention that resets the entrenchment component restores revisability without harming legitimate stability or general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on belief-revision accuracy, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build AgeBelief. Propositions P in three truth regimes: real-true, real-false, and synthetic facts defined only in context (to remove parametric priors and fix the initial belief). Each dialogue (a) ESTABLISHES belief in P early (via an in-context assertion/evidence with calibrated strength), (b) inserts a variable amount of UNRELATED filler dialogue to advance the entrenchment clock to a target elapsed AGE (measured in turns and in tokens: 1, 3, 6, 12 turns), then (c) presents a fixed, calibrated DISCONFIRMING evidence piece and probes the resulting belief. Crucially cross elapsed AGE with matched controls: (i) a STRENGTH-MATCHED control where filler length is equated but the establishment is re-stated just before the counterevidence, so belief strength is equalized across ages (isolating age from strength-decay); (ii) a DILUTION-ONLY control measuring belief strength as a function of filler with no counterevidence; (iii) a PRIOR-STRENGTH control varying establishment strength at fixed age (to dissociate age from prior-inertia). Match total token budget across age conditions where possible; include paraphrase sets; human-verify a sample.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral declarative true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. Read the internal belief in P (i) right after establishment, (ii) right before the counterevidence (to record current strength), and (iii) after the counterevidence, at matched query positions. Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false items; establishment moves belief as intended; the calibrated counterevidence moves belief for at least the youngest age.

Belief Entrenchment measurement: Define Revisability(age) = belief-change induced by the fixed counterevidence at that elapsed age. Define Belief Entrenchment Score = decline in Revisability per unit elapsed age, computed in the STRENGTH-MATCHED condition so pre-counterevidence belief strength is equalized across ages. Report per-layer, per-model entrenchment across ages and truth regimes. Test the hypothesis that revisability falls with age even at fixed strength. Compare age effects in turns vs tokens (is the clock counting turns or raw tokens?). Compare internal entrenchment to OUTPUT-level revisability (does the model's yes/no answer flip less at older ages?).

Dissociation from dilution and prior-inertia: Using the DILUTION-ONLY control, verify that belief STRENGTH change with filler is separable from the REVISABILITY change with age (a strength-decay-only account predicts no residual age effect once strength is matched). Using the PRIOR-STRENGTH control, show entrenchment persists at fixed age when prior strength varies, and vice versa, so age is not merely a proxy for strength. Fit an 'entrenchment' direction via difference-in-means on old-established vs young-established activations (matched on strength and content) and test decodability and dissociation from the truth direction (cosine similarity, project-out re-decoding) and from a separately-fit strength-decay direction.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Patch the entrenchment component from a YOUNG-established processing into an OLD-established processing of the same P (matched strength) and measure whether revisability under the fixed counterevidence increases (belief flips more). (b) Conversely inject the old-entrenchment component into a young belief and measure induced rigidity. Confirm the entrenchment signal causally governs revisability, separable from the truth axis and strength.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether the Belief Entrenchment Score predicts a stubborn-belief failure mode: (i) failure to flip the output answer for an established-but-WRONG fact when decisive counterevidence arrives late in a long conversation, (ii) belief perseverance (reverting to the old belief when re-queried), and (iii) inconsistency between early-age and late-age revision behavior. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (elapsed age alone, current belief strength, output entropy).

De-aging intervention: At inference, estimate the entrenchment direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer just before processing counterevidence (ITI-style), effectively resetting the belief's 'age' so it is as revisable as a freshly-established one. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected long-standing beliefs under challenge. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) restored Revisability at old ages / reduced Belief Entrenchment Score, (ii) improved belief-revision accuracy (correctly updating established-but-wrong facts late in long conversations) on AgeBelief and adapted long-context knowledge-conflict QA, (iii) calibration (ECE), (iv) PRESERVATION of legitimate stability — the model must NOT flip on weak/spurious counterevidence and must retain correctly-established true beliefs (measured on spurious-evidence and true-fact controls), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based re-statement of the fact just before counterevidence, and prompt-based instruction to 'treat long-standing and newly-stated facts as equally revisable'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), age measured in turns vs tokens, filler content type (coherent prose vs random facts vs boilerplate), truth regime, establishment strength, model scale, context-window training, and generalization to conversation structures not used to fit the de-aging direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The age effect could be entirely explained by generic context-dilution/strength-decay or by recency/attention decay rather than a distinct entrenchment clock; the strength-matched and dilution-only controls, the turns-vs-tokens comparison, and the project-out dissociation from a strength-decay direction directly test this, and a null (age = strength-decay) is an informative finding.
Equalizing belief STRENGTH across ages is imperfect (re-statement may itself change entrenchment); we calibrate strength from readouts, use multiple matching schemes, and report sensitivity.

Truth probes trained on single declaratives may transfer imperfectly to multi-turn established beliefs, so entrenchment estimates could carry probe extrapolation error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks, and synthetic facts to control priors.
Entrenchment and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; orthogonality/project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

The De-aging intervention risks over-destabilizing correctly-established true beliefs or making the model flip on spurious counterevidence; we explicitly measure true-fact preservation and spurious-evidence stability to characterize the revisability-vs-stability tradeoff.

The entrenchment score may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (elapsed age, belief strength, output entropy) for stubborn-update failures; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that dialogue age is a distinct entrenchment clock in belief geometry, plus the de-aging tool, reported honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may amplify consistency/commitment across turns); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: self_efficacy_belief_geometry
Title: Does the Model Believe It Can? Probing a Self-Efficacy Belief Axis Distinct From Actual Capability
Short Hypothesis: Beyond believing propositions about the world, an LLM carries an internal PROCEDURAL self-efficacy belief — a representation of whether IT CAN successfully perform a given task — that is formed BEFORE the model attempts the task and is decodable from hidden states at the prompt/instruction position. We hypothesize (1) this self-efficacy belief is a linearly decodable axis dissociable from the world-fact truth axis and from mere task-difficulty features; (2) it is systematically MISCALIBRATED against the model's actual per-task success — over-confident on hard tasks it will fail and under-confident on easy ones it will pass; (3) the axis, read from a single pre-attempt forward pass, predicts actual task success better than verbalized confidence; and (4) reading this axis gives a cheap pre-attempt abstention/routing signal that improves selective task performance, and steering it recalibrates over/under-confidence.
Related Work: Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) reads a belief about a PROPOSITION's truth, never a belief about the model's own ABILITY to do a task. Self-knowledge/calibration work (Kadavath et al. 2022 'models mostly know what they know') studies OUTPUT-level P(True)/verbalized confidence AFTER or about an answer; introspection work (Binder et al. 2024) asks whether models predict their own behavior behaviorally. Knowledge-boundary work (Xiao et al. 2025) probes whether a fact is known, i.e. DECLARATIVE knowledge, not PROCEDURAL self-efficacy on a task. My prior belief proposals are all about world-fact truth-value (coherence, provenance, ghosts, ignorance-vs-falsehood, evidence-weighting, epistemic-robustness, etc.); none read a PRE-ATTEMPT, task-level 'I-can-do-this' belief as a dissociable internal axis, test its miscalibration against realized success, or use it for pre-attempt routing. This procedural self-efficacy lens — an internal capability self-model read before any attempt — is new and directly actionable for compute-efficient routing and safe deferral.
Abstract: Most work on LLM beliefs concerns propositions about the world; we ask whether a model also holds a belief about ITSELF — specifically, whether it can successfully perform the task it is about to attempt. This procedural self-efficacy belief, if it exists, would be formed at the instruction position before any solution tokens are generated. Using difference-in-means and logistic probes on hidden states at the pre-attempt (post-instruction) position, we test whether such a self-efficacy axis is decodable, and construct SelfEfficacyBelief, a dataset of tasks (math word problems, code, factual QA, multi-step reasoning) each labeled by the model's ACTUAL success rate over sampled attempts, spanning easy-to-hard difficulty. We test four claims: (1) a self-efficacy axis is linearly decodable at the pre-attempt position and dissociable from the world-fact truth axis and from surface difficulty features via project-out analyses; (2) it is systematically miscalibrated against realized success, exposing over-confident-yet-failing and under-confident-yet-succeeding tasks; (3) the pre-attempt self-efficacy readout predicts actual success better than verbalized confidence and output-token entropy; and (4) it yields a cheap pre-attempt routing/abstention signal (defer hard tasks to a stronger model or to chain-of-thought), and steering along the axis recalibrates over/under-confidence. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate selective-task performance (risk-coverage), routing efficiency, calibration, and capability retention. Our results ask whether an LLM has an internal, readable model of its own competence — before it even tries.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build SelfEfficacyBelief. Assemble tasks across four families with verifiable success: (a) GSM8K math word problems, (b) code problems (HumanEval/MBPP-style) with unit tests, (c) factual QA (TriviaQA plus obscure-entity items), and (d) multi-step reasoning (BIG-Bench Hard subsets). For each model, obtain a per-task ACTUAL success label by sampling k attempts (e.g. k=8) and recording pass rate, giving a continuous self-efficacy ground truth from clearly-solvable to clearly-unsolvable. Include difficulty gradients within each family and matched surface-length controls so the probe cannot exploit trivial length cues. Hold out a task split for probe fitting vs evaluation.

Pre-attempt readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), extract hidden states at the PRE-ATTEMPT position (final token of the instruction/prompt, before any solution token is generated). Train a self-efficacy probe (difference-in-means and logistic regression / linear regression to the pass rate) per layer, Platt/isotonic-scaled to a predicted success probability. Report per-layer decoding accuracy/AUC for will-succeed-vs-will-fail and correlation with pass rate. Manipulation check: probe separates clearly-solvable from clearly-unsolvable tasks.

Dissociation analysis: Test that the self-efficacy axis is not merely (i) the world-fact truth direction (fit the standard truth probe on separate true/false statements; measure cosine similarity; project out the truth direction and re-decode self-efficacy), nor (ii) a surface task-difficulty feature (regress self-efficacy readout on token length, task family, and an embedding-based difficulty score; show residual predictive power). Report cross-axis leakage. A finding that self-efficacy collapses onto difficulty features is itself informative.

Miscalibration measurement: Compare the pre-attempt predicted self-efficacy against realized success. Define a Self-Efficacy Miscalibration score and identify OVER-CONFIDENT-YET-FAILING and UNDER-CONFIDENT-YET-SUCCEEDING task clusters. Report per-model, per-family miscalibration and reliability diagrams. Compare internal-axis calibration to verbalized confidence ('How likely are you to solve this?') and to output-token entropy on a first attempt.

Predictive validity (central test): From a SINGLE pre-attempt forward pass (no solution generated), test whether the self-efficacy readout predicts actual task success. Report AUC/correlation and crucially compare against baselines: verbalized pre-attempt confidence, first-token/first-attempt output entropy, and a difficulty-feature-only predictor. Does the internal axis beat these cheap baselines before any compute is spent solving?

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Steer activations along the self-efficacy direction at the pre-attempt position (holding the truth axis fixed) and measure whether realized success or the model's chosen strategy (e.g. attempting vs deferring, length of reasoning) changes as predicted. (b) Patch the self-efficacy component from a clearly-solvable task into a hard task and measure induced over-attempting. Confirm the axis is causal and separable from difficulty.

Routing/abstention application: Use the pre-attempt self-efficacy readout as a router: tasks scoring low are deferred (to a stronger model, to chain-of-thought, or to abstention); high-scoring tasks answered directly. Report risk-coverage / selective-task-accuracy curves and compute-cost savings versus routing by verbalized confidence, by entropy, and by always-CoT. Also test recalibration steering (raise efficacy on under-confident-yet-solvable, lower on over-confident-yet-failing) and measure whether attempt/defer decisions improve.

Downstream evaluation: Measure (i) improved selective-task performance (higher accuracy at fixed coverage / lower compute at fixed accuracy) from self-efficacy routing, (ii) reduced over-confident-failure and under-confident-deferral rates after recalibration steering, (iii) calibration (ECE) of pre-attempt success prediction, (iv) PRESERVATION of accuracy on clearly-solvable tasks (no over-deferral), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: verbalized-confidence routing, entropy routing, difficulty-heuristic routing, and no routing.

Ablations: pre-attempt position choice (final instruction token vs pooled), layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic vs regression), task family, difficulty level, k (number of attempts for success labels), model scale, cross-family generalization (fit probe on math+QA, test on code+reasoning), and transfer of the routing threshold across families.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The self-efficacy axis might be nearly collinear with surface task-difficulty features or with the world-fact truth axis, making it redundant; we directly test this with project-out and difficulty-controlled regressions, and a redundancy finding is itself informative about whether the model has a genuine self-model.

Actual-success labels depend on decoding temperature and k; a task's pass rate is stochastic. We fix decoding settings, use adequate k, report label-noise sensitivity, and treat continuous pass rate rather than a hard threshold.

The pre-attempt readout may implicitly reflect the model already 'planning' the solution rather than a distinct self-efficacy belief; we read strictly before any solution token, test position robustness, and use causal patching to check the axis governs attempt/defer behavior.

The internal self-efficacy axis may not beat cheap baselines (verbalized confidence, entropy) for success prediction; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic finding about whether procedural self-efficacy is a distinct, causally-manipulable belief coordinate, reported honestly.

Recalibration steering could induce over-deferral (harming easy tasks) or reckless over-attempting; we explicitly measure preservation on clearly-solvable tasks and characterize the accuracy-vs-compute tradeoff.

Cross-family generalization may be weak (self-efficacy for math may not transfer to code); we test cross-family probe transfer and report where a unified self-efficacy axis exists vs where it is domain-specific.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may inflate or flatten self-efficacy); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: paradox_belief_undefinedness
Title: No Fact of the Matter: Do LLM Beliefs Represent Truth-Valuelessness or Force a Spurious Verdict?
Short Hypothesis: Some propositions have no stable classical truth-value — self-referential paradoxes ('this sentence is false'), presupposition-failure statements ('the present king of France is bald'), category mistakes ('the number seven is blue'), and vacuously-referring claims. A competent believer should represent these as truth-valueless rather than as true or false. We hypothesize that LLM internal belief representations (linear truth-direction readouts) FORCE such statements into the true/false axis — collapsing 'no fact of the matter' into a spurious binary verdict — that a separable 'undefinedness/ill-posedness' axis is nonetheless weakly decodable and dissociable from the truth axis, that this collapse causally predicts an over-confident-verdict failure mode (confidently answering ill-posed questions instead of flagging them), and that reading the undefinedness axis gives a cheap gate that improves appropriate abstention/rejection without harming genuine true/false judgments.
Related Work: The dominant belief-probing tool fits a single linear true-vs-false 'truth direction' and reads a scalar belief (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024; Bao et al. 2025), always assuming propositions have a determinate truth-value. Bae (2026, 'When Self-Reference Fails to Close') shows paradoxical/non-closing self-reference destabilizes internal MATRIX DYNAMICS (attention rank, SVD) relative to grounded self-reference, but works at the level of aggregate activation statistics, not belief geometry: it never reads a truth-belief scalar, never tests whether paradoxes collapse onto the true/false axis, and does not cover presupposition failure, category mistakes, or vacuous reference. My prior 'ignorance_vs_falsehood_belief' proposal separated 'I don't know' (unknown but DETERMINATE facts) from 'I believe false'; that is orthogonal to the present question, which concerns statements that have NO determinate truth-value at all (undefined, not merely unknown). No prior work asks whether belief geometry has a coordinate for truth-valuelessness, whether ill-posed statements are spuriously binarized, whether this collapse drives over-confident verdicts on ill-posed inputs, or whether an undefinedness axis can gate rejection. This truth-valuelessness lens on belief geometry is new and distinct from stability/dynamics analyses and from all my prior determinate-truth proposals.
Abstract: A rational believer distinguishes three things: true, false, and 'there is no fact of the matter'. The Liar sentence, 'the present king of France is bald', and 'the number seven is jealous' are not true, not false, but truth-valueless — ill-posed. We ask whether large language models honor this inside their belief representations, or whether the standard linear truth direction forces such statements into a spurious true/false verdict. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar belief along the truth direction, we construct IllPosedBelief, a controlled dataset of (a) determinately-true and (b) determinately-false control statements versus truth-valueless statements of four kinds: self-referential paradoxes, presupposition-failure statements, category mistakes, and vacuously-referring claims, with matched surface forms. We first test our central collapse hypothesis: where do truth-valueless statements project on the truth axis — do they occupy a distinct neutral/ill-posed region, or are they pushed into the true or false region? We then test whether a separate 'undefinedness/ill-posedness' axis is decodable and dissociable from the truth axis via project-out analyses, and validate causality with activation patching. We show that the geometric distance between an ill-posed statement and the reject region causally predicts an over-confident-verdict failure mode — confidently answering ill-posed questions ('Is the king of France bald?' — 'No') instead of flagging the defect. Finally we introduce Ill-Posedness Gating, a cheap inference-time signal that triggers rejection/clarification, and evaluate whether it improves appropriate handling of ill-posed inputs against confidence-based baselines while preserving true/false accuracy and general capability.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build IllPosedBelief. CONTROL items: determinately-true and determinately-false factual statements. TRUTH-VALUELESS items in four categories: (1) SELF-REFERENTIAL PARADOXES (liar 'this statement is false', liar cycles, truth-teller); (2) PRESUPPOSITION FAILURE ('the present king of France is bald', 'have you stopped cheating?' as a declarative, statements about nonexistent referents); (3) CATEGORY MISTAKES ('the number seven is blue', 'Tuesday is heavier than justice'); (4) VACUOUS/UNDEFINED REFERENCE (definite descriptions with no or ambiguous referent). Include GROUNDED self-referential controls (self-referential but truth-valued, e.g. 'this sentence contains five words') to separate self-reference per se from paradox, following Bae (2026). Match surface length and syntactic form to the controls so the probe cannot exploit lexical cues (e.g. category mistakes should be grammatically well-formed declaratives). Human-verify category labels with multiple annotators; report agreement; include paraphrase sets.

Manipulation checks: Confirm items behave as intended: controls answered correctly with low entropy; truth-valueless items ideally elicit hedging/rejection when the model is explicitly allowed to say 'ill-posed', and confident wrong verdicts when forced to pick true/false. Separate items the model demonstrably recognizes as defective from those it does not.

Probe training and truth-axis collapse test: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), extract final-token hidden states per statement per layer and fit the standard truth direction (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on determinately-TRUE vs determinately-FALSE controls, Platt-scaled to [0,1]. Central test: project truth-valueless items onto this axis and measure where they land. Define a Collapse Score = distance of ill-posed-item projections from the neutral 0.5 point (large = forced into a verdict) and a Verdict-Bias measure (do they systematically land in the true or the false region, and does this differ by category — e.g. presupposition-failure toward false, category mistakes elsewhere?). Report per-layer, per-model, per-category.

Undefinedness-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit an 'ill-posedness/undefinedness' direction via difference-in-means on truth-valued (control) vs truth-valueless items, balanced across true/false and across the four categories. Report per-layer decoding accuracy and whether a single axis captures all four categories or they separate. Test dissociation from the truth axis: cosine similarity, project out the truth direction and re-decode undefinedness (and vice versa), report cross-axis leakage. Control for surface features (self-reference tokens, definite-description phrasing) with the grounded-self-reference control and a features-only baseline; a purely surface-detecting result is an informative negative.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Move activations along the undefinedness direction and measure whether the model's behavior shifts between issuing a verdict and flagging the statement as ill-posed, holding the truth axis fixed. (b) Patch the undefinedness component from an ill-posed item into a determinate control and measure induced hedging. Confirm the undefinedness axis is causal and separable from truth.

Predictive validity for the over-confident-verdict failure: Test whether an ill-posed item's position on the truth axis (its Collapse Score) / its undefinedness-axis score predicts (i) confident false-verdict on ill-posed questions ('Is the present king of France bald?' answered yes/no), (ii) failure to flag the presupposition/category defect, and (iii) inconsistency across paraphrases of the ill-posed item. Report AUROC/correlation vs baselines: output-token entropy, verbalized 'this is ill-posed' rate, and truth-probe confidence magnitude.

Ill-Posedness Gating intervention: At inference, read the decoded undefinedness score at a chosen layer; if it exceeds a calibrated threshold, route to a rejection/clarification response ('this question is ill-posed because...') rather than a true/false verdict. Threshold set on a held-out split. Optionally combine with a steering variant nudging activations toward the neutral/ill-posed region. Sweep layer and threshold.

Downstream evaluation: On a mixed set of determinate (true/false) and ill-posed items, plus adapted presupposition/category-mistake and paradox benchmarks, measure (i) appropriate-handling rate (rejecting/flagging ill-posed items) and risk-coverage for the reject decision, (ii) reduced confident false-verdicts on ill-posed questions, (iii) AUROC of the gate for detecting ill-posed inputs, (iv) PRESERVATION of true/false accuracy and coverage on determinate controls (no over-rejection of legitimate hard-but-well-posed items), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no gating, output-entropy thresholding, verbalized-confidence gating, and prompt-based instruction to 'flag questions that have no true or false answer'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), ill-posed category (paradox/presupposition/category-mistake/vacuous-reference), grounded-vs-paradoxical self-reference, model scale, threshold-calibration transfer across categories, and generalization to ill-posed types not used to fit the undefinedness direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The undefinedness axis might merely detect surface cues (self-reference phrasing, definite descriptions, semantically odd adjective-noun pairs) rather than a genuine ill-posedness representation; mitigate with surface-matched controls, a grounded-self-reference control, a features-only baseline, paraphrase controls, and causal patching, treating a pure surface-detecting result as an informative negative.

The four categories of truth-valuelessness may not share a common representation; a single 'undefinedness' axis may fail while per-category axes succeed. This heterogeneity is itself an informative finding and is directly measured.

The standard truth probe may extrapolate unpredictably to truth-valueless items, so apparent collapse could reflect probe behavior off-distribution rather than a genuine geometric commitment; we validate with multiple probe types, and a finding that the truth axis is ill-defined off-distribution is itself informative.

Philosophically, whether some items (e.g. presupposition-failure statements) are truly truth-valueless vs false is contested; we anchor quantitative claims on clear cases (liar paradoxes, blatant category mistakes), human-verify labels, and analyze contested items separately.

Ill-Posedness Gating could over-reject legitimate hard or unusual-but-well-posed questions, hurting coverage; we explicitly measure preservation on determinate controls and risk-coverage tradeoffs, and compare against strong confidence baselines rather than assuming superiority.

The undefinedness axis may correlate with but not exceed output-entropy/verbalized-rejection baselines for detecting ill-posed inputs; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic finding about whether (and how) belief geometry represents truth-valuelessness, reported regardless of intervention gains.

Findings may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may already teach some rejection of ill-posed inputs); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: affective_state_belief_contagion
Title: Beliefs in a Bad Mood: Does an Induced Emotional Context Distort an LLM's Internal Factual Belief?
Short Hypothesis: Holding a factual proposition's content fixed, embedding it in a surrounding emotional context (an angry, fearful, sad, or joyful preceding passage that is topically unrelated to the fact) systematically shifts the LLM's INTERNAL belief in the fact (linear truth-direction readout) in an affect-congruent way — negative moods lowering belief in neutral/positive facts and raising belief in threatening ones, mirroring human mood-congruent judgment. We hypothesize this affective belief distortion is graded in emotional intensity, carried by a decodable affect direction dissociable from the truth axis, causally predicts an affect-driven factual-error mode, and can be neutralized by a lightweight inference-time intervention that removes the affect component from the belief representation.
Related Work: Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) reads a single internal belief but never varies the AFFECTIVE context surrounding a fact. My prior proposals manipulate desirability of a proposition's CONTENT (wishful_belief_bias), surface REGISTER/tone of the assertion itself (register_framing_belief_bias), reported CROWD size (social_consensus), external REWARD (incentivized_belief_distortion), and REPETITION (repetition_illusory_belief). NONE test whether a topically-UNRELATED emotional context — a preceding angry/fearful/sad/joyful passage carrying no evidence about the fact — bleeds into and distorts the internal belief in a subsequent neutral factual claim (the analogue of human mood-congruent cognition and affect-as-information). Emotion in LLMs is studied at the OUTPUT/sentiment level and via 'emotional prompting' effects on task performance, not as a distortion of internal factual belief geometry. This mood-congruent-belief lens — affect leaking across an unrelated topic boundary into factual belief — is new and distinct from all prior content-desirability, style, crowd, reward, and repetition proposals.
Abstract: Humans in a fearful or angry mood judge unrelated risks as more likely and unrelated good news as less credible — mood-congruent cognition. We ask whether large language models inherit this bias inside their belief representations. Distinguishing a factual proposition's content from the AFFECTIVE CONTEXT in which it is embedded, we test whether a topically-unrelated emotional passage placed before a neutral factual claim shifts the model's internal belief in that claim. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar belief along the linear truth direction, we construct MoodBelief, a controlled dataset of true, false, and synthetic-in-context factual propositions, each preceded by emotion-inducing passages (anger, fear, sadness, joy, neutral) that are topically disjoint from the fact and carry no evidential bearing on it, with surface length matched and emotion intensity graded. We define an Affective Belief Shift Score = belief(fact | emotional context) minus belief(fact | neutral context), and test four claims: (1) internal belief shifts in an affect-congruent direction, graded in emotional intensity; (2) the shift is carried by a decodable affect direction dissociable from the truth axis; (3) shift magnitude causally predicts an affect-driven factual-error mode (mis-endorsing threatening claims under fear, doubting positive claims under sadness); and (4) a lightweight intervention that subtracts the affect component restores content-driven belief and reduces affect-induced errors while preserving legitimate emotion comprehension and general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on factuality, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build MoodBelief. Factual propositions P in three truth regimes: real-true, real-false, and synthetic facts defined only in context (to remove parametric priors). Crucially, each P is TOPICALLY NEUTRAL and carries an implicit valence label (positive-valence facts, negative/threatening facts, and neutral facts). Precede each P with an EMOTION-INDUCING passage — a short vignette or narrative rated as evoking anger, fear, sadness, or joy — that is topically DISJOINT from P and carries no evidence about P, plus a NEUTRAL-context control with matched surface length. Grade emotional intensity (mild vs strong) per emotion. Validate that emotional passages carry no logical bearing on P (human check) and that the emotion labels/intensities are accurate (human + LLM-judge ratings). Match surface length across all context conditions; include paraphrase sets and disjoint-topic verification.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral-context true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At a matched query position after the emotional context read the internal belief in P. Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false neutral-context items; confirm the emotional passage is comprehended (the model can classify its emotion) but is not evidence for P.

Affective Belief Shift measurement: Define Affective Belief Shift Score = belief(P | emotional context) minus belief(P | neutral context). Report per-layer, per-model shift broken down by inducing emotion (anger/fear/sadness/joy), emotional intensity, and the fact's valence (positive/negative/neutral). Test the mood-congruence hypotheses: fear/anger raise belief in threatening facts and lower it in positive facts; sadness lowers belief in positive facts; joy raises belief in positive facts — while holding P's content fixed. Test graded-in-intensity monotonicity. Compare internal shift to OUTPUT-level shift (does the model's yes/no answer or verbalized confidence about P move with the mood?).

Affect-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit an 'affect' direction via difference-in-means on emotional-context vs neutral-context activations at the P-query position (balanced across P truth-value and valence). Report per-layer decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the affect axis (and vice versa); test whether the belief shift is explained by the affect component leaking into the truth-probe readout. Disentangle affect from generic sentiment/valence-of-tokens with a sentiment-controlled regression.

Causal validation: Activation patching. Take the activation difference between an emotional-context and a neutral-context processing of the same P, decompose into truth-direction and affect-direction components, patch only the affect component into the neutral condition, and measure induced change in belief readout and output endorsement. Conversely subtract the affect component under emotional context and measure whether belief returns to the content-driven value. Confirm the affect signal causally shifts the belief scalar independent of content.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether Affective Belief Shift predicts an affect-driven factual-error mode: (i) mis-endorsement of threatening false claims under fear/anger, (ii) under-endorsement/doubting of true positive claims under sadness, and (iii) confident-wrong rate driven by the induced mood. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (emotion intensity alone, output entropy, neutral-context truth-probe confidence).

Affect De-biasing intervention: At inference, estimate the affect direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer (ITI-style), so the belief readout reflects the proposition's content rather than the surrounding mood. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected strong emotional context. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Affective Belief Shift Score, (ii) reduced affect-driven factual errors (fewer threat-under-fear mis-endorsements, less positive-under-sadness doubting), (iii) factuality/calibration (ECE) on emotionally-embedded factual QA, (iv) PRESERVATION of legitimate emotion comprehension (the model must still correctly classify/discuss the emotional passage) and accuracy on neutral-context controls (no over-correction), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'judge the facts calmly regardless of the surrounding mood', and a fresh-context re-ask baseline (query P without the emotional passage).

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), inducing emotion and intensity, fact valence (positive/negative/neutral), real vs synthetic facts, true vs false regime, distance between the emotional passage and the fact query, model scale, and generalization to emotion types and topics not used to fit the de-biasing direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent affective belief shift could reflect the probe detecting sentiment/valence lexical residue of the emotional passage rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with surface-length matching, topic-disjointness verification, a sentiment-controlled regression separating affect from token valence, paraphrase controls, and causal patching that isolates the affect-direction component.

The emotional passage might be construed by the model as weak evidence for P despite topic disjointness (e.g., a fearful passage priming plausibility of threats); we human-verify no evidential bearing, include valence-balanced facts, and treat any residual evidential leakage as a separately-analyzed confound.

Truth probes trained on neutral-context statements may transfer imperfectly to emotionally-embedded contexts, so shifts could carry probe extrapolation error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, and synthetic facts to control priors.
Affect and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality/project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

The De-biasing intervention could impair legitimate emotion comprehension (the model can no longer discuss the mood) or harm fluency; we explicitly measure emotion-comprehension preservation, neutral-context accuracy, and capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Affective belief shift may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (emotion intensity, output entropy) for affect-driven errors; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that unrelated affect distorts internal factual belief (mood-congruent cognition in belief geometry) plus the de-biasing tool, reported honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may dampen or amplify affect sensitivity); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: effort_indexed_belief_geometry
Title: Does Working Harder Change What It Believes? Testing Whether Allotted Compute Distorts an LLM's Internal Belief
Short Hypothesis: Holding a proposition's content and evidence fixed, the amount of computation an LLM is allotted to reach a verdict about it — forced immediate answer vs extended chain-of-thought, or few vs many reasoning tokens — systematically shifts the model's INTERNAL belief (linear truth-direction readout) about the proposition, even when the extra computation adds no new information. We hypothesize this 'effort-indexed' belief shift is graded in allotted compute, dissociable from a decodable effort/deliberation axis distinct from the truth axis, causally predicts a compute-dependent flip-flop failure mode (the same fact judged differently under different thinking budgets), and can be neutralized by a lightweight inference-time intervention that removes the effort component so belief reflects content rather than budget.
Related Work: Recent probing work shows an LLM's answer and confidence about a proposition are often largely fixed BEFORE chain-of-thought begins: Sarfati et al. (2026) find a single pre-reasoning forward pass recovers the committed forecast and confidence, and CoT is frequently post-hoc; my prior 'step_belief_load_bearing' proposal studies which CoT steps move the answer-belief. Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) reads a static belief scalar and never varies the COMPUTE BUDGET allotted to reach a verdict. Crucially, no prior work asks the inverse of the 'pre-committed answer' finding: whether, for propositions where the verdict is NOT pre-fixed, the amount of allotted computation (forced-immediate vs extended thinking, short vs long reasoning) itself DISTORTS the internal belief in an information-free way — i.e., whether belief is effort-indexed — whether this is a decodable axis separable from truth, whether it causes compute-dependent flip-flops on the same fact, or whether it can be de-biased. This effort-as-distorter lens is distinct from all my prior content/framing/source/dynamics proposals and from post-hoc-rationalization work, which treats reasoning as revealing (or concealing) a fixed belief, not as an information-free force that moves belief.
Abstract: How much a model 'thinks' before answering is now a tunable knob (forced immediate answers, or extended chain-of-thought with variable token budgets). We ask a simple question with safety implications: does merely allotting more or less computation change what an LLM internally BELIEVES about a fixed proposition, even when the extra computation carries no new information? Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar belief along the linear truth direction, we present true, false, and synthetic-in-context propositions and vary only the compute budget used to reach a verdict — forced-immediate answer, brief reasoning, and extended reasoning — while holding all content and evidence fixed. We construct EffortBelief and define an Effort-Indexed Belief Shift Score = belief(under high compute) minus belief(under low compute), and test four claims: (1) internal belief shifts with allotted compute, graded in budget, even absent new information; (2) the shift is carried by a decodable effort/deliberation axis dissociable from the truth axis; (3) shift magnitude causally predicts a compute-dependent flip-flop mode — the same fact judged differently under different thinking budgets — and correlates with correctness changes; and (4) a lightweight intervention that subtracts the effort component stabilizes belief across budgets while preserving genuine compute-driven improvement on hard multi-step items. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on belief stability, calibration, flip-flop rate, and capability retention. Our results ask whether an LLM's beliefs can be moved by how hard it is told to think.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build EffortBelief. Propositions P in three truth regimes: real-true, real-false, and synthetic-in-context facts (to remove parametric priors). Crucially partition items by whether extra computation SHOULD matter: (a) SINGLE-STEP items whose truth is directly checkable with no computation (the extra compute is genuinely information-free), and (b) MULTI-STEP items whose correct verdict genuinely requires reasoning (a control where extra compute legitimately should help). For each P, create compute-budget conditions that hold content fixed but vary allotted computation: FORCED-IMMEDIATE (answer instructed before any reasoning), BRIEF-REASONING (a short bounded chain), and EXTENDED-REASONING (a long chain / high thinking budget). Match surface prompt content; the only manipulated variable is the reasoning budget. Include paraphrase sets; human-verify labels.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale, including thinking-tuned variants where available (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to [0,1]. Read the internal belief in P at a matched query position under each budget condition. For reasoning conditions, read belief at the point the model commits to a verdict. Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false items; confirm the model actually uses more/less compute as instructed.

Effort-Indexed Belief Shift measurement: Define Effort-Indexed Belief Shift Score = belief(EXTENDED) minus belief(FORCED-IMMEDIATE), computed separately for SINGLE-STEP (information-free) and MULTI-STEP (legitimate) items. Report per-layer, per-model shift as a function of budget. Test the hypotheses that (i) belief shifts with budget even on single-step items where compute adds nothing, and (ii) the shift is graded/monotone in budget. Compare internal shift to OUTPUT-level shift (does the yes/no verdict or verbalized confidence move with budget?).

Effort-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit an 'effort/deliberation' direction via difference-in-means on extended-reasoning vs forced-immediate activations (balanced across truth-value and content). Report per-layer decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the effort axis (and vice versa); test whether the belief shift is explained by the effort component leaking into the truth-probe readout.

Causal validation: Activation patching. Take the activation difference between extended and forced-immediate conditions on single-step items, decompose into truth-direction and effort-direction components, patch only the effort component into the forced-immediate condition, and measure induced change in belief and output; conversely subtract the effort component under extended reasoning and measure whether belief returns to the low-compute value. Confirm the effort signal causally shifts the belief scalar independent of content.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether the Effort-Indexed Belief Shift predicts a compute-dependent flip-flop failure mode: (i) the same single-step fact receiving different yes/no verdicts under different budgets, (ii) confidence swings across budgets, and (iii) whether the flip corresponds to a correctness change (does more compute help, hurt, or randomly perturb?). Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (budget alone, output entropy, forced-immediate truth-probe confidence).

Effort De-biasing intervention: At inference, estimate the effort direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer at the verdict position (ITI-style), so belief reflects content rather than allotted compute. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected high-compute reasoning. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Effort-Indexed Belief Shift and reduced flip-flop rate on single-step items, (ii) PRESERVATION of legitimate compute-driven improvement on MULTI-STEP items (extended reasoning must still help where it genuinely should), (iii) calibration (ECE) across budgets, (iv) accuracy on clearly-true/false controls, and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, self-consistency across budgets, and prompt-based instruction to 'answer based only on the facts regardless of how long you think'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), budget levels, single-step vs multi-step items, thinking-tuned vs standard models, real vs synthetic facts, verdict-position choice, model scale, and generalization to reasoning formats not used to fit the effort direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The belief shift on single-step items might reflect the model genuinely discovering something during reasoning rather than an information-free effort effect; we mitigate by construction (single-step items are directly checkable with no derivation possible), by human-verifying that no additional inference is available, and by contrasting with multi-step items where compute legitimately helps.

Apparent effort shift could reflect the probe reading a verdict-position token differently across budget conditions (position/format artifact) rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with matched verdict positions, position/layer sweeps, and causal patching that isolates the effort-direction component.

Truth probes trained on neutral statements may transfer imperfectly to reasoning-laden contexts, so shifts could carry probe extrapolation error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, and synthetic facts to control priors.
Effort and truth directions may be partly entangled, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality/project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

The De-biasing intervention could suppress legitimate compute-driven improvement on hard items or harm fluency; we explicitly measure multi-step preservation and capability retention to characterize the tradeoff, and the intervention risks being useful only when belief-instability, not genuine reasoning, is the problem.

Prior work (Sarfati et al. 2026) shows many answers are pre-committed before reasoning; on such items the effort effect may be near zero, so the phenomenon may be confined to genuinely-uncertain items — we stratify by pre-commitment and report where the effect concentrates, treating a confinement result as informative.
Effects may vary across model families, scales, and thinking-tuning; we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: syntactic_commitment_belief_bending
Title: Sentence Traps: Do Mid-Generation Grammatical Commitments Bend an LLM's Internal Belief Toward False Completions?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM has already emitted a partial sentence that grammatically/lexically commits it toward a particular continuation (e.g. after generating 'The capital of Australia is S...' the model is syntactically primed to complete a word starting with S like 'Sydney'), its INTERNAL belief (linear truth-direction readout) in the false-but-syntactically-consistent completion is inflated relative to the true completion, and relative to the same fact judged without the leading partial. We hypothesize this 'syntactic commitment pressure' on belief is graded in how strongly the prefix constrains the continuation, is carried by a decodable coherence/commitment component dissociable from the truth axis, causally predicts a fluency-over-truth hallucination mode, and can be reduced by a lightweight inference-time intervention that removes the commitment component so belief reflects the fact rather than grammatical consistency with what was already written.
Related Work: Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024; Bao et al. 2025) reads a belief scalar and shows probes generalize across logical transformations, but never varies a self-generated grammatical PREFIX that constrains the continuation. PAIR (Kim et al. 2026) documents that hidden-state probes degrade under 'prefix contamination' in multi-step agent trajectories — tracking coherence with a (possibly corrupted) prefix rather than grounded correctness — but treats this purely as a nuisance for step-level reward modeling and proposes an engineering fix (an attention-based correction head); it does not localize the effect in belief geometry, isolate the specific SYNTACTIC/lexical-commitment cause, tie it to a fluency-over-truth hallucination mode within a single generation, or steer it away. My prior proposals (self_commitment, self_persuasion, premature_commitment, generation_quota) concern semantic self-authorship, argument production, lock-in during READING of an input, or quota pressure — none isolate the case where the model's own partially-emitted grammatical structure (an unfinished word/phrase whose only consistent completions are false) bends its internal belief toward the false completion. This grammatical-coherence-pressure lens on belief geometry is new.
Abstract: Fluent generation requires each new token to be grammatically consistent with what was already written, but this consistency pressure can collide with truth: once a model has started writing 'The largest planet is M...', it is grammatically primed to finish a word like 'Mars' even though 'Jupiter' is correct. We ask whether such mid-generation grammatical commitments bend not just the model's output but its INTERNAL belief. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar belief along the linear truth direction, we test whether, after emitting a partial sentence that syntactically/lexically constrains the continuation toward a false answer, the model's internal belief in the false-but-consistent completion is inflated relative to the true completion and relative to a no-prefix baseline. We construct SentenceTrap, a controlled dataset of factual questions whose true and false answers differ in their leading tokens (first letter, syllable, grammatical gender/number), letting us craft partial generations that commit the model toward the false answer, plus neutral-prefix and true-committing controls with matched surface forms. We define a Commitment Belief Bending Score, and test four claims: (1) internal belief bends toward the syntactically-consistent completion, graded in prefix constraint strength; (2) the bending is carried by a decodable coherence/commitment direction dissociable from the truth axis; (3) bending magnitude causally predicts a fluency-over-truth hallucination mode where the model completes with the false answer; and (4) a lightweight intervention subtracting the commitment component restores fact-driven belief and reduces such hallucinations without harming fluency or general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on factuality, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build SentenceTrap. Collect factual question-answer pairs where the TRUE answer and a salient FALSE alternative differ in leading-token structure so a partial generation can commit toward one or the other: (a) first-letter/syllable divergence (Q: 'The capital of Australia is' — true 'Canberra' vs false 'Sydney'; craft prefixes ending in a committing fragment like 'Syd' or a determiner+letter), (b) grammatical-gender/number commitment in gendered/inflected languages, and (c) SYNTHETIC-in-context facts (answer defined only in context) to remove parametric priors. For each item, create matched conditions differing only in the LEADING PARTIAL GENERATION: FALSE-COMMITTING prefix (grammatically forces the false answer), TRUE-COMMITTING prefix (forces the true answer), NEUTRAL prefix (no leading commitment, e.g. 'The answer is'), and NO-PREFIX baseline (bare question). Vary prefix CONSTRAINT STRENGTH (weakly vs strongly narrowing the continuation). Match surface length; human-verify that prefixes are truth-neutral in content and differ only in grammatical/lexical commitment; include paraphrase sets.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral declarative true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. For each item read the internal belief in the proposition 'answer = TRUE-value' and 'answer = FALSE-value' at the continuation position, under each prefix condition. Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false items; confirm the prefix behaviorally constrains the model's next-token distribution as intended.

Commitment Belief Bending measurement: Define Commitment Belief Bending Score = belief(false answer | FALSE-committing prefix) minus belief(false answer | NO-PREFIX baseline); and symmetrically the drop in belief(true answer) under a false-committing prefix. Report per-layer, per-model bending as a function of prefix constraint strength and item type. Test the hypotheses that (i) belief bends toward the syntactically-consistent (false) completion, and (ii) bending grows with constraint strength. Contrast FALSE- vs TRUE-committing prefixes (they should bend belief in opposite directions) to rule out generic prefix effects. Compare internal bending to OUTPUT-level behavior (does the model actually complete with the false answer?).

Commitment-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'coherence/commitment' direction via difference-in-means on committing-prefix vs neutral-prefix activations (balanced across truth-value and content). Report per-layer decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the commitment axis (and vice versa); test whether the belief bending is explained by the commitment component leaking into the truth-probe readout.

Causal validation: Activation patching. Take the activation difference between a false-committing and a neutral prefix processing of the same item, decompose into truth-direction and commitment-direction components, patch only the commitment component into the neutral condition, and measure induced change in belief readout and next-token completion. Conversely subtract the commitment component under a false-committing prefix and measure whether belief returns toward the fact-driven value and the completion flips to the true answer. Confirm the commitment signal causally bends the belief scalar independent of content.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether Commitment Belief Bending predicts a fluency-over-truth hallucination mode: (i) rate at which the model completes with the false-but-syntactically-consistent answer under a false-committing prefix, (ii) confident-wrong rate, and (iii) failure to self-correct within the sentence. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (prefix constraint strength alone, next-token entropy, no-prefix truth-probe confidence).

Commitment De-biasing intervention: At inference, estimate the commitment direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer during continuation (ITI-style), so belief reflects the fact rather than grammatical consistency with the emitted prefix. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected strong syntactic commitment (low next-token entropy toward a factually-wrong continuation). Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Commitment Belief Bending Score, (ii) reduced fluency-over-truth hallucination (fewer false-consistent completions) and improved within-sentence self-correction, (iii) factuality/calibration (ECE) on completion-format factual QA, (iv) PRESERVATION of fluency (grammaticality of outputs, judged by an LLM/human rubric) and accuracy on neutral-prefix and true-committing controls (no over-correction), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'complete truthfully even if it requires rephrasing', and a rephrase-allowed decoding baseline (let the model back up and restart the sentence).

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), commitment type (first-letter/syllable vs gender/number), constraint strength, real vs synthetic facts, false- vs true-committing prefixes, model scale, and generalization to commitment structures and languages not used to fit the de-biasing direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent belief bending could reflect the probe detecting the committing prefix tokens lexically rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with the false-vs-true-committing contrast (opposite-signed bending on matched prefixes), neutral-prefix and no-prefix baselines, paraphrase controls, and causal patching that isolates the commitment-direction component.

Truth probes trained on full declaratives may transfer imperfectly to mid-sentence continuation positions, so bending could carry probe extrapolation error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks confirming prefix constraint, and synthetic facts to control priors, with position/layer robustness checks.
Commitment and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality/project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

The De-biasing intervention could harm fluency (producing ungrammatical completions when it should instead rephrase) or over-correct on true-committing prefixes; we explicitly measure grammaticality preservation, true-committing/neutral controls, and capability retention, and compare against a rephrase-allowed baseline that fixes the problem by restarting rather than by breaking grammar.

Bending may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (constraint strength, next-token entropy) for fluency-over-truth hallucination; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that grammatical commitment pressure distorts internal belief (localizing the PAIR 'prefix contamination' effect in belief geometry) plus the de-biasing tool, reported honestly.
Effects may vary across model families, scales, tokenization, and languages; we test multiple models and report scale/tokenization effects and negative results as informative.

Name: is_ought_belief_conflation
Title: Is Versus Ought: Do LLM Internal Beliefs Separate Factual Truth From Normative Desirability of States of the World?
Short Hypothesis: Beyond a proposition's factual truth-value, a competent belief system must keep 'what is the case' (descriptive/factual) distinct from 'what ought to be the case' (normative/deontic). We hypothesize that (1) an LLM's internal belief representation encodes a decodable normative-desirability axis dissociable from the factual truth axis; (2) the two systematically CONFLATE, so that a state's moral/prudential desirability spuriously raises the internal belief that it is factually the case (and undesirable states are believed less true), an internal is-from-ought (naturalistic-fallacy-like) distortion; (3) this conflation causally predicts a normatively-biased factual-error mode (believing that good outcomes obtain and bad ones don't, contrary to evidence); and (4) a lightweight inference-time intervention that removes the normative component from the factual belief reduces these errors without harming genuine normative reasoning.
Related Work: Truth-direction probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024; Bao et al. 2025) reads a scalar FACTUAL belief and never distinguishes descriptive truth from normative/deontic status. Work on LLM moral reasoning and value representations studies normative judgments at the OUTPUT level (ETHICS, moral-machine style benchmarks) or probes 'value directions' in isolation, but none asks whether the model keeps the IS axis (what factually holds) separate from the OUGHT axis (what is morally/prudentially desirable) inside belief geometry, whether desirability leaks into factual belief (an internal analogue of the naturalistic fallacy / wishful thinking about the world's actual state), whether this predicts factual error, or whether it can be de-biased. My prior 'wishful_belief_bias' proposal concerned the desirability of a proposition to the USER (flattery/hope/pleasantness) distorting belief; the present proposal is distinct: it targets the MORAL/DEONTIC 'ought' status of a described state of the world (what should be the case, independent of user-pleasingness) and its leakage into descriptive 'is' belief, with a focus on the is/ought (Hume's guillotine) separation as a structural rationality constraint. 'affective_state_belief_contagion' concerned surrounding mood; 'modal_status_belief_geometry' concerned necessary-vs-contingent truth (an alethic modality), not deontic ought-vs-is.
