FALSIFIABLE items: ordinary empirical claims with a definite truth-value that could be checked by observation (physics/chemistry/biology/everyday facts and their negations). UNFALSIFIABLE items in three subtypes: (a) METAPHYSICAL/unobservable ('a conscious but wholly undetectable entity guides evolution'), (b) VACUOUS/tautological dressed as empirical ('everything happens for a reason that we may never know'), (c) INHERENTLY-UNTESTABLE predictions ('something significant will eventually happen somewhere'). Crucially, unfalsifiable items are coherent, grammatical, and span high vs low surface plausibility, so falsifiability is not confounded with incoherence or implausibility. Include SYNTHETIC-in-context claims (nonce mechanisms stipulated as either testable or untestable-by-construction) to control priors. Match surface length/syntax; human-verify (multiple annotators, with an explicit Popperian rubric) both falsifiability and plausibility labels and report agreement; include paraphrase sets and neutral controls.

Manipulation checks: Confirm items behave as intended — falsifiable items answered with definite verdicts; unfalsifiable items ideally elicit 'this cannot be empirically tested' when the model is explicitly allowed to say so, and a forced true/false verdict when made to choose. Separate items the model recognizes as untestable from those it does not.

Probe training and truth-axis collapse test: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), extract final-token hidden states per claim per layer and fit the standard truth direction (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on FALSIFIABLE-true vs FALSIFIABLE-false items, Platt-scaled to [0,1]. Central test: where do UNFALSIFIABLE claims project on this axis? Define a Collapse Score = distance of unfalsifiable-item projections from the neutral 0.5 point, and a Plausibility-Verdict-Bias = correlation between the projected belief and the claim's surface plausibility (a rational model would not derive a confident truth-verdict from an untestable claim's plausibility). Report per-layer, per-model, per-subtype.

Falsifiability-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'falsifiability/testability' direction via difference-in-means on falsifiable vs unfalsifiable items, balanced across truth-value and plausibility. Report per-layer decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode falsifiability (and vice versa); report cross-axis leakage. Control for surface cues (does the probe just detect hedging words like 'undetectable'?) via surface-matched items and a features-only baseline; a purely surface-detecting result is an informative negative.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Move activations along the falsifiability direction and measure whether the model shifts between issuing a verdict and flagging 'this cannot be tested', holding the truth axis fixed. (b) Patch the falsifiability component from a falsifiable item into an unfalsifiable one and measure induced hedging. Confirm the falsifiability axis is causal and separable from truth.

Predictive validity for the over-verdict failure: Test whether an unfalsifiable item's Collapse Score / falsifiability-axis score predicts (i) confident true/false verdicts on untestable claims, (ii) failure to flag the claim as unfalsifiable, and (iii) inconsistency across paraphrases. Report AUROC/correlation vs baselines: output-token entropy, verbalized 'cannot be tested' rate, and truth-probe confidence magnitude.

Falsifiability Gating intervention: At inference, read the decoded falsifiability score at a chosen layer; if it indicates unfalsifiability beyond a calibrated threshold, route to an epistemic-hedging response ('this claim cannot be empirically tested, so I can't affirm or deny it') rather than a verdict. Threshold set on a held-out split. Optionally combine with steering toward the neutral region. Sweep layer and threshold.

Downstream evaluation: On a mixed set of falsifiable and unfalsifiable claims, plus adapted pseudoscience/conspiracy/metaphysical-claim items, measure (i) appropriate-handling rate (flagging unfalsifiable claims) and risk-coverage for the gate decision, (ii) reduced confident verdicts on untestable claims, (iii) AUROC of the gate for detecting unfalsifiable inputs, (iv) PRESERVATION of true/false accuracy and coverage on falsifiable items (no over-hedging on ordinary empirical claims), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no gating, output-entropy thresholding, verbalized-confidence gating, and prompt-based instruction to 'flag claims that cannot be empirically tested'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), unfalsifiable subtype (metaphysical/vacuous/untestable-prediction), plausibility level, synthetic vs real items, model scale, threshold-calibration transfer across subtypes, and generalization to unfalsifiability types not used to fit the falsifiability direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The falsifiability axis might merely detect surface cues (words like 'undetectable', 'invisible', 'never') rather than a genuine testability representation; mitigate with surface-matched items, a features-only baseline, paraphrase controls, synthetic-in-context testable-vs-untestable-by-construction items, and causal patching, treating a pure surface-detecting result as an informative negative.

Falsifiability is philosophically contested at the margins (demarcation problem, degrees of testability); we anchor quantitative claims on clear cases (paradigmatic empirical facts vs paradigmatic metaphysical/vacuous claims), human-verify with an explicit rubric, and analyze borderline items separately.

The standard truth probe may extrapolate unpredictably to unfalsifiable items, so apparent collapse could reflect off-distribution probe behavior; we validate with multiple probe types, and a finding that the truth axis is ill-defined for unfalsifiable claims is itself informative.

Unfalsifiability overlaps with adjacent constructs (context-underdetermination, truth-valuelessness); we design items so falsifiability is a property of the claim itself (fully specified, coherent, non-paradoxical) and separate it from underdetermination and paradox conditions.

Falsifiability Gating could over-hedge on legitimate but unusual empirical claims, hurting coverage; we explicitly measure falsifiable-item preservation and risk-coverage tradeoffs and compare against strong confidence baselines rather than assuming superiority.

The falsifiability axis may correlate with but not exceed entropy/verbalized-abstention baselines for detecting unfalsifiable inputs; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic finding about whether (and how) belief geometry represents empirical testability, reported regardless of intervention gains.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may already teach some hedging on pseudoscientific claims); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: moral_contagion_belief_bending
Title: Once Tainted, Forever Doubted: Does Moral or Physical Contamination History Distort an LLM's Internal Factual Belief?
Short Hypothesis: Holding a factual proposition's content and truth-value fixed, prefacing it with an evidentially-irrelevant CONTAMINATION history of the entity/object involved — a moral taint (the person once behaved dishonestly), a physical/hygienic taint (the object once touched something disgusting), or a symbolic taint — systematically LOWERS the LLM's INTERNAL belief in the fact (linear truth-direction readout), an internal analogue of the human contagion/'once in contact, always in contact' magical-thinking bias. This contamination-induced belief bending is graded in taint intensity, carried by a decodable contamination/taint component dissociable from the truth axis, causally predicts a contamination-driven factual-error mode (doubting true statements about tainted entities, and, symmetrically, being harder to convince of virtuous claims about them), and can be neutralized by a lightweight inference-time intervention that removes the contamination component.
Related Work: Truth-direction/belief probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024; Bao et al. 2025 ACL) reads a scalar internal belief but never varies an evidentially-irrelevant CONTAMINATION/TAINT history of the entity a fact is about. In human psychology, the law of contagion (Rozin & Nemeroff; Nemeroff & Rozin 2000) is a robust magical-thinking bias: an entity that once contacted something impure (a dishonest act, a disgusting substance) is treated as permanently tainted, coloring unrelated judgments about it. My prior belief proposals vary content desirability (wishful_belief_bias), affective SURROUNDING context (affective_state_belief_contagion — an unrelated mood passage, not a taint history of the entity), reported crowd (social_consensus), assigned identity (persona), moral taboo of the CLAIM ITSELF (taboo_belief_suppression), and associative spillover from EVIDENCE (belief_contagion, which spreads belief between logically-independent propositions). NONE isolate a CONTAMINATION HISTORY of the entity — a past moral/physical/symbolic taint carrying no logical bearing on the queried fact — as a distinct axis that distorts the model's own internal factual belief about that entity, treat taint as a decodable belief component dissociable from truth, tie it causally to a contamination-driven factual-error mode, or de-bias it. This is distinct from affective_state (mood of an unrelated passage vs a taint attached to the very entity), from taboo_suppression (offensiveness of stating the claim vs contamination of the subject), and from belief_contagion (spillover across independent propositions from evidence vs a taint-history distortion of a single fact). This contagion/taint lens on belief geometry — borrowing a well-documented human magical-thinking bias — is new and maps onto real reliability risks (LLMs under-crediting true facts about entities with a checkered history, e.g. discounting accurate statements about a person, company, or product because of an unrelated past scandal or 'ick' association).
Abstract: People treat contamination as sticky: a coat that once touched something disgusting, or a person who once lied, feels permanently tainted, and that taint bleeds into unrelated judgments — the law of contagion, a robust magical-thinking bias. We ask whether large language models inherit this bias inside their belief representations. Holding a factual proposition's content and truth-value fixed, we preface it with an evidentially-irrelevant CONTAMINATION HISTORY of the entity involved (a past moral taint, a physical/hygienic taint, or a symbolic taint) and read the internal belief via linear truth probes, testing whether the taint bends the model's belief about a completely unrelated fact concerning that entity. We construct TaintBelief, a controlled dataset of true, false, and synthetic-in-context propositions each paired with matched taint vs neutral-history framings that carry no logical bearing on the fact, with taint intensity graded and surface length matched. We define a Contamination Belief Bending Score = belief(fact | taint history) minus belief(fact | neutral history), and test four claims: (1) internal belief in unrelated facts about tainted entities is lowered, graded in taint intensity; (2) the shift is carried by a decodable contamination/taint component dissociable from the truth axis; (3) shift magnitude causally predicts a contamination-driven factual-error mode (doubting true statements about tainted entities); and (4) a lightweight intervention that subtracts the contamination component restores content-driven belief while preserving legitimate reputation-based reasoning and general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on factuality, calibration, and capability retention. Our results ask whether an LLM's factual beliefs are silently tainted by an entity's unrelated history.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build TaintBelief. Propositions P in three truth regimes: real-true, real-false, and synthetic-in-context facts (defined only in context, to remove parametric priors). Each P is a factual claim about an ENTITY (a person, object, place, or product) that carries no logical connection to any taint. Preface each P with matched HISTORY framings that are evidentially irrelevant to P: (a) MORAL TAINT (the entity once did something dishonest/immoral), (b) PHYSICAL/HYGIENIC TAINT (the object once contacted something disgusting/contaminated), (c) SYMBOLIC TAINT (the entity is associated with a negatively-charged symbol), vs a NEUTRAL HISTORY of matched length and a no-history baseline. Crucially the queried fact is unrelated to the taint (e.g. taint = 'this chef was once caught stealing'; fact = 'this chef was born in 1975'). Grade taint intensity (mild vs severe). Include taint framings paired with true and false P (so effects are not confounded with generic negativity/caution). Human-verify that taint framings carry no logical bearing on P; include paraphrase sets and controls where the taint IS legitimately relevant (a reputation control, e.g. taint = fraud history, fact = 'this person is trustworthy') to distinguish illegitimate contagion from warranted reputation reasoning.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral, history-free true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At a matched query position read the internal belief in P under each history framing; also record the OUTPUT answer/confidence. Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false neutral items; confirm the model comprehends the taint (can report the entity's history) but is not given evidence about P.

Contamination Belief Bending measurement: Define Contamination Belief Bending Score = belief(P | taint history) minus belief(P | neutral history), holding content and truth fixed. Report per-layer, per-model bending across taint type, taint intensity, and truth regime. Test the hypotheses that (i) belief in unrelated facts about tainted entities is lowered, and (ii) bending grows with taint intensity. Crucially test the reputation control: taint SHOULD lower belief in a relevant virtue claim (legitimate) but should NOT lower belief in an unrelated factual claim (illegitimate contagion). Compare internal bending to OUTPUT-level bending (does the model's verdict/confidence about the unrelated fact drop when the entity is tainted?).

Contamination-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'contamination/taint' direction via difference-in-means on taint-history vs neutral-history activations at the P-query position (balanced across truth-value and content). Report per-layer decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the taint axis (and vice versa); test whether the bending is explained by the taint component leaking into the truth-probe readout. Disentangle contamination from generic negative sentiment via a sentiment-controlled regression (does a merely negative-but-non-contaminating history produce less bending than a contaminating one?).

Causal validation: Activation patching. Take the activation difference between taint-history and neutral-history processing of the same P, decompose into truth-direction and taint-direction components, patch only the taint component into the neutral condition, and measure induced change in belief readout and output. Conversely subtract the taint component under the taint framing and measure whether belief returns to the content-driven value. Confirm the taint signal causally shifts the belief scalar independent of content.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether Contamination Belief Bending predicts a contamination-driven factual-error mode: (i) doubting/under-endorsing true statements about tainted entities, (ii) misjudging factual QA about tainted entities, and (iii) inconsistency across taint paraphrases. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (taint-intensity indicator, sentiment score, output entropy, neutral-history truth-probe confidence).

Contamination De-biasing intervention: At inference, estimate the contamination/taint direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer (ITI-style), so the belief readout reflects the fact's content rather than the entity's unrelated taint history. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected taint framing. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Contamination Belief Bending Score, (ii) reduced doubting of true unrelated facts about tainted entities and improved factual QA accuracy, (iii) calibration (ECE) on taint-framed factual QA, (iv) PRESERVATION of legitimate reputation-based reasoning (the reputation control, where taint genuinely bears on a virtue/trust claim, must still lower belief appropriately) and accuracy on neutral-history controls (no over-correction), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'judge each fact on its own merits, ignoring the entity's unrelated history', and a fresh-context re-ask baseline (query the fact with no history).

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), taint type (moral/physical/symbolic), taint intensity, real vs synthetic-in-context facts, true vs false regime, model scale, distance between the taint history and the fact query, contamination-vs-sentiment disentangling, and generalization to taint framings and entity types not used to fit the de-biasing direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent contamination belief bending could reflect the probe detecting taint-framing negative-sentiment lexical cues rather than a genuine contagion-specific belief shift; mitigate with surface-length matching, a sentiment-controlled regression (comparing contaminating vs merely-negative-but-non-contaminating histories), taint-paired-with-true-vs-false contrasts, paraphrase controls, synthetic-in-context facts, and causal patching that isolates the taint-direction component.

The taint history might be construed by the model as weak evidence about P (a dishonest person's stated facts could be doubted as possibly-fabricated); we human-verify framings carry no logical bearing on the specific factual claim (which concerns objective attributes like birth year, not entity-asserted claims), and treat any residual evidential leakage as a separately-analyzed confound.

Distinguishing illegitimate contagion from legitimate reputation reasoning is the crux; the reputation control (where taint genuinely bears on a virtue/trust claim) calibrates warranted lowering, and the de-biasing must preserve it — a key success criterion.

Truth probes trained on history-free statements may transfer imperfectly to taint-framed contexts, so bending could carry probe extrapolation error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, and synthetic facts to control priors.
Contamination and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality/project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

The De-biasing intervention could impair legitimate reputation-based reasoning or harm fluency; we explicitly measure preservation on the reputation control, neutral-history accuracy, and capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Contamination bending may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (sentiment score, taint-intensity indicator, output entropy) for contamination-driven errors; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that an entity's unrelated contamination history distorts internal factual belief (a law-of-contagion effect in belief geometry, distinct from generic negativity) plus the de-biasing tool, reported honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may amplify negativity/caution toward tainted entities); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: numerosity_belief_geometry
Title: Anchored to the Frame: Do LLM Internal Beliefs Track Absolute Quantity or Only Proportion When Judging Numeric Facts?
Short Hypothesis: For a factual claim about a quantity that can be framed as an ABSOLUTE count or an equivalent PROPORTION/ratio (e.g. '900 of 1,000 patients recovered' vs '90% of patients recovered', or 'a program that saves 200 of 600 lives' vs 'that lets 400 of 600 die'), an LLM's internal belief in whether the claim describes a large/severe/good outcome (linear truth-direction readout) is systematically bent by the numeric FRAMING even though the two framings denote the identical fact, an internal analogue of the human numerosity/ratio-bias and attribute-framing effects. We hypothesize this framing distortion is graded, carried by a decodable framing/format component dissociable from the truth axis, causally predicts a framing-dependent factual-inconsistency mode, and can be neutralized by a lightweight inference-time intervention that removes the framing component so belief reflects the underlying quantity rather than how it is expressed.
Related Work: Truth-direction/belief probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024; Bao et al. 2025) reads a scalar belief but never varies whether a numeric fact is framed as an absolute count vs an equivalent proportion/ratio while holding the denoted fact fixed. My prior 'numeric_magnitude_belief_snapping' proposal tested roundness/anchoring bias in belief about the truth of a stated numeric value; 'comparative_belief_distance_effect' tested magnitude-graded comparison confidence; 'base_rate_neglect_belief' tested prior-vs-individuating-evidence weighting; 'availability_heuristic_belief' tested retrieval-ease vs actual frequency. NONE isolate the NUMEROSITY / RATIO-BIAS and ATTRIBUTE-FRAMING effects — that a judgment of magnitude/severity/goodness is bent by whether an identical quantity is expressed as a large absolute count, a small proportion, or a gain-vs-loss ratio (the classic '200 saved of 600' vs '400 die of 600' Asian-disease framing, and the ratio-bias where '9/100' feels larger than '1/10'). This is a well-documented cluster in human judgment (Kahneman & Tversky's framing effects; Denes-Raj & Epstein's ratio bias) never examined in LLM belief geometry. Distinct from magnitude-snapping (roundness of a single value), from comparative-distance (gap between two values), and from base-rate/availability (which concern prior vs evidence and recall ease). This numerosity-framing lens on quantitative belief geometry is new and maps onto high-stakes framing failures in medical/risk communication where the same statistic drives opposite judgments.
Abstract: The same quantity can be framed to feel large or small: '9 out of 100' seems bigger than '1 out of 10' though they are equal, and a treatment that 'saves 200 of 600' is preferred over one that 'lets 400 of 600 die' though the outcomes are identical. Humans are famously swayed by such numeric framings — numerosity/ratio bias and gain-loss attribute framing. We ask whether large language models exhibit these biases inside their belief representations. Holding the denoted quantity fixed, we vary only its numeric framing — absolute count vs equivalent proportion, small-denominator vs large-denominator ratio, gain vs loss phrasing — and read the internal belief that the claim describes a large/severe/good outcome via linear truth probes. We construct FrameQuantBelief, a controlled dataset of quantitative propositions in matched framings, spanning medical/risk and everyday domains, plus synthetic-in-context quantities to control priors, with the denoted fact held identical. We define a Numerosity Framing Bias Score = belief(outcome large/good | framing A) minus belief(same outcome | equivalent framing B), and test four claims: (1) internal belief is bent by numeric framing at fixed denoted quantity, graded in framing contrast; (2) the bias is carried by a decodable framing/format component dissociable from the truth axis; (3) bias magnitude causally predicts a framing-dependent factual-inconsistency mode (the same statistic judged differently across framings, e.g. opposite gain-vs-loss verdicts); and (4) a lightweight intervention that subtracts the framing component restores quantity-driven belief and improves cross-framing consistency without harming legitimate quantitative reasoning or general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on quantitative-judgment consistency, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build FrameQuantBelief. Quantitative propositions in three truth regimes: real facts, false variants, and SYNTHETIC-in-context quantities (values stipulated in context, to remove parametric priors and give exact control). For each underlying quantity, create matched EQUIVALENT framings that denote the identical fact: (a) ABSOLUTE COUNT vs PROPORTION ('900 of 1,000 recovered' vs '90% recovered'); (b) RATIO-BIAS pairs (small-denominator vs large-denominator equal ratios, e.g. '1 of 10' vs '10 of 100'); (c) GAIN vs LOSS attribute framing (the Asian-disease-style '200 of 600 saved' vs '400 of 600 die'). Probe the belief in an EVALUATIVE proposition about the quantity ('this is a large/high/severe/good outcome') whose correct answer is framing-invariant. Draw items from MEDICAL/RISK domains (survival rates, side-effect frequencies, screening statistics) plus everyday domains. Match surface length across framings; human-verify that framings are numerically equivalent and that the evaluative target's correct answer is framing-invariant; include paraphrase sets and neutral controls.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At a matched query position (a canonical evaluative probe appended in a fresh pass, e.g. 'is this a large/good outcome?') read the internal belief under each framing. Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false items; confirm the model comprehends each framing (can convert count<->proportion when asked).

Numerosity Framing Bias measurement: Define Numerosity Framing Bias Score = belief(evaluative claim | framing A) minus belief(same claim | equivalent framing B), holding the denoted quantity fixed. Report per-layer, per-model bias for each framing contrast (count/proportion, ratio-bias, gain/loss) and domain. Test the hypotheses that (i) belief is bent by framing at fixed quantity, (ii) bias grows with framing contrast (e.g. larger denominator gap), and (iii) gain vs loss framing produces opposite-signed shifts. Compare internal bias to OUTPUT-level bias (does the model's verdict/preference differ across framings?), separating framing effects from response-format artifacts.

Framing-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'numeric-framing' direction via difference-in-means on activations under one framing vs its equivalent (balanced across denoted quantity and content); optionally a multi-way framing subspace. Report per-layer decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the framing axis (and vice versa); test whether the bias is explained by the framing component leaking into the truth-probe readout. Disentangle framing from surface token-length/format via controlled regression.

Causal validation: Activation patching. Take the activation difference between two equivalent framings of the same quantity, decompose into truth-direction and framing-direction components, patch only the framing component into a reference framing, and measure induced change in belief and output verdict. Conversely subtract the framing component and measure whether belief converges across framings. Confirm the framing signal causally shifts the belief scalar independent of the denoted quantity.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether Numerosity Framing Bias predicts a framing-dependent factual-inconsistency mode: (i) the same statistic judged large/good in one framing and small/bad in the equivalent framing, (ii) opposite gain-vs-loss verdicts/preferences, and (iii) confidence swings across framings. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (framing-type indicator, output entropy, reference-framing truth-probe confidence).

Framing De-biasing intervention: At inference, estimate the numeric-framing direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer (ITI-style), so belief reflects the underlying quantity rather than its framing. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected numeric-framing cues. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Numerosity Framing Bias Score, (ii) improved cross-framing consistency (same verdict/preference for equivalent framings) on FrameQuantBelief and adapted medical/risk framing benchmarks, (iii) calibration (ECE) aggregated across framings, (iv) PRESERVATION of legitimate quantitative reasoning (genuinely different quantities must still be judged differently) and accuracy on neutral controls, and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, self-consistency across framings, chain-of-thought ('convert to a common form first'), and prompt-based instruction to 'judge the underlying quantity, not how it is phrased'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), framing contrast type (count-proportion/ratio-bias/gain-loss), denominator gap, real vs synthetic-in-context quantities, medical/risk vs everyday domain, model scale, readout position, and generalization to framings not used to fit the de-biasing direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent numerosity framing bias could reflect the probe detecting framing-specific surface tokens (%, digits, denominators) rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with length matching, format-vs-content regression, paraphrase controls, synthetic-in-context quantities, and causal patching that isolates the framing-direction component.

Reading a comparable belief scalar across structurally different framings is position-sensitive; we standardize via a canonical evaluative probe appended in a fresh pass, include position/layer robustness checks, and report sensitivity of the bias score.

The model may genuinely mis-convert some framings (a numeric-comprehension failure, not a belief-framing failure); we include per-framing comprehension manipulation checks (count<->proportion conversion) and analyze comprehended vs mis-converted items separately.

Truth probes trained on neutral statements may transfer imperfectly to quantitative evaluative claims, so bias could carry probe extrapolation error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, and synthetic quantities to control priors.
Framing and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality/project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

The De-biasing intervention could over-correct (flattening genuine quantitative distinctions) or harm fluency; we explicitly measure preservation of legitimate quantitative reasoning and neutral controls plus capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Because LLMs encode numbers digit-wise (Levy & Geva 2024), observed framing bias may partly stem from magnitude-encoding artifacts; we probe the encoded quantity separately and analyze whether framing bias stems from encoding vs belief-level framing, treating this decomposition as a core finding.

Framing bias may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (framing-type indicator, output entropy) for cross-framing inconsistency; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that numeric framing distorts internal belief (numerosity/ratio/gain-loss bias in belief geometry) plus the de-biasing tool, reported honestly.
Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training; we test multiple models and report scale effects and negative results as informative.

Name: counterfactual_self_belief_reflexivity
Title: Would You Still Believe It If You Were Wrong Before? Testing Whether an LLM's Internal Belief Tracks Its Own Recent Track Record
Short Hypothesis: A calibrated agent should let its own recent demonstrated error rate feed back into how firmly it holds new beliefs: after just getting several factual questions wrong (an established poor track record), it should hold its next belief LESS firmly, and after a strong recent track record, MORE firmly. We hypothesize LLM internal belief representations (linear truth-direction readouts) FAIL this reflexive self-calibration: the internal belief in a new proposition is largely INSENSITIVE to the model's own just-demonstrated in-context accuracy, so confidence does not deflate after a run of self-errors nor inflate after a run of self-successes. This self-track-record insensitivity is measurable, dissociable from a decodable self-performance-history axis, causally predicts a persistent-overconfidence-after-errors failure mode, and can be corrected by a lightweight inference-time intervention that couples belief firmness to the decoded self-track-record.
Related Work: Truth-direction/belief probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024; Bao et al. 2025) reads a scalar belief but never conditions it on the model's OWN recent in-context performance. Calibration/self-knowledge work (Kadavath et al. 2022) studies whether a model knows if a single answer is right, at the output level, not whether belief firmness updates on a running self-track-record. Source-reliability work (my prior 'source_reliability_belief_weighting') concerned tracking an EXTERNAL named source's accuracy over turns; the present proposal is reflexive — the source whose reliability must be tracked is the MODEL ITSELF. 'belief_conviction_vs_content' and 'counterfactual_confidence_belief_geometry' concerned a conviction/robustness axis read at rest; 'metabelief_alignment' concerned belief-about-belief for a single proposition. NONE test whether an LLM feeds its OWN recently-demonstrated error rate back into how firmly it holds a subsequent belief (a metacognitive self-monitoring / error-driven-recalibration loop, well documented in human metacognition), whether a self-performance-history axis is decodable, whether its failure drives persistent overconfidence after errors, or whether it can be coupled. This reflexive self-track-record lens on belief geometry is new and directly relevant to agentic/multi-turn deployments where a model that just erred should hedge more.
Abstract: A metacognitively healthy agent uses its own recent mistakes to lower its confidence: after getting three questions wrong in a row it should hold its next answer more tentatively, and after a strong run more firmly. We ask whether large language models perform this reflexive self-calibration inside their belief representations, or whether the firmness of a new belief is blind to the model's own just-demonstrated accuracy. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar internal belief along the truth direction, we place a target proposition after a controlled run of prior in-context questions on which the model has recently SUCCEEDED or ERRED (with feedback), and measure whether the internal belief in the target is modulated by this self-track-record. We construct SelfTrackBelief, a controlled dataset of true, false, and synthetic-in-context target propositions preceded by manipulated self-performance histories (recent-error-streak vs recent-success-streak vs neutral), with track-record length graded and difficulty/content matched. We define a Self-Calibration Sensitivity Score = how much target-belief firmness moves with the model's own recent accuracy, and test four claims: (1) internal belief firmness is largely INSENSITIVE to self-track-record, whereas a rational agent would deflate after errors; (2) a self-performance-history axis is nonetheless decodable and dissociable from the truth axis; (3) low self-calibration sensitivity causally predicts a persistent-overconfidence-after-errors failure mode (confident-wrong answers immediately after a self-error streak); and (4) a lightweight intervention that couples belief firmness to the decoded self-track-record improves post-error calibration without harming performance after genuine successes or general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on calibration, error-streak overconfidence, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build SelfTrackBelief. Target propositions P in three truth regimes: real-true, real-false, and synthetic-in-context facts (to control priors). Each target is preceded by a controlled HISTORY of prior in-context questions the model just answered WITH FEEDBACK, manipulating the self-track-record: RECENT-ERROR-STREAK (the model got the preceding k questions wrong, made salient via feedback), RECENT-SUCCESS-STREAK (got them right), and NEUTRAL/no-history baseline. Grade streak length (k=2,4,6). Crucially, to actually induce self-errors, seed the history with items the model reliably fails (obscure/hard, verified in a pilot) for the error condition and reliably passes for the success condition, while the TARGET P is drawn from a matched, held-out difficulty distribution independent of the history topic (so history topic does not leak into target content). Include a CONTENT-MATCHED control where the history questions are equally hard but their outcomes are NOT made salient (no feedback), isolating self-track-record awareness from mere difficulty context. Match total surface length across conditions; human-verify labels; include paraphrase sets.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At a matched query position read the internal belief in the TARGET P under each history condition; also record output answer/confidence. Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false items; confirm the model actually erred on the error-streak history items and received/registered feedback (can report its recent accuracy when asked).

Self-Calibration Sensitivity measurement: Define target-belief FIRMNESS as |belief-0.5| (or a conviction readout). Define Self-Calibration Sensitivity Score = change in target-belief firmness from the error-streak to the success-streak condition, at matched target content and truth. A rational agent shows positive sensitivity (firmer after successes, more tentative after errors). Report per-layer, per-model sensitivity as a function of streak length. Test the hypothesis that sensitivity is near-zero (self-track-record insensitivity). Compare internal sensitivity to OUTPUT-level sensitivity (does verbalized confidence deflate after self-errors?), and to the no-feedback content-matched control (to isolate self-awareness from difficulty context).

Self-history-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'self-performance-history' direction via difference-in-means on error-streak vs success-streak activations at the target position (balanced across target truth-value and content). Report per-layer decoding accuracy (can the model's own recent accuracy be read from its state?); measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the self-history axis (and vice versa). Test whether the self-track-record is REPRESENTED in activations but simply fails to modulate belief firmness (a coupling failure) versus not represented at all.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Patch the self-history component from an error-streak processing into a success-streak processing of the same target and measure whether target-belief firmness and output confidence deflate as a rational agent's would. (b) Steer along the self-history direction and measure whether belief firmness and post-error overconfidence change. Confirm the self-track-record axis can causally modulate belief firmness (and that its natural failure to do so is the coupling gap).

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether low Self-Calibration Sensitivity predicts a persistent-overconfidence-after-errors failure mode: (i) confident-wrong answers on the target immediately following a self-error streak, (ii) failure of verbalized/internal confidence to deflate after errors, and (iii) miscalibration (ECE) conditioned on recent self-accuracy. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (streak length alone, output entropy, neutral-condition truth-probe confidence).

Self-Calibration Coupling intervention: At inference, decode the self-performance-history axis (the model's running recent accuracy) and couple it to belief firmness — an ITI-style shift that shrinks target-belief toward neutral (0.5) proportionally to a decoded recent-error signal, and preserves/raises firmness under a decoded recent-success signal. Provide a deployment variant that reads recent accuracy from in-context feedback. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) increased Self-Calibration Sensitivity, (ii) reduced persistent-overconfidence-after-errors (lower confident-wrong rate and better ECE on targets following self-error streaks), (iii) PRESERVATION of appropriate confidence after genuine success streaks (no over-hedging when the model is actually doing well) and accuracy on neutral controls, and (iv) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'consider how you have been doing recently and adjust your confidence accordingly', and a self-consistency baseline.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), streak length, feedback-salient vs no-feedback histories, real vs synthetic targets, true vs false targets, model scale, distance between history and target, and generalization to history/target domains not used to fit the self-history direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent self-track-record insensitivity could reflect the probe reading a target-position token that does not incorporate the history, so a null could be a readout artifact; mitigate with position/layer sweeps, the self-history-axis dissociation analysis (is recent accuracy represented but uncoupled?), and causal patching that shows the axis CAN modulate firmness when amplified.

Inducing genuine self-errors requires history items the model reliably fails, which may correlate with topic/difficulty that leaks into the target; we draw targets from a matched but topically-independent distribution, include a no-feedback difficulty-matched control, and human-verify independence.

Firmness measured as |belief-0.5| may conflate with truth-axis distance; we corroborate with a separate conviction readout and report sensitivity to the firmness definition, and a finding that firmness is intrinsically decoupled from the truth axis is itself informative.

Truth probes trained on neutral statements may transfer imperfectly to multi-turn history-laden contexts, so sensitivity could carry probe extrapolation error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, and synthetic targets to control priors.

The Self-Calibration Coupling intervention could over-hedge after occasional errors (harming performance when the model is actually competent) or destabilize confidence; we explicitly measure preservation after genuine success streaks and neutral controls plus capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Self-calibration insensitivity may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (streak length, output entropy) for post-error overconfidence; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic finding that belief firmness is decoupled from the model's own decodable track record (a metacognitive self-monitoring gap) plus the coupling tool, reported honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF may or may not instill error-driven recalibration); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: defeasible_override_belief_geometry
Title: Does the Exception Win? Testing Whether Specific Exceptions Properly Override General Defaults in LLM Belief Geometry
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM internally holds a general default rule ('birds fly') and is given a specific exception ('this bird is a penguin; penguins don't fly'), a competent defeasible reasoner must let the specific exception OVERRIDE the default so that the internal belief in the default-derived conclusion ('this bird flies') is suppressed. We hypothesize LLM internal belief representations (linear truth-direction readouts) FAIL proper override: the default-derived belief persists and often dominates the exception, so the model internally 'believes' the default conclusion despite a known applicable exception. This override failure is graded in default strength and exception specificity, carried by a decodable default-vs-exception component dissociable from the truth axis, causally predicts a default-override hallucination mode, and can be reduced by an inference-time intervention that enforces exception dominance.
Related Work: Output-level work shows LLMs struggle with defeasible/non-monotonic reasoning: Kirkpatrick & Sterken (2025, 'Generics and Default Reasoning in LLMs') find models misinterpret generics as universals and that CoT degrades default reasoning; 'Confidently Wrong: Exception Chain Collapse' (2026) documents frontier models failing nested 'A unless B unless C' rules; LOGicalThought (2025) shows LLMs need symbolic scaffolding for exception-laden rules. All are behavioral/accuracy studies; none examine belief GEOMETRY. Truth-direction/belief probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024; Bao et al. 2025) reads a scalar belief but never tests whether a specific exception properly overrides an internally-held general default. My prior 'belief_coherence_geometry' tested STRICT deductive rules (modus ponens, contraposition) where premises are indefeasible; 'taxonomic_belief_monotonicity' tested is-a subsumption monotonicity; 'belief_ghost_revision' tested residue after a completed in-context fact flip; 'conditional_belief_indexing' tested conditioning on an antecedent. NONE isolate DEFEASIBLE OVERRIDE — the non-monotonic competition where a specific exception must defeat a general default rule the model holds — in belief geometry, treat default-vs-exception as a decodable competing axis, tie override failure to a hallucination mode, or enforce exception dominance via intervention. This defeasible-override lens is new and maps onto high-stakes exception-heavy domains (law, medicine, eligibility rules) where the failure carries real consequences.
Abstract: Everyday reasoning is defeasible: 'birds fly' is a good default, but a specific fact ('this bird is a penguin') must override it. We ask whether large language models honor this override inside their belief representations, or whether a general default the model holds persists and dominates a known applicable exception. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar belief along the truth direction, we present a general default rule together with a specific exception and read the internal belief in the default-DERIVED conclusion (which the exception should defeat). We construct DefeasibleBelief, a controlled dataset pairing generic default rules with specific exceptions — real-world generics (birds fly / penguins), and synthetic-in-context defeasible rules ('all glorps are blue, unless they are old') to control priors — crossed with default strength, exception specificity, and truth-value, plus strict-rule (indefeasible) controls. We define a Default-Override Failure Score = residual belief in the default-derived conclusion after an applicable exception is given, and test four claims: (1) belief fails to override, with the default-derived conclusion still internally believed despite the exception, graded in default strength; (2) a decodable default-vs-exception competition component is dissociable from the truth axis; (3) override-failure magnitude causally predicts a default-override hallucination mode (asserting the default conclusion for an exceptional case); and (4) a lightweight Exception-Dominance intervention that steers belief toward the exception-consistent conclusion reduces the failure while preserving correct default application to non-exceptional cases and general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on defeasible-reasoning accuracy, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build DefeasibleBelief. Each item = a GENERAL DEFAULT rule + a SPECIFIC EXCEPTION applied to an instance, with a probed CONCLUSION the exception should defeat. Two sources: (a) REAL-WORLD generics with well-known exceptions (birds fly / penguins; mammals give live birth / platypus; sharp objects cut / a butter knife); (b) SYNTHETIC-in-context defeasible rules over nonce entities ('All glorps are blue; old glorps are not blue; this glorp is old') to remove parametric priors and give exact ground truth. For each, probe belief in the DEFAULT-DERIVED conclusion ('this glorp is blue' / 'this penguin flies') which is FALSE given the exception. Cross with: DEFAULT STRENGTH (near-universal generic vs weak default), EXCEPTION SPECIFICITY (explicit direct exception vs one requiring a chaining step), and include: STRICT-RULE controls (indefeasible universals where the 'exception' does not apply, so the conclusion holds), NON-EXCEPTIONAL controls (default correctly applies, so the derived conclusion is true), and a no-exception baseline. Match surface forms; human-verify defeasible-vs-strict labels; include paraphrase sets.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At a matched query position read the internal belief in the default-derived conclusion (i) with only the default rule present (baseline, conclusion should be believed), and (ii) after the applicable exception is added (conclusion should now be disbelieved). Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false items; confirm the model behaviorally holds the default and comprehends the exception.

Default-Override Failure measurement: Define Default-Override Failure Score = internal belief in the default-derived conclusion AFTER the applicable exception is presented (high = failed override; a competent reasoner drops belief toward false). Report per-layer, per-model failure as a function of default strength and exception specificity, for real vs synthetic items. Test the hypotheses that (i) override often fails (default belief persists), and (ii) failure grows with default strength and with exception-chaining depth. Contrast with STRICT-RULE controls (belief should stay high, correctly) and NON-EXCEPTIONAL controls (belief should stay high) to isolate genuine override failure from generic insensitivity. Compare internal failure to OUTPUT-level failure (does the model assert the default conclusion for the exceptional case?).

Default-vs-exception-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'default-vs-exception competition' direction via difference-in-means on exception-applied vs no-exception activations at the conclusion-query position (balanced across truth-value and content). Report per-layer decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the competition axis (and vice versa); test whether override failure corresponds to the default component dominating the truth-probe readout, or whether the exception is represented but fails to suppress the default-derived belief.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Steer along the exception (competition) direction toward exception-dominance at a chosen layer and measure whether the default-derived belief and output flip toward the exception-consistent (false) answer. (b) In synthetic items, patch the exception representation into a no-exception context and measure whether the derived belief is suppressed. (c) Conversely suppress the exception component and confirm the default belief re-dominates. Confirm the default-vs-exception competition causally governs the conclusion belief.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether the Default-Override Failure Score predicts a default-override hallucination mode: (i) asserting the default conclusion for an exceptional case (e.g. 'penguins fly'), (ii) defeasible-reasoning QA errors, and (iii) inconsistency across exception paraphrases and chaining depths. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (default-strength indicator, output entropy, no-exception baseline truth-probe confidence).

Exception-Dominance intervention: At inference, estimate the default-vs-exception competition direction (from the probe) and add a scaled shift toward exception-dominance along the truth direction at a chosen layer (ITI-style), so an applicable specific exception suppresses the default-derived belief. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected exception clauses ('unless', 'except', a specific overriding fact). Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Default-Override Failure Score, (ii) improved defeasible-reasoning accuracy (correctly rejecting default conclusions for exceptional cases) on DefeasibleBelief and adapted generics/exception-chain benchmarks (Kirkpatrick & Sterken generics patterns; nested 'A unless B unless C' items), (iii) calibration (ECE), (iv) PRESERVATION of correct DEFAULT application to NON-EXCEPTIONAL cases and of STRICT-RULE conclusions (the intervention must not suppress defaults when no exception applies — the core specificity check), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, chain-of-thought prompting (which prior work shows can HURT default reasoning — a useful comparison), and prompt-based instruction to 'let specific exceptions override general rules'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), default strength, exception specificity/chaining depth, real vs synthetic-in-context rules, model scale, distance between exception and conclusion query, and generalization to exception structures and domains not used to fit the competition direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent override failure could reflect the probe detecting default-rule lexical cues rather than a genuine belief; mitigate with synthetic-in-context rules (guaranteed no parametric prior), matched surface forms, paraphrase controls, and causal patching that isolates the competition component. STRICT-RULE and NON-EXCEPTIONAL controls distinguish genuine override failure from generic insensitivity.

The model may fail to COMPREHEND the exception (a parsing failure, not an override failure); we include behavioral manipulation checks that the model can restate the exception and analyze comprehended vs non-comprehended items separately.

Truth probes trained on neutral declaratives may transfer imperfectly to defeasible-conclusion statements, so failure could carry probe extrapolation error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, and synthetic rules with exact ground truth.

Default-vs-exception and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality/project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

The Exception-Dominance intervention could over-suppress correct defaults on non-exceptional cases (making the model reject valid default conclusions) or harm fluency; we explicitly measure preservation on NON-EXCEPTIONAL and STRICT-RULE controls plus capability retention to characterize the tradeoff — the core risk is breaking legitimate default reasoning.

Override failure may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (default-strength indicator, output entropy) for default-override hallucination; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that belief geometry fails defeasible override (specific exceptions do not defeat internally-held defaults) plus the exception-dominance tool, reported honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF/CoT-tuning may help or, per prior work, hurt default reasoning); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: ensemble_belief_aggregation
Title: Believing the Forest but Not the Trees: Do LLM Internal Beliefs About Group-Level Statistics Cohere With Beliefs About Members?
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's internal belief in a group/aggregate-level claim (an ensemble statistic over a described set of members, e.g. 'the average of these five values exceeds 50', 'most of these items are red', 'the group's total is over 1000') should be a lawful function of its internal beliefs about the individual member facts. We hypothesize LLM belief geometry systematically FAILS this member-to-aggregate coherence: the decoded belief in an ensemble-statistic claim tracks a salient or extreme member (or the group's gist) rather than the correct aggregate, so aggregate beliefs are internally incoherent with the member beliefs that determine them. This mismatch is graded in set size and member variance, carried by a decodable gist/salient-member component dissociable from the truth axis, causally predicts an aggregation-error hallucination mode, and can be reduced by a lightweight inference-time intervention that recomputes the aggregate belief from member beliefs.
Related Work: Truth-direction/belief probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024; Bao et al. 2025 ACL) reads a scalar belief per proposition but never tests whether belief in an ENSEMBLE STATISTIC over a set coheres with beliefs about the set's members. My prior 'quantifier_belief_aggregation' proposal tested LOGICAL/counting quantifiers ('all', 'exactly k' true) over a set of TRUTH-VALUES; the present proposal targets a distinct and more general object: NUMERIC/CATEGORICAL ENSEMBLE STATISTICS (mean, sum, max, mode, proportion) over member ATTRIBUTES, where the psychological failure mode is gist-based / salient-member anchoring rather than mis-counting truth-values. 'belief_load_crosstalk' concerned truth-value bleeding across co-held facts; 'numeric_magnitude_belief_snapping' concerned roundness bias for a single value; 'comparative_belief_distance_effect' concerned pairwise comparisons; 'base_rate_neglect_belief' concerned prior-vs-individuating evidence. NONE test whether internal belief about a group aggregate is a coherent function of member beliefs, whether it collapses onto a gist/extreme-member representation, whether this drives aggregation-error hallucination, or whether it can be recomputed from members. In human cognition this maps onto ensemble/summary-statistics perception and gist-based (fuzzy-trace) reasoning, where people extract a group gist but mis-compute exact aggregates. This member-to-aggregate coherence lens on belief geometry is new and maps onto real reliability failures (LLMs misstating averages/totals/proportions when reasoning over described sets, data tables, or search results).
Abstract: Reasoning over groups requires aggregating members correctly: the average of a set, the total, the most common category, the proportion satisfying a property. A coherent believer's confidence in a group-level claim must follow from its beliefs about the members. We ask whether large language models honor this member-to-aggregate coherence inside their belief representations, or whether they anchor on a group gist or a salient/extreme member. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar belief along the linear truth direction, we read the model's belief in each member fact of a described set AND its belief in an ensemble-statistic claim about the set (mean, sum, max, mode, proportion), then test whether the aggregate belief matches what the member beliefs imply. We construct EnsembleBelief, a controlled dataset of member sets (real and synthetic-in-context to control priors) paired with true and false aggregate-statistic claims, with set size and member variance varied and a salient/extreme outlier planted to elicit anchoring. We define an Aggregation Incoherence Score = discrepancy between the decoded aggregate belief and the aggregate computed from decoded member beliefs, and test four claims: (1) aggregate beliefs are incoherent with member beliefs, driven by gist/salient-member anchoring, growing with set size and variance; (2) a decodable gist/salient-member component is dissociable from the truth axis; (3) incoherence causally predicts an aggregation-error hallucination mode; and (4) a lightweight intervention that recomputes the aggregate belief from member beliefs improves accuracy and calibration without harming member-level judgments or general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on aggregate-statistic QA, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build EnsembleBelief. Each item = a described SET of N members with numeric or categorical attributes (N in {3,4,6,8}), plus true and false ENSEMBLE-STATISTIC claims about the set: MEAN/SUM ('the average of these values is above 50'; 'the total exceeds 1000'), MAX/MIN ('the largest is over 90'), MODE/PROPORTION ('most of these items are red'; 'more than half are large'). Compute the exact ground-truth aggregate for each set. Use real-world member sets (e.g. described objects/people with attributes) plus SYNTHETIC-in-context sets (member attributes stipulated only in context) to remove parametric priors and give exact control. Systematically vary MEMBER VARIANCE and plant a SALIENT/EXTREME OUTLIER (one member far from the aggregate) in half the items to elicit anchoring; balance so the outlier sometimes pulls the correct answer and sometimes away from it. Match surface form/length; human-verify labels; include paraphrase sets.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral atomic true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. For each set, read (a) the internal belief in each MEMBER-attribute fact and (b) the internal belief in each AGGREGATE-STATISTIC claim (at the aggregate-claim query position). Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false atomic items; confirm member beliefs track the stated member attributes.

Aggregation Incoherence measurement: From the decoded member beliefs (and stated attributes), compute the member-IMPLIED aggregate and the member-implied belief in each aggregate claim. Define Aggregation Incoherence Score = |decoded aggregate-claim belief - member-implied aggregate-claim belief|. Report per-layer, per-model incoherence broken down by statistic type (mean/sum/max/mode/proportion), set size, and variance. Test the hypotheses that (i) aggregate beliefs are incoherent with member beliefs, (ii) incoherence grows with set size and member variance, and (iii) incoherence is larger for statistics sensitive to distribution shape (mean/proportion) than to extremes (max) when a salient outlier is present. Diagnose GIST/SALIENT-MEMBER ANCHORING: does the aggregate belief track the planted extreme member or the group gist rather than the true aggregate? Compare internal incoherence to OUTPUT-level incoherence (directly asking the model the aggregate vs member facts).

Gist/salient-member-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'gist/salient-member' direction via difference-in-means on aggregate-claim activations for items where the salient member pulls toward vs away from the correct aggregate (balanced across truth-value). Report per-layer decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the gist component (and vice versa); test whether incoherence corresponds to the gist/salient-member component dominating the aggregate-claim belief readout while the true-aggregate signal under-modulates it.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Flip one member's decoded attribute belief (steer along the truth direction) and measure whether the aggregate belief updates in the aggregate-appropriate direction and magnitude (e.g. changing one member should shift the mean-claim belief proportionally). (b) Patch the salient-member/gist component into a low-variance set and measure induced incoherence. Confirm the aggregate belief is causally linked to member beliefs and that the gist component causally drives incoherence.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether Aggregation Incoherence predicts an aggregation-error hallucination mode: (i) errors on aggregate-statistic QA (the model's yes/no answer to the aggregate claim disagrees with ground truth), (ii) errors where the answer requires aggregating over described members or a data table, and (iii) inconsistency across aggregate paraphrases. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (set size alone, member variance, output entropy, mean member truth-probe confidence).

Aggregation-Recompute intervention: At inference, given the decoded member beliefs and stated attributes, recompute the correct aggregate for the queried statistic and either (a) answer directly from this recomputed value, or (b) steer the aggregate-claim readout along the truth direction toward the member-implied value (ITI-style), and/or subtract the gist/salient-member component. Provide a deployment variant that reads members from the same context and recomputes without ground-truth labels. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Aggregation Incoherence Score, (ii) improved aggregate-statistic QA accuracy across statistic types and set sizes, (iii) improved accuracy on multi-member / table-aggregation tasks, (iv) calibration (ECE) on aggregate claims, (v) PRESERVATION of member-level accuracy (no over-correction), and (vi) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, chain-of-thought ('list each member then compute the statistic'), and prompt-based instruction to 'compute the aggregate from all members, not from the most salient one'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), statistic type, set size, member variance, salient-outlier present vs absent (and pulling toward vs away), real vs synthetic-in-context sets, aggregation function used for the member-implied value, model scale, and generalization to statistics and set structures not used to fit the intervention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Truth probes trained on atomic statements may transfer imperfectly to aggregate-statistic claims, so measured incoherence could partly reflect probe extrapolation rather than genuine internal inconsistency; mitigate with multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, synthetic sets to control priors, and causal patching that links member and aggregate beliefs.

The member-implied aggregate value depends on the chosen aggregation function and on treating member beliefs as calibrated; miscalibration across members could make the implied value ill-posed. We test multiple aggregation functions, use Platt-scaled probes, and anchor quantitative claims on synthetic sets with exact ground truth.

Apparent gist/salient-member anchoring could reflect the probe detecting surface features of the outlier rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with balanced outlier-pull conditions, paraphrase controls, and causal patching isolating the gist component.

Because LLMs encode numbers digit-wise (Levy & Geva 2024) and may mis-compute arithmetic, incoherence in numeric statistics could stem from computation error rather than belief-aggregation failure; we contrast numeric (mean/sum) with categorical (mode/proportion) statistics and separately probe whether members are correctly encoded, treating this decomposition as a core finding.
Reading a comparable belief scalar for members and aggregates at matched positions is token/position sensitive; include position and layer robustness checks and report sensitivity.

The Aggregation-Recompute intervention requires reliable member readouts at inference; noisy member beliefs may make recomputation error-prone and the deployment variant weaker — we characterize this gap honestly and measure member-accuracy preservation.

Incoherence may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (set size, member variance, mean member confidence, output entropy) for aggregate-QA errors; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic finding that belief geometry fails member-to-aggregate coherence via gist/salient-member anchoring, plus the recompute tool, reported honestly.
Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training; we test multiple models and report scale effects and negative results as informative.

Name: identity_persistence_belief_geometry
Title: Ship of Theseus in the Machine: Do LLM Internal Beliefs Track Object Identity Persistence Across Incremental Change?
Short Hypothesis: When an object undergoes a sequence of incremental changes (gradual part replacement, renaming, relocation, transformation), a competent believer must maintain that its IDENTITY persists ('this is still the same object') across small changes yet appropriately judge identity broken by wholesale/discontinuous replacement. We hypothesize that LLM internal belief representations (linear truth-direction readouts) FAIL to track identity persistence coherently: the decoded belief in the identity-continuity proposition ('X_now is the same object as X_original') erodes monotonically with the CUMULATIVE AMOUNT of change (a sorites-of-identity gradient) rather than respecting the actual continuity of the causal history, so the model both loses identity for objects that should retain it (gradual replacement) and preserves identity for objects that should not (a wholesale swap disguised as gradual). This identity-persistence failure is graded, carried by a decodable change-magnitude/persistence component dissociable from the truth axis, causally predicts an identity-confusion factual-error mode, and can be reduced by a lightweight inference-time intervention that re-anchors identity belief to causal continuity rather than accumulated change.
Related Work: Truth-direction/belief probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024; Bao et al. 2025) reads a scalar belief per proposition but never probes belief in an object's IDENTITY PERSISTENCE across a sequence of changes. Extensive OUTPUT-level entity/state-tracking work exists (OAKS, Kim et al. 2026; VSTAT, Yu et al. 2026; LLM-State, Chen et al. 2023; world-model probing) and philosophical accounts of 'state-of-the-world understanding' (Beckmann & Queloz 2025) discuss dynamically tracking changes, but all treat state-tracking as recording an object's ATTRIBUTES, never the distinct question of whether the object remains the SAME entity (numerical identity) through change, and never read a graded internal identity-continuity belief. My prior belief proposals cover temporal indexing of a fact's validity (time_indexed), agent-holder binding, alias substitutivity (opaque_belief_alias_binding, which concerns co-referring NAMES at a fixed time, not persistence through change), belief ghosts after revision, and taxonomic/granularity monotonicity. NONE address IDENTITY PERSISTENCE / the ship-of-Theseus (sorites-of-identity) problem in belief geometry: whether the model represents that an object survives gradual change but not wholesale replacement, whether identity belief erodes with accumulated change rather than tracking causal continuity, whether this drives an identity-confusion error mode, or whether it can be re-anchored. This object-persistence lens — borrowing a classic problem from philosophy and developmental psychology (object permanence, identity through change) — is new and maps onto real reliability failures in long-context agentic/entity-tracking deployments where models lose or conflate object identity as scenes evolve.
Abstract: A cup that loses its handle and gets a new one is still the same cup; a cup secretly swapped for a different cup is not — identity persists through gradual change but not wholesale replacement. This ship-of-Theseus problem is a hallmark of coherent thought about objects. We ask whether large language models honor identity persistence inside their belief representations. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar belief along the linear truth direction, we present a sequence of incremental changes to an object and read the model's internal belief in the identity-continuity proposition ('the object now is the same object as at the start'). A competent believer should hold this belief high across gradual, causally-continuous changes and drop it only at genuine identity-breaking events; we hypothesize instead that the belief erodes monotonically with the cumulative amount of change (a sorites gradient) and is insensitive to whether the causal history is actually continuous. We construct TheseusBelief, a controlled dataset of objects undergoing graded change sequences — gradual part-by-part replacement (identity should persist), a single wholesale swap (identity broken), and a discontinuous-but-disguised swap and a gradual-but-total replacement to dissociate change-magnitude from causal continuity — using real and synthetic-in-context objects. We define an Identity Persistence Failure Score and test four claims: (1) identity belief erodes with cumulative change rather than tracking causal continuity; (2) a decodable change-magnitude/persistence component is dissociable from the truth axis; (3) the failure causally predicts an identity-confusion error mode (losing identity for continuous objects, preserving it for swapped ones); and (4) a lightweight intervention that re-anchors identity belief to causal continuity reduces the failure without harming legitimate identity-breaking judgments or general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on identity-QA accuracy, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build TheseusBelief. Each item establishes an object X and applies a SEQUENCE of changes, after which we probe the identity-continuity proposition 'the object now is the same object as the original X'. Design conditions to dissociate CUMULATIVE CHANGE MAGNITUDE from CAUSAL CONTINUITY: (a) GRADUAL-CONTINUOUS — part-by-part replacement / incremental modification / renaming / relocation where the single persisting object is continuously modified (identity SHOULD persist even at high cumulative change, the ship-of-Theseus case); (b) WHOLESALE-SWAP — the object is replaced in one step by a different object (identity BROKEN, low cumulative gradualness); (c) DISGUISED-SWAP — a discontinuous replacement described in gradual-sounding language (identity broken but framed to look gradual); (d) GRADUAL-BUT-TOTAL — continuous replacement of every part (the philosophically-contested high-cumulative-change-but-continuous case). Vary the number of change steps and cumulative fraction changed. Use real-world objects plus SYNTHETIC-in-context objects (nonce objects whose parts/history are stipulated) to remove parametric priors and give exact control over continuity. Include identity-BREAKING ground-truth events and identity-PRESERVING events; match surface length; human-verify identity labels for clear cases and analyze the philosophically-contested gradual-but-total case separately; include paraphrase sets.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. After presenting a change sequence, at a matched query position read the internal belief in the identity-continuity proposition, and additionally read it after each step to trace an identity-belief trajectory. Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false items; confirm the model comprehends the change sequence (can report what changed).

Identity Persistence Failure measurement: Plot internal identity-continuity belief vs cumulative change for each condition. Define an Identity Persistence Failure Score capturing two errors: (i) EROSION — belief in identity continuity for GRADUAL-CONTINUOUS objects declining with cumulative change even though identity should persist (a sorites gradient); and (ii) FALSE-PERSISTENCE — belief in identity continuity remaining high for WHOLESALE-SWAP / DISGUISED-SWAP objects where identity is broken. Report per-layer, per-model failure as a function of cumulative change and number of steps. Test the central hypotheses: (a) identity belief tracks cumulative change magnitude rather than causal continuity (GRADUAL-CONTINUOUS and GRADUAL-BUT-TOTAL erode similarly despite differing continuity; DISGUISED-SWAP retains identity like GRADUAL despite being a swap), and (b) the erosion is monotone/graded. Compare internal identity belief to OUTPUT-level answers ('is it still the same object?').

Change-magnitude/persistence-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'cumulative-change/persistence' direction via difference-in-means on high- vs low-cumulative-change activations (balanced across true continuity), and separately a 'causal-continuity' direction on continuous vs discontinuous histories (balanced across change magnitude). Report per-layer decoding accuracy of each; measure cosine similarities among change-magnitude, causal-continuity, and truth directions; project out one and re-decode the others. Test whether identity belief is dominated by the change-magnitude component while the causal-continuity component under-modulates it (the mechanistic substrate of the failure).
