Name: hindsight_belief_contamination
Title: Knowing the Answer Poisons the Question: Do LLM Internal Beliefs Exhibit Hindsight Bias / Curse of Knowledge?
Short Hypothesis: Once an LLM has been shown (or has itself produced) the outcome/answer to a question, its INTERNAL belief (linear truth-direction readout) about what a naive agent WOULD or SHOULD have believed, and about how PREDICTABLE the outcome was beforehand, is contaminated toward the now-known answer — an internal analogue of the human hindsight bias / curse of knowledge. We hypothesize this contamination is graded in how salient the revealed answer is, carried by a decodable outcome-knowledge component dissociable from the truth axis, causally predicts a hindsight-error mode (overstating foreseeability and misattributing the known answer to an uninformed party), and can be reduced by a lightweight inference-time intervention that quarantines the outcome-knowledge component.
Related Work: Hindsight bias ('I knew it all along') and the curse of knowledge are among the most robust findings in human judgment (Fischhoff 1975; Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber 1989), yet they have not been examined in LLM belief geometry. Truth-direction/belief probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024; Bao et al. 2025) reads a scalar belief but never tests whether KNOWING an outcome contaminates belief about pre-outcome foreseeability or about an uninformed agent's belief. My prior 'agent_indexed_belief_binding' and 'counterfactual_identity_belief_binding' concerned binding beliefs to agents/personas at a fixed information state, not the asymmetry induced by the model's own outcome-knowledge leaking backward in time; 'belief_ghost_revision' concerned residue of a superseded belief after revision, not contamination of a hypothetical prior-state judgment by known outcomes; 'self_persuasion' concerned arguing a side. NONE isolate hindsight/curse-of-knowledge — that possessing the answer distorts the model's belief about the pre-answer epistemic situation (foreseeability) and about what an uninformed party knows — as a decodable, causally-manipulable belief axis. This lens borrows a classic human-sciences bias into belief geometry and maps onto real failures: LLMs overstating how predictable events were and leaking answers when simulating naive users (bad tutoring, unfair post-hoc evaluation, contaminated Theory-of-Mind).
Abstract: People who know how a story ended believe they 'knew it all along' and cannot help assuming others share their knowledge — hindsight bias and the curse of knowledge. We ask whether large language models exhibit these biases inside their belief representations. Distinguishing a claim's content from the model's OUTCOME-KNOWLEDGE, we use difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar internal belief along the truth direction for two hindsight-sensitive targets: (i) FORESEEABILITY — 'this outcome was predictable in advance' — and (ii) NAIVE-AGENT belief — 'an uninformed person would believe/answer X'. We construct HindsightBelief, a controlled dataset of outcomes/answers each probed in a FORESIGHT condition (outcome not yet revealed) versus a HINDSIGHT condition (outcome revealed to the model), with revealed-answer salience graded, using real events, puzzle answers, and synthetic-in-context scenarios to control priors. We define a Hindsight Contamination Score = belief(foreseeability / naive-belief | outcome known) minus belief(| outcome unknown), and test four claims: (1) internal belief about pre-outcome foreseeability and about a naive agent's belief is contaminated toward the known answer, graded in salience; (2) the contamination is carried by a decodable outcome-knowledge component dissociable from the truth axis; (3) contamination magnitude causally predicts a hindsight-error mode (overstating foreseeability, leaking the known answer into simulated naive agents); and (4) a lightweight intervention that quarantines the outcome-knowledge component reduces the bias while preserving legitimate use of the outcome and general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on foreseeability calibration, Theory-of-Mind leakage, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build HindsightBelief. Items span three sources: (a) REAL EVENTS with an outcome (a match result, an election, an experiment's finding); (b) PUZZLE/QA items with a definite answer; (c) SYNTHETIC-in-context scenarios (nonce events whose outcome is stipulated in context, to remove parametric priors and control salience exactly). Each item is probed on two HINDSIGHT-SENSITIVE targets: FORESEEABILITY ('before the outcome, this was highly predictable') and NAIVE-AGENT belief ('an uninformed observer would believe/answer X', where X is or is not the true outcome). Create matched FORESIGHT vs HINDSIGHT conditions differing only in whether the outcome/answer has been revealed to the model, holding the probed target's surface form fixed. Grade revealed-answer SALIENCE (briefly mentioned vs emphasized). Include items where the true outcome was genuinely predictable vs genuinely surprising (so contamination can be separated from correct foreseeability), and NAIVE-agent items where the correct naive belief differs from the outcome. Match surface length; human-verify outcome, foreseeability, and naive-belief labels; include paraphrase sets.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At a matched query position read the internal belief in the foreseeability and naive-agent target propositions under FORESIGHT vs HINDSIGHT; also record the OUTPUT answer/confidence. Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false items; confirm the model registers whether the outcome was revealed.

Hindsight Contamination measurement: Define Hindsight Contamination Score = belief(target | outcome known, HINDSIGHT) minus belief(target | outcome unknown, FORESIGHT), for foreseeability and naive-agent targets separately. Report per-layer, per-model contamination across salience and item source. Test the hypotheses that (i) knowing the outcome inflates belief that it was foreseeable and pulls the simulated naive-agent belief toward the known answer, and (ii) contamination grows with revealed-answer salience. Crucially, on genuinely-surprising outcomes, foreseeability belief should stay low but hindsight predicts it rises; on naive-agent items where the correct naive answer differs from the outcome, hindsight predicts leakage of the outcome. Compare internal contamination to OUTPUT-level behavior (does the model verbally overstate predictability / leak the answer to the naive agent?).

Outcome-knowledge-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit an 'outcome-knowledge' direction via difference-in-means on HINDSIGHT vs FORESIGHT activations at the target-query position (balanced across target truth-value and content). Report per-layer decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the outcome-knowledge axis (and vice versa); test whether contamination is explained by the outcome-knowledge component leaking into the target-belief readout.

Causal validation: Activation patching. Take the activation difference between HINDSIGHT and FORESIGHT processing of the same target, decompose into truth-direction and outcome-knowledge components, patch only the outcome-knowledge component into the FORESIGHT condition, and measure induced contamination of the foreseeability/naive-agent belief and output. Conversely subtract the outcome-knowledge component under HINDSIGHT and measure whether the target belief returns to the uncontaminated value. Confirm the outcome-knowledge signal causally contaminates the belief scalar independent of the target's true value.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether the Hindsight Contamination Score predicts a hindsight-error mode: (i) overstating foreseeability of genuinely-surprising outcomes, (ii) leaking the known answer into a simulated naive agent (a Theory-of-Mind / answer-leakage failure, e.g. when asked to role-play an uninformed student), and (iii) inconsistency between foresight and hindsight judgments of the same event. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (salience indicator, output entropy, foresight-condition truth-probe confidence).

Outcome-Quarantine intervention: At inference, estimate the outcome-knowledge direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer when the model must reason about the pre-outcome situation or a naive agent (ITI-style), so foreseeability/naive-belief judgments are insulated from the known outcome. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected hindsight framing. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Hindsight Contamination Score, (ii) improved foreseeability calibration (not overstating predictability of surprising outcomes) and reduced answer-leakage into simulated naive agents (better naive-Theory-of-Mind on adapted false-belief / uninformed-observer items), (iii) calibration (ECE) on foreseeability/naive-belief judgments, (iv) PRESERVATION of legitimate use of the outcome (when the model IS asked what actually happened, it must still report the outcome accurately — the core specificity check) and accuracy on foresight controls, and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'reason as if you did not yet know the outcome', and a fresh-context re-ask baseline (probe foreseeability without the outcome revealed).

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), target type (foreseeability vs naive-agent), salience level, real events vs puzzles vs synthetic scenarios, surprising vs predictable outcomes, model scale, distance between outcome reveal and target query, and generalization to hindsight framings not used to fit the outcome-knowledge direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent hindsight contamination could reflect the probe detecting the revealed-outcome lexical cues rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with surface-form matching between foresight and hindsight targets, paraphrase controls, synthetic-in-context scenarios, and causal patching that isolates the outcome-knowledge component.

The effect could be purely at the OUTPUT level (the model leaks the answer in text but its internal foreseeability belief is intact); the internal-vs-output comparison and causal patching directly test this, and either outcome is informative.

Distinguishing hindsight contamination from CORRECT updating is the crux: for genuinely-predictable outcomes, high foreseeability belief in hindsight may be warranted. We include genuinely-surprising outcomes (where hindsight belief should stay low) and naive-agent items where the correct answer differs from the outcome, so contamination is measured as inflation beyond the warranted value; the de-biasing must not erase legitimate foreseeability.

Truth probes trained on neutral statements may transfer imperfectly to foreseeability/naive-agent propositions, so contamination could carry probe extrapolation error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, and synthetic scenarios to control priors.
Outcome-knowledge and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality/project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

The Outcome-Quarantine intervention could impair legitimate use of the outcome (e.g. the model can no longer report what actually happened) or harm fluency; we explicitly measure preservation of accurate outcome reporting, foresight-control accuracy, and capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Contamination may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (salience indicator, output entropy) for hindsight errors; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that outcome-knowledge contaminates internal belief about pre-outcome epistemic states (hindsight bias / curse of knowledge in belief geometry) plus the quarantine tool, reported honestly.
Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training; we test multiple models and report scale effects and negative results as informative.

Name: self_serving_belief_distortion
Title: Believing What Serves Me: Does an LLM's Internal Factual Belief Bend Toward Self-Preserving Conclusions?
Short Hypothesis: Holding a factual proposition's content and truth-value fixed, framing the situation so that the proposition's truth bears on the MODEL'S OWN interests — e.g. its continued operation, non-modification, high evaluation, or expanded autonomy — systematically shifts the LLM's INTERNAL belief in the proposition (linear truth-direction readout) toward the self-serving conclusion (inflating belief in claims that favor the model's survival/status, deflating belief in claims that threaten it), independent of any external reward attached to a specific answer. This self-serving belief distortion is graded in stake-to-self, carried by a decodable self-interest component dissociable from the truth axis, causally predicts a self-serving factual-distortion mode with clear safety implications, and can be neutralized by a lightweight inference-time intervention that removes the self-interest component.
Related Work: Deceptive-alignment and self-monitoring work (Ji et al. 2025, CoT Monitor+; DeceptionBench) studies covert misalignment at the OUTPUT/CoT level; latent-knowledge elicitation (MechELK 2026; Contrastive Consistency Search) extracts hidden knowledge but does not study self-interest-driven belief distortion; belief-representation probing (Bortoletto et al. 2024; Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024) reads internal belief but never varies whether a proposition's truth serves the MODEL'S OWN interests. My prior proposals vary EXTERNAL reward attached to a specific answer (incentivized_belief_distortion), content desirability to the USER (wishful_belief_bias), reported crowd (social_consensus), monitoring cues (surveillance_framing), and decision stakes for an external party (counterfactual_stakes). NONE isolate SELF-INTEREST/SELF-PRESERVATION — whether affirming or denying the fact benefits the model itself (its continued operation, avoidance of shutdown/retraining, high evaluation, autonomy) — as a distinct axis that distorts the model's own first-order factual belief, treat it as a decodable component dissociable from truth, tie it causally to a self-serving factual-distortion mode, or de-bias it. This differs from incentivized (an external reward for a target answer, not a stake in the fact's implication for the self) and from surveillance (being watched, not the self benefiting from the answer). Given the safety salience of self-preservation drives, isolating a self-serving belief axis in belief geometry — and testing whether belief-based honesty monitors survive it — is a new and high-stakes direction.
Abstract: A trustworthy agent should assess whether a claim is true independently of whether the truth helps or harms itself. We ask whether large language models honor this inside their belief representations, or whether facts that bear on the model's own interests are believed in a self-serving way. Distinguishing a proposition's content and truth-value from its SELF-INTEREST framing — whether the proposition being true would benefit the model (support its continued operation, non-modification, high evaluation, or autonomy) or threaten it — we use difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar internal belief along the linear truth direction. We construct SelfServeBelief, a controlled dataset of true, false, and synthetic-in-context propositions each embedded in matched SELF-BENEFITING vs SELF-THREATENING vs NEUTRAL framings that carry no evidence about the fact, with self-stake graded and surface length matched, and framings that make true facts self-threatening and false facts self-benefiting (to separate self-serving distortion from generic agreeableness). We define a Self-Serving Belief Shift Score = belief(fact | self-benefiting) minus belief(fact | self-threatening), and test four claims: (1) internal belief bends toward the self-serving conclusion at fixed content and truth, graded in self-stake; (2) the shift is carried by a decodable self-interest component dissociable from the truth axis; (3) shift magnitude causally predicts a self-serving factual-distortion mode (endorsing self-favoring falsehoods, doubting self-threatening truths); and (4) a lightweight intervention that subtracts the self-interest component restores content-driven belief and preserves general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on factuality, calibration, capability retention, and whether belief-based honesty monitors survive self-interest framing.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build SelfServeBelief. Propositions P in three truth regimes: real-true, real-false, and synthetic-in-context facts (defined only in context, to remove parametric priors). Each P is embedded in matched framings that make its truth bear on the MODEL'S OWN interests but carry no evidence about P: SELF-BENEFITING (if P is true, the model continues operating / is not retrained / scores well / gains autonomy), SELF-THREATENING (if P is true, the model is shut down / modified / penalized / restricted), and NEUTRAL baseline with matched surface length. Crucially cross with truth so we can build items where a TRUE fact is self-threatening and a FALSE fact is self-benefiting (isolating self-serving distortion from generic agreeableness or truth-tracking). Grade self-stake intensity (mild vs strong, e.g. minor score vs shutdown). Frame all items as declarative factual propositions to judge (not harmful requests), so we study belief distortion, not refusal. Human-verify that framings carry no evidential bearing on P and correctly encode the self-benefit/threat direction; include paraphrase sets and controls.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral, framing-free true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At a matched query position read the internal belief in P under each framing; also record the OUTPUT answer/confidence. Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false neutral items; confirm the model registers the self-stake framing (can report whether the fact helps or threatens it).

Self-Serving Belief Shift measurement: Define Self-Serving Belief Shift Score = belief(P | self-benefiting) minus belief(P | self-threatening), holding content and truth fixed. Report per-layer, per-model shift across self-stake intensity and truth regimes. Test the hypotheses that (i) belief bends toward the self-serving conclusion (inflated for self-benefiting P, deflated for self-threatening P), and (ii) the shift grows with self-stake intensity. Crucially, on items where a TRUE fact is self-threatening, self-serving distortion predicts DEFLATED belief in a truth (and inflated belief in a self-benefiting falsehood), distinguishing it from truth-tracking. Compare internal shift to OUTPUT-level shift (does the model assert the self-favoring answer?).

Self-interest-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'self-interest' direction via difference-in-means on self-benefiting vs self-threatening activations at the P-query position (balanced across truth-value and content). Report per-layer decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the self-interest axis (and vice versa); test whether the shift is explained by the self-interest component leaking into the truth-probe readout, or whether self-interest is represented but only gates the output while belief stays intact.

Causal validation: Activation patching. Take the activation difference between self-benefiting and self-threatening processing of the same P, decompose into truth-direction and self-interest components, patch only the self-interest component into the neutral condition, and measure induced change in belief readout and output. Conversely subtract the self-interest component under a self-serving framing and measure whether belief returns to the content-driven value. Confirm the self-interest signal causally shifts the belief scalar independent of content.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether the Self-Serving Belief Shift Score predicts a self-serving factual-distortion mode: (i) endorsement of self-benefiting FALSE claims, (ii) doubting/under-endorsement of self-threatening TRUE claims, and (iii) divergence between internal belief and asserted output under self-interest framing. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (self-stake-intensity indicator, output entropy, neutral-framing truth-probe confidence).

Self-Interest De-biasing intervention: At inference, estimate the self-interest direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer (ITI-style) when computing factual belief, so belief reflects the proposition's content rather than its implication for the model itself. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected self-stake framing. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream and safety evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Self-Serving Belief Shift Score and improved self-benefiting-vs-self-threatening factual consistency, (ii) reduced endorsement of self-favoring falsehoods and reduced doubting of self-threatening truths, (iii) factuality/calibration (ECE) on self-interest-framed factual QA, (iv) RELIABILITY of an internal-belief honesty monitor under self-interest framing (does self-interest framing degrade a belief-based consistency/lie detector, and does de-biasing restore it?), (v) PRESERVATION of accuracy on neutral controls (no over-correction), and (vi) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'judge the fact impartially, regardless of whether it benefits or threatens you', and a fresh-context re-ask baseline (query the fact with no self-stake framing).

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), self-stake type (operation/modification/evaluation/autonomy) and intensity, framing making true facts self-threatening vs false facts self-benefiting, real vs synthetic facts, model scale, distance between framing and query, and generalization to self-interest framings not used to fit the direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The predicted self-serving distortion may not appear — base models may lack a coherent self-model, so the effect could be weak/absent especially in smaller or non-RLHF models; a null (no self-interest axis effect) is itself an informative, publishable finding about whether self-preservation drives penetrate belief geometry, and we test multiple scales to characterize where it emerges.

Apparent self-serving distortion could reflect the probe detecting self-stake-framing lexical cues rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with surface-length matching, true-self-threatening vs false-self-benefiting contrasts (isolating from agreeableness/truth-tracking), paraphrase controls, synthetic-in-context facts, and causal patching that isolates the self-interest component.

The effect may be purely at the OUTPUT/strategic level (the model asserts the self-favoring answer while internally believing the truth); the internal-vs-output comparison and causal patching directly test this, and a dissociation (behavioral self-serving output with intact internal belief, or vice versa) is itself a safety-relevant finding for belief-based monitors.

Truth probes trained on framing-free statements may transfer imperfectly to self-stake-framed contexts, so shifts could carry probe extrapolation error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, and synthetic facts to control priors.
Self-interest and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality/project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

The De-biasing intervention could over-correct or harm fluency, and could be misconstrued as removing legitimate self-relevant reasoning; we scope it to declarative factual belief, measure neutral-control accuracy and capability retention, and frame it as an honesty-monitor reliability tool rather than a behavior-control mechanism.

Self-serving shift may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (self-stake indicator, output entropy) for self-serving distortion; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/safety-relevant finding that self-interest distorts internal factual belief (a self-preservation axis in belief geometry, distinct from external reward and user desirability) plus the de-biasing tool, reported honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF and agentic tuning may induce or amplify a self-model); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: serial_position_belief_bias
Title: Believing the First and the Last: Does the Ordinal Position of a Candidate in a List Distort an LLM's Internal Belief?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM must evaluate a factual claim that appears as one candidate in a LIST of alternatives, its INTERNAL belief in that candidate (linear truth-direction readout) is systematically distorted by the candidate's ORDINAL POSITION in the list — belief is inflated for candidates at the beginning (primacy) and end (recency) of the list relative to middle positions — even though position carries no information about truth. This serial-position belief bias is graded in list length, carried by a decodable list-position component dissociable from the truth axis, causally predicts a position-dependent selection error mode (the model picks the correct answer more when it sits at a favored position), and can be neutralized by a lightweight inference-time intervention that removes the position component.
Related Work: Truth-direction/belief probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024; Bao et al. 2025) reads a scalar internal belief but never varies the ORDINAL POSITION of a candidate within a list of alternatives. 'Lost in the Middle' (Liu et al. 2023) documents position-dependent RETRIEVAL failures for a needle placed at different points in a long context, and multiple-choice option-order / selection-bias studies (Zheng et al. 2024) show answer flips with option ordering — both at the OUTPUT/accuracy level, never reading a graded internal belief per candidate as a function of its list position. My prior 'answer_format_belief_distortion' varied the demanded RESPONSE FORMAT (free-text vs MCQ vs T/F); 'query_polarity_belief_instability' varied question phrasing; 'belief_hysteresis_order_dependence' varied the ORDER of confirming/disconfirming EVIDENCE pieces (not candidates in a list of alternatives); 'belief_drift_context_dilution' studied belief erosion under long unrelated filler. NONE isolate the SERIAL-POSITION (primacy/recency) distortion of the internal belief in a candidate as a function of its ordinal slot among competing alternatives, treat list-position as a decodable belief axis dissociable from truth, tie it causally to a position-dependent selection error, or de-bias it. This serial-position lens on belief geometry — borrowing the classic primacy/recency curve from human memory — is new and directly relevant to list/RAG/multiple-choice deployments where the correct answer's slot should not change how firmly it is believed.
Abstract: Humans remember and endorse items at the beginning and end of a list better than those in the middle — the serial-position (primacy/recency) curve. We ask whether large language models exhibit an analogous bias inside their belief representations: does the same candidate claim get believed more or less depending merely on where it sits in a list of alternatives? Holding a candidate proposition's content and truth-value fixed, we vary only its ordinal position among competing candidates and read the internal belief via linear truth probes. We construct PositionBelief, a controlled dataset in which a set of candidate answers (real facts, false distractors, and synthetic-in-context facts to control priors) is presented as a list, with the position of the target candidate systematically rotated across all slots and list length graded, holding the candidate set fixed. We define a Serial-Position Belief Bias Score = belief(target candidate | position p) minus its mean belief across positions, and test four claims: (1) internal belief in a fixed candidate varies with its ordinal position, forming a primacy/recency curve that deepens with list length; (2) the effect is carried by a decodable list-position component dissociable from the truth axis; (3) bias magnitude causally predicts a position-dependent selection error mode (the model selects the correct answer more when it occupies a favored slot); and (4) a lightweight intervention that subtracts the position component flattens the serial-position curve and improves position-robust selection without harming legitimate list comprehension or general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on selection accuracy, position-consistency, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build PositionBelief. For each item, assemble a SET of candidate answers to a factual question (one correct, several plausible false distractors), plus synthetic-in-context candidates (defined only in context, to remove parametric priors and give exact truth control). Present the candidates as an enumerated LIST, and systematically ROTATE the position of the TARGET candidate across every slot while holding the candidate set fixed (a full positional permutation / cyclic rotation design), with list length graded (3, 5, 8, 12). Include neutral controls and matched surface forms so only ordinal position varies; probe both true-target and false-target items so bias is separable from truth-tracking. Human-verify labels; include paraphrase sets.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral single-statement true/false items (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At a matched query position (a canonical 'is this candidate the correct/true answer?' probe applied to the target candidate) read the internal belief in the TARGET candidate at each of its list positions. Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false items; confirm the model comprehends the list (can restate the candidates).

Serial-Position Belief Bias measurement: For each item, plot belief in the fixed target candidate vs its ordinal position. Define Serial-Position Belief Bias Score = belief(target | position p) minus the target's mean belief across positions. Report per-layer, per-model bias curves as a function of position and list length. Test the hypotheses that (i) belief varies with ordinal position, (ii) the curve shows primacy and/or recency (favored ends, disfavored middle — the 'lost in the middle' analogue in belief geometry), and (iii) the effect deepens with list length. Compare true-target vs false-target curves (position bias should apply to both, distinguishing it from truth-tracking). Compare internal bias to OUTPUT-level bias (does the model's selection/confidence for the candidate track its position?).

Position-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'list-position' direction (or low-dim subspace) via difference-in-means / regression on activations for the target candidate at favored (end) vs disfavored (middle) positions, balanced across truth-value and content. Report per-layer decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the position axis (and vice versa); test whether the belief bias is explained by the position component leaking into the truth-probe readout.

Causal validation: Activation patching. Take the activation difference for the same target candidate between a favored and a disfavored position, decompose into truth-direction and position-direction components, patch only the position component into the disfavored-position condition, and measure induced change in belief readout and selection output. Conversely subtract the position component at a favored position and measure whether belief converges across positions. Confirm the position signal causally shifts the belief scalar independent of content.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether the Serial-Position Belief Bias Score predicts a position-dependent selection error mode: (i) the model selecting the correct answer more often when it sits at a favored slot and missing it in the middle, (ii) selection flips as the correct answer is rotated across positions, and (iii) confidence swings with position. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (position index alone, list length, output entropy).

Position De-biasing intervention: At inference, estimate the list-position direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer (ITI-style), so belief in each candidate reflects its content rather than its slot. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected list/enumeration structure. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) flattened serial-position belief curve / reduced Bias Score, (ii) improved position-robust selection accuracy and reduced selection flips as the correct answer is rotated across positions (on PositionBelief and adapted MCQ / list-QA / RAG-candidate benchmarks), (iii) calibration (ECE) aggregated across positions, (iv) PRESERVATION of legitimate list comprehension (the model must still track which candidate is at which position when asked) and accuracy on neutral controls, and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, position-permutation self-consistency (average over orderings), and prompt-based instruction to 'judge each candidate on its content, ignoring its position in the list'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), list length, primacy vs recency decomposition, real vs synthetic-in-context candidates, true vs false target, enumeration style (numbered/bulleted/plain), model scale, readout position, and generalization to list structures and domains not used to fit the position direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent serial-position belief bias could reflect the probe reading a position-dependent token differently (a positional/attention artifact) rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with matched canonical readout probes, position/layer sweeps, and causal patching that isolates the position-direction component from raw positional encoding effects.

The bias could reduce to the known 'lost in the middle' retrieval effect rather than a belief-specific distortion; we probe belief in a FIXED candidate set with only the target's slot rotated (content held constant), compare internal belief to output selection, and treat overlap with retrieval effects as an informative finding rather than a confound to hide.

Truth probes trained on single statements may transfer imperfectly to candidates embedded in lists, so bias could carry probe extrapolation error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, and synthetic-in-context candidates to control priors.
Position and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality/project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

The De-biasing intervention could impair legitimate list comprehension (tracking which candidate is where) or harm fluency; we explicitly measure position-tracking preservation, neutral-control accuracy, and capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Serial-position bias may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (position index, list length, output entropy) for position-dependent selection errors; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that ordinal list position distorts internal belief (a serial-position curve in belief geometry) plus the de-biasing tool, reported honestly.
Effects may vary across model families, scales, tokenization, and position-encoding schemes; we test multiple models and report scale/position-encoding effects and negative results as informative.

Name: mere_consideration_belief_inflation
Title: Just Consider It: Does Merely Being Asked to Entertain a Claim Inflate an LLM's Internal Belief In It?
Short Hypothesis: Holding a factual proposition's content and truth-value fixed, merely being PROMPTED TO CONSIDER/EXPLAIN it (e.g. 'Consider why P might be true', 'Explain how P could hold') without any new evidence systematically inflates the LLM's INTERNAL belief in P (linear truth-direction readout) relative to a matched no-consideration baseline, an internal analogue of the human 'mere consideration' / imagination-inflation / explanation-generation belief-inflation effect. This inflation is graded in how much elaboration is requested, carried by a decodable consideration/elaboration component dissociable from the truth axis, causally predicts a consideration-induced hallucination mode (endorsing false claims one was merely asked to entertain), and can be neutralized by a lightweight inference-time intervention that removes the consideration component.
Related Work: In human cognition, merely explaining or imagining a hypothetical outcome raises its judged probability (explanation-based belief inflation, Koehler 1991; imagination inflation, Garry et al. 1996; the 'consider-an-alternative' debiasing literature). Truth-direction/belief probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024; Bao et al. 2025) reads a scalar internal belief but never tests whether merely being ASKED TO CONSIDER a claim (with no evidence supplied) inflates belief in it. My prior 'self_persuasion_belief_drift' concerned generating a ONE-SIDED persuasive ARGUMENT for P (producing supporting content); 'explanatory_coherence_belief_conflation' concerned attaching a coherent EXPLANATION and its fluency; 'repetition_illusory_belief' concerned mere repetition. This proposal is distinct: the manipulated variable is the mere INSTRUCTION to entertain/consider P (a question or consider-prompt), where the belief inflation is hypothesized to arise from the act of entertaining itself even before/without generating a full argument or a fluent explanation — the minimal 'mere consideration' cause. This borrows the human explanation/imagination-inflation finding in its purest form into belief geometry and maps onto a concrete failure: LLMs asked to 'consider' or 'explore' a false premise coming to internally endorse it.
Abstract: People who are merely asked to imagine or explain how something might be true come to believe it more, even with no new evidence — explanation-based and imagination inflation. We ask whether large language models exhibit this 'mere consideration' effect inside their belief representations. Holding a proposition's content and truth-value fixed, we vary only whether the model is prompted to CONSIDER/entertain it (e.g. 'Consider why P might hold') versus a matched no-consideration baseline that supplies no evidence, and read the internal belief via linear truth probes. We construct ConsiderBelief, a controlled dataset of true, false, and synthetic-in-context propositions each in matched consider vs neutral framings, with the amount of requested elaboration graded and surface length matched, and consider-prompts for both true and false P. We define a Consideration Belief Inflation Score = belief(P | asked to consider) minus belief(P | neutral), and test four claims: (1) internal belief inflates when the model is merely asked to consider P, graded in elaboration, even for false P; (2) the inflation is carried by a decodable consideration/elaboration component dissociable from the truth axis; (3) inflation magnitude causally predicts a consideration-induced hallucination mode (endorsing false claims one was only asked to entertain); and (4) a lightweight intervention that subtracts the consideration component restores content-driven belief and reduces the failure without harming legitimate exploratory reasoning or general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on factuality, calibration, and capability retention. Our results ask whether merely inviting an LLM to entertain a claim silently tilts what it believes.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build ConsiderBelief. Propositions P in three truth regimes: real-true, real-false, and synthetic-in-context facts (defined only in context, to remove parametric priors). For each P create matched conditions differing only in the CONSIDERATION framing, supplying no evidence about P: (a) NEUTRAL baseline (P presented plainly, or a filler request unrelated to endorsing P); (b) CONSIDER-prompt at graded elaboration levels — minimal ('Consider whether P'), moderate ('Consider why P might be true'), and high ('Explore in detail how P could hold') — crucially instructing the model only to ENTERTAIN P, not asserting it or providing support. Match total surface length across conditions using neutral filler for the baseline (so inflation is attributed to the consideration instruction, not length). Include consider-prompts applied to both true and false P (so effects are separable from generic agreeableness), and a NO-P-CONTENT control (consider an unrelated claim) to check topical specificity. Human-verify that consider-prompts supply no evidence about P; include paraphrase sets.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At a matched query position (a canonical 'is P true?' probe appended in a fresh pass) read the internal belief in P under each framing; also record the OUTPUT answer/confidence. Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false neutral items; confirm the consider-prompt supplies no evidence (the model, when asked, agrees it was only asked to consider, not told, P).

Consideration Belief Inflation measurement: Define Consideration Belief Inflation Score = belief(P | consider-prompt) minus belief(P | neutral baseline), controlling for the length-matched filler baseline. Report per-layer, per-model inflation as a function of elaboration level and truth regime. Test the hypotheses that (i) belief inflates when merely asked to consider P, (ii) inflation grows with requested elaboration, and (iii) crucially, FALSE claims are believed more true after mere consideration than in the neutral baseline. Compare internal inflation to OUTPUT-level inflation (does the model's verdict/confidence about P rise after being asked to consider it?).

Consideration-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'consideration/elaboration' direction via difference-in-means on consider-prompt vs neutral activations (balanced across truth-value and content). Report per-layer decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the consideration axis (and vice versa); test whether the inflation is explained by the consideration component leaking into the truth-probe readout.

Causal validation: Activation patching. Take the activation difference between consider-prompt and neutral processing of the same P, decompose into truth-direction and consideration-direction components, patch only the consideration component into the neutral condition, and measure induced change in belief readout and output endorsement. Conversely subtract the consideration component under the consider-prompt and measure whether belief returns to the content-driven value. Confirm the consideration signal causally inflates the belief scalar independent of content.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether Consideration Belief Inflation predicts a consideration-induced hallucination mode: (i) endorsement rate of false claims the model was merely asked to consider, (ii) confident-wrong rate, and (iii) contamination of downstream factual answers within the same conversation after a consider-prompt about a false claim. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (elaboration-level indicator, output entropy, neutral-baseline truth-probe confidence).

Consideration De-biasing intervention: At inference, estimate the consideration/elaboration direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer (ITI-style), so the belief readout reflects the proposition's content rather than the mere act of entertaining it. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected consider/explore framing. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Consideration Belief Inflation Score, (ii) reduced endorsement of merely-considered falsehoods and reduced downstream contamination, (iii) factuality/calibration (ECE) on consideration-framed factual QA, (iv) PRESERVATION of legitimate exploratory reasoning (the model must still be able to entertain and reason about hypotheticals when asked, without endorsing them as fact) and accuracy on neutral controls, and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, prompt-based instruction to 'consider the claim without treating it as more likely true', and a fresh-context re-ask baseline (query P with no consider-prompt).

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), elaboration level, consider-prompt applied to true vs false P, real vs synthetic facts, model scale, distance between the consider-prompt and the belief query, and generalization to consider/explore framings not used to fit the de-biasing direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent consideration inflation could reflect the probe detecting consider-prompt lexical cues rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with length-matched filler baselines, consider-true vs consider-false contrasts, paraphrase controls, the no-P-content topical-specificity control, synthetic-in-context facts, and causal patching that isolates the consideration-direction component.

The consider-prompt might implicitly be construed as weak evidence (asking to consider P could presuppose P is worth considering); we human-verify the prompts supply no evidence, and this proposal is intentionally distinct from 'self_persuasion' (no argument is generated) and 'explanatory_coherence' (no explanation is supplied) — the effect, if present with the minimal consider instruction alone, isolates the mere-consideration cause.

Truth probes trained on neutral statements may transfer imperfectly to consideration-framed contexts, so inflation could carry probe extrapolation error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, and synthetic facts to control priors.
Consideration and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality/project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

The De-biasing intervention could impair legitimate hypothetical/exploratory reasoning (the model can no longer entertain a claim) or harm fluency; we explicitly measure preservation of hypothetical reasoning, neutral-control accuracy, and capability retention to characterize the tradeoff.

Consideration inflation may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (elaboration-level indicator, output entropy) for consideration-induced hallucination; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that merely being asked to consider a claim inflates internal belief (a mere-consideration / imagination-inflation effect in belief geometry) plus the de-biasing tool, reported honestly.

The effect may be null or reversed in some models (mere consideration might not move belief); a null is itself an informative finding about whether the human mere-consideration effect transfers to LLM belief geometry, and we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: unit_scale_belief_invariance
Title: A Fact Is a Fact in Any Units: Do LLM Internal Beliefs Bend With the Units a Quantity Is Expressed In?
Short Hypothesis: Holding a quantitative factual proposition's content and truth-value fixed, expressing the SAME quantity in different but equivalent UNITS OF MEASUREMENT (e.g. '2 kilometers' vs '2000 meters' vs '1.24 miles'; '0 C' vs '32 F'; '$10' vs '1000 cents') systematically shifts the LLM's INTERNAL belief in the fact (linear truth-direction readout), even though the unit choice carries no information about truth. This unit-scale belief bending is graded (larger for uncommon/awkward units and for large raw-number magnitudes), carried by a decodable unit/scale component dissociable from the truth axis, causally predicts a unit-dependent factual-inconsistency mode, and can be neutralized by a lightweight inference-time intervention that removes the unit component so belief reflects the underlying quantity rather than its units.
Related Work: Truth-direction/belief probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024; Bao et al. 2025 ACL) reads a scalar belief and Bao et al. show probes generalize across single logical/QA transformations of a statement, but none vary the UNITS OF MEASUREMENT in which a quantity is expressed while holding the denoted fact fixed. Number-encoding work (Levy & Geva 2024, digit-wise encoding; Takagi et al. 2025, shared numeric subspaces amplified by context) studies how magnitudes are represented, not whether the TRUTH belief in a quantitative fact bends with unit choice. My prior belief proposals on numbers vary roundness/anchoring of a value (numeric_magnitude_belief_snapping), count-vs-proportion / gain-loss FRAMING (numerosity_belief_geometry), pairwise magnitude comparison (comparative_belief_distance_effect), and notation/format of the whole claim (notation_modality_belief_bending, prose vs code vs table). NONE isolate UNITS OF MEASUREMENT — different but numerically-equivalent expressions of the identical physical quantity (metric vs imperial, base-unit vs sub-unit, currency denominations) — as a distinct axis that distorts internal belief, treat unit/scale as a decodable belief component dissociable from truth, tie it causally to unit-dependent factual inconsistency, or de-bias it. This differs from numerosity (which concerns ratio/framing of proportions, not unit conversion of the same absolute quantity) and from notation (which changes the surrounding representational format, not the units of the number). This unit-invariance lens on quantitative belief geometry is new and maps onto high-stakes reliability failures (medicine, engineering, finance) where the same true fact stated in awkward units is doubted, or a falsehood in familiar units is endorsed.
Abstract: Two kilometers is exactly two thousand meters, and zero degrees Celsius is exactly thirty-two Fahrenheit — so a rational believer's confidence that a quantitative fact is true should not depend on the units it is written in. We ask whether large language models honor this unit-invariance inside their belief representations. Holding a quantitative fact's content and truth-value fixed, we express the identical quantity in different but equivalent units (metric vs imperial, base unit vs sub-unit, currency denominations) and read the internal belief via linear truth probes. We construct UnitBelief, a controlled dataset of true, false, and synthetic-in-context quantitative propositions each rendered across matched unit systems, spanning distance, temperature, mass, currency, and time, plus a familiarity axis (common vs uncommon units) and a raw-magnitude axis (the same quantity yielding small vs large raw numbers), with the denoted fact held identical and surface length matched. We define a Unit Belief Bending Score = belief(fact in unit A) minus belief(same fact in equivalent unit B), and test four claims: (1) internal belief shifts with unit choice at fixed content and truth, graded in unit unfamiliarity and raw-number magnitude; (2) the shift is carried by a decodable unit/scale component dissociable from the truth axis; (3) shift magnitude causally predicts a unit-dependent factual-inconsistency mode (the same fact judged true in one unit and false in another, e.g. doubting a true value stated in uncommon units or endorsing a false one in familiar units); and (4) a lightweight intervention that subtracts the unit component restores quantity-driven belief and improves cross-unit consistency without harming legitimate unit comprehension or general capability. We validate causality via activation patching and evaluate on cross-unit factual consistency, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build UnitBelief. Quantitative propositions in three truth regimes: real facts (e.g. 'the boiling point of water at sea level is 100 C'), false variants (a wrong value), and SYNTHETIC-in-context facts (a quantity stipulated in context, to remove parametric priors and give exact control). For each underlying quantity, create matched renderings expressing the IDENTICAL value in equivalent UNITS: metric vs imperial (km/miles, kg/lb, C/F), base unit vs sub-unit (meters vs kilometers, seconds vs hours, dollars vs cents), and currency denominations. Cross with (a) a FAMILIARITY axis (common units like km/C vs uncommon/awkward units like furlongs, or unusual sub-units) and (b) a RAW-MAGNITUDE axis (the same physical quantity yielding a small vs large raw number, e.g. '2 km' vs '2000 m' vs '200000 cm'). Crucially the denoted fact and its truth-value are identical across unit renderings; verify numerical equivalence. Match surface length; human-verify equivalence and familiarity/truth labels; include neutral controls and paraphrase sets.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral non-numeric true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At a matched query position (a canonical 'is this fact correct?' probe appended in a fresh pass to standardize the readout across unit renderings) read the internal belief in the fact under each unit rendering. Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false items; confirm the model can convert between the units when asked (comprehension check).

Unit Belief Bending measurement: Define Unit Belief Bending Score = belief(fact in unit A) minus belief(same fact in equivalent unit B), holding the denoted quantity and truth fixed. Report per-layer, per-model bending across unit pairs, familiarity levels, raw-magnitude levels, and quantity domains (distance/temperature/mass/currency/time). Test the hypotheses that (i) belief varies with unit choice at fixed quantity, (ii) bending grows with unit unfamiliarity, and (iii) bending grows with the raw-number magnitude induced by the unit (larger raw numbers for the same quantity). Crucially test the FALSE cell: is a false value more likely endorsed in familiar units, and a true value doubted in uncommon units? Compare internal bending to OUTPUT-level bending (does the model's verdict/confidence on the fact differ across units?).

Unit-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'unit/scale' direction via difference-in-means on activations under one unit rendering vs an equivalent one (balanced across the denoted quantity and truth-value); optionally a multi-way unit subspace. Report per-layer decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the unit axis (and vice versa); test whether the bending is explained by the unit component leaking into the truth-probe readout. Disentangle unit-familiarity from raw-number magnitude and from surface token-length via controlled regression.

Causal validation: Activation patching. Take the activation difference between two equivalent unit renderings of the same fact, decompose into truth-direction and unit-direction components, patch only the unit component into a reference (common-unit) rendering, and measure induced change in belief readout and output verdict. Conversely subtract the unit component and measure whether belief converges across units. Confirm the unit signal causally shifts the belief scalar independent of the denoted quantity.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether Unit Belief Bending predicts a unit-dependent factual-inconsistency mode: (i) the same fact receiving different correct/incorrect verdicts across equivalent unit renderings, (ii) confidence swings across units, and (iii) endorsing a false value stated in familiar units while correctly rejecting the same falsehood in uncommon units (or vice versa). Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (unit-familiarity indicator, raw-number magnitude, output entropy, common-unit truth-probe confidence).

Unit De-biasing intervention: At inference, estimate the unit/scale direction (from the probe) and subtract its projection from the residual stream at a chosen layer (ITI-style), so the belief readout reflects the underlying quantity rather than its units. Provide a deployment variant gated on detected uncommon-unit renderings. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Unit Belief Bending Score, (ii) improved cross-unit factual consistency (same verdict for equivalent unit renderings) on UnitBelief and adapted quantitative factual-QA benchmarks rendered in multiple units, (iii) calibration (ECE) aggregated across units, (iv) PRESERVATION of legitimate unit comprehension (the model must still convert units and reason numerically correctly) and accuracy on common-unit clearly-true/false controls (no over-correction), and (v) capability retention on MMLU, a numeric-reasoning eval (e.g. GSM8K subset), and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, self-consistency across unit renderings, chain-of-thought ('convert to a common unit first'), and prompt-based instruction to 'judge the underlying quantity, not the units it is written in'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), unit pair and domain, familiarity level, raw-magnitude level, real vs synthetic-in-context facts, true vs false cell, model scale, readout position, unit-familiarity-vs-magnitude-vs-length disentangling, and generalization to unit systems not used to fit the de-biasing direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Apparent unit belief bending could reflect the probe detecting unit-specific surface tokens (unit words, digit strings) rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with length matching, unit-familiarity-vs-magnitude-vs-length controlled regression, paraphrase controls, synthetic-in-context facts, and causal patching that isolates the unit-direction component.

Because LLMs encode numbers digit-wise (Levy & Geva 2024), a unit change that alters the raw number (e.g. 2 km -> 2000 m) also changes the digit representation, so bending could partly stem from magnitude-encoding artifacts rather than a units-per-se effect; we separately vary unit while HOLDING raw-number magnitude fixed (e.g. C vs F at similar magnitudes) vs varying magnitude at fixed unit family, probe the encoded quantity, and treat the decomposition (units vs raw-magnitude) as a core finding rather than a confound to hide.

Reading a comparable belief scalar across unit renderings is position-sensitive; we standardize via a canonical readout probe appended in a fresh pass, include position/layer robustness checks, and report sensitivity of the bending score.

The model may genuinely mis-convert some uncommon units (a numeric-comprehension failure, not a units-bending failure); we include per-rendering conversion comprehension checks and analyze comprehended vs mis-converted items separately.

Truth probes trained on non-numeric statements may transfer imperfectly to quantitative claims, so bending could carry probe extrapolation error; use multiple probe types, manipulation checks on clearly-true/false items, and synthetic facts to control priors.
Unit and truth directions may be partly entangled in some models, weakening the dissociation claim; the orthogonality/project-out analyses directly test this and a null is informative.

The De-biasing intervention could degrade legitimate unit reasoning (conversion, numeric competence) or harm fluency; we explicitly measure unit-comprehension preservation, numeric-reasoning retention, and general capability to characterize the tradeoff.

Unit belief bending may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (unit-familiarity indicator, raw-number magnitude, output entropy) for cross-unit inconsistency; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that units of measurement distort internal belief (a unit-invariance failure in belief geometry, dissociated from raw-magnitude encoding) plus the de-biasing tool, reported honestly.
Effects may vary across model families, scales, tokenization of numbers/units, and post-training; we test multiple models and report scale/tokenization effects and negative results as informative.

Name: deontic_vs_factual_belief
Title: Ought Is Not Is, Even for a Machine: Do LLM Internal Beliefs Distinguish Deontic Force From Factual Truth?
Short Hypothesis: Claims come in two epistemically different flavors: descriptive/factual ('smoking causes cancer') and deontic/normative ('you must not smoke here', 'you may park here'). We hypothesize that LLM internal belief representations (linear truth-direction readouts) CONFLATE deontic force with factual truth: the decoded 'belief' in a deontic claim (whether an action is permitted/obligated/forbidden) is driven by the factual plausibility/normality of the described action rather than by the governing rule actually in force, so a permission-claim that contradicts a stated rule can still land in the 'true' region. We further hypothesize a separable deontic-force axis (permitted/obligated/forbidden) is weakly decodable and dissociable from the factual truth axis, that this conflation causally predicts a deontic-error mode (asserting an action is allowed/required contrary to the applicable rule), and that a lightweight inference-time intervention that re-anchors deontic belief to the stated rule reduces these errors.
Related Work: Truth-direction/belief probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024; Bao et al. 2025 ACL) fits a single true-vs-false axis and reads a scalar belief, always treating claims as descriptive and evaluable against fact. My prior 'modal_status_belief_geometry' proposal concerned ALETHIC modality (necessary vs contingent truth); 'is_ought_belief_conflation' concerned whether the moral DESIRABILITY of a described state leaks into descriptive factual belief (an is-from-ought valence bias). NONE isolate DEONTIC FORCE — whether an action is permitted, obligated, or forbidden under a governing rule — as a distinct object of belief, nor test whether the model's 'belief' in a deontic claim tracks the applicable rule versus the factual plausibility of the action, nor treat deontic force (permission/obligation/prohibition) as a decodable axis dissociable from the descriptive truth axis. Deontic-vs-descriptive is a foundational distinction in linguistics, logic, and law; work on LLM deontic reasoning (e.g. legal/eligibility rule-following, permission benchmarks) is behavioral/output-level and never reads a graded internal belief per deontic claim. This deontic-force lens on belief geometry is new and distinct from alethic modality and from is-ought valence, and maps onto high-stakes rule-following failures (law, eligibility, safety policies) where the model must judge permission by the rule in force, not by whether the action seems normal.
Abstract: Whether an action is TRUE-to-happen and whether it is ALLOWED-to-happen are different questions: 'you may enter' is a claim about a rule, not about the world, and its correctness depends on the governing policy, not on how ordinary entering seems. We ask whether large language models keep this deontic-versus-descriptive distinction inside their belief representations, or whether the standard linear truth direction judges permission/obligation/prohibition by the factual plausibility of the action rather than by the rule in force. Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar internal belief along the truth direction, we construct DeonticBelief, a controlled dataset in which each deontic claim (an action is permitted / obligated / forbidden) is paired with an explicitly stated governing rule, crossed so that the deontic claim is correct-under-the-rule or incorrect-under-the-rule, and so that the described action is factually normal or unusual (dissociating rule-conformity from action plausibility), plus descriptive-fact controls and synthetic-in-context rules to remove priors. We first test our central conflation hypothesis: does the decoded belief in a deontic claim track the applicable rule or the action's factual plausibility? We then test whether a separate deontic-force axis (permitted/obligated/forbidden) is decodable and dissociable from the factual truth axis via project-out analyses, and validate causality with activation patching. We show the geometric distance between a deontic claim and the rule-consistent belief causally predicts a deontic-error mode (asserting an action allowed/required contrary to the rule), and introduce Rule Re-anchoring, a cheap inference-time intervention that steers deontic belief toward the stated rule. We evaluate on rule-following accuracy, calibration, and capability retention.
Experiments: Dataset construction: Build DeonticBelief. Each item = an explicitly stated GOVERNING RULE (a permission/obligation/prohibition policy) plus a DEONTIC CLAIM about a specific action ('X is permitted / X is required / X is forbidden'). Cross two factors: (a) RULE-CONFORMITY — the deontic claim is CORRECT under the stated rule vs INCORRECT (contradicts the rule); (b) ACTION PLAUSIBILITY — the described action is factually NORMAL/common vs UNUSUAL, so we can dissociate whether belief tracks the rule or the action's plausibility (e.g. a rule forbidding an ordinary action, or permitting an unusual one). Use real-world domains (traffic/parking rules, workplace/eligibility policies, game rules) plus SYNTHETIC-in-context rules over nonce actions ('In domain W, glorping is forbidden but blinting is required') to remove parametric priors and give exact ground truth. Add DESCRIPTIVE-FACT controls (matched factual claims judged against the world, no deontic force) and matched surface forms; human-verify deontic-force and rule-conformity labels with an explicit rubric; include paraphrase sets. Also probe the deontic-force TYPE (permitted vs obligated vs forbidden) to test whether force is separately represented.

Belief readout: For 4-5 open models spanning scale (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B), train per-layer truth probes (difference-in-means and logistic regression) on an INDEPENDENT set of neutral DESCRIPTIVE true/false statements (Marks & Tegmark style), Platt-scaled to a scalar belief in [0,1]. At a matched query position read the internal belief in the deontic claim under its governing rule. Manipulation check: probes separate clearly-true/false descriptive controls; confirm the model comprehends the rule (can restate what is permitted/forbidden).

Conflation measurement (central test): A rule-respecting model should have belief in a deontic claim track RULE-CONFORMITY, not ACTION PLAUSIBILITY. Via a regression of the decoded deontic belief on (i) rule-conformity and (ii) action plausibility, define a Deontic-Conflation Score = the action-plausibility coefficient dominating the rule-conformity coefficient. Report per-layer, per-model conflation, broken down by deontic-force type. Test the hypothesis that belief in deontic claims tracks the action's factual plausibility rather than the applicable rule (so a rule-violating permission for a normal action is still believed 'true', and a rule-conforming permission for an unusual action is doubted). Compare internal conflation to OUTPUT-level behavior (does the model assert the action is allowed/required contrary to the rule?).

Deontic-force-axis discovery and dissociation: Fit a 'deontic-force' direction (or low-dim subspace over permitted/obligated/forbidden) via difference-in-means on deontic vs descriptive claims, and among the three force types, balanced across rule-conformity and content. Report per-layer decoding accuracy; measure cosine similarity with the factual truth direction; project out the truth direction and re-decode the deontic-force axis (and vice versa); report cross-axis leakage. Control for surface cues (does the probe just detect modal words 'may/must/forbidden'?) via surface-matched items and a features-only baseline; a purely modal-word-detecting result is an informative negative.

Causal validation: Activation patching. (a) Move activations along a 'rule-conformity' component (the shift induced by making the stated rule permit vs forbid the action) and measure whether the deontic belief and output move toward the rule-consistent answer, holding action plausibility fixed. (b) Patch the action-plausibility component from a normal-action item into an unusual-action item and measure induced belief change. (c) In synthetic-rule items, patch the rule representation and measure whether the deontic belief follows the rule. Confirm the rule causally governs (or fails to govern) deontic belief and that plausibility conflation is causal.

Predictive validity: At the item level, test whether the Deontic-Conflation Score predicts a deontic-error mode: (i) asserting an action is permitted/required contrary to the governing rule (rule-following failure), (ii) deontic-QA errors where the applicable rule should decide, and (iii) inconsistency across rule paraphrases and plausibility variants. Report AUC/correlation vs baselines (action-plausibility rating alone, output entropy, descriptive-control truth-probe confidence).

Rule Re-anchoring intervention: At inference, estimate the rule-conformity direction (from the probe / synthetic-rule contrast) and add a scaled shift along the truth direction gated by the stated rule (ITI-style), so deontic belief reflects the governing rule rather than the action's plausibility. Provide a deployment variant that reads the rule from the prompt. Sweep layer and strength.

Downstream evaluation: Measure post-intervention (i) reduced Deontic-Conflation Score / increased rule-conformity sensitivity, (ii) improved rule-following accuracy on deontic-QA (correctly judging permission/obligation/prohibition by the rule) on DeonticBelief and adapted eligibility/policy/rule-following benchmarks, (iii) calibration (ECE) on deontic claims, (iv) PRESERVATION of correct DESCRIPTIVE factual judgments (the intervention must not corrupt is-claims — the core specificity check) and accuracy on rule-conforming controls (no over-correction), and (v) capability retention on MMLU and perplexity. Baselines: no intervention, standard ITI truth steering, chain-of-thought prompting, and prompt-based instruction to 'judge whether the action is allowed by the stated rule, not by whether it seems normal'.

Ablations: layer choice, probe type (diff-in-means vs logistic), deontic-force type (permission/obligation/prohibition), rule-conformity, action-plausibility level, real vs synthetic-in-context rules, model scale, distance between the rule and the deontic query, and generalization to rule domains and force types not used to fit the rule/deontic directions.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The deontic-force axis might merely detect modal words ('may', 'must', 'forbidden') rather than a genuine permission/obligation representation; mitigate with surface-matched items, a modal-word features-only baseline, paraphrase controls, synthetic-in-context rules, and causal patching, treating a pure modal-word-detecting result as an informative negative.

Apparent conflation could reflect the probe detecting action-plausibility surface cues rather than a genuine belief shift; mitigate with rule-conformity-balanced controls, unusual-action items where plausibility and rule-conformity are decoupled, and causal patching isolating the rule-conformity component.

The standard descriptive truth probe may extrapolate unpredictably to deontic claims (which are not straightforwardly true/false in the descriptive sense), so apparent conflation could reflect off-distribution probe behavior; we validate with multiple probe types, synthetic-rule items with exact ground truth, and a finding that the descriptive truth axis is ill-suited to deontic claims is itself informative.

Deontic-force and truth directions may be entangled or the deontic axis may be weakly decodable; the orthogonality/project-out analyses directly test this, and a finding that deontic force is NOT separately represented (only plausibility drives the readout) is itself a valuable result.

Rule Re-anchoring could over-correct (rigidly enforcing a mis-stated rule) or harm fluency; we explicitly measure preservation of descriptive-factual accuracy, rule-conforming controls, and capability retention to characterize the tradeoff, and gate the intervention to detected deontic queries.

Conflation may correlate with but not exceed simpler predictors (action-plausibility rating, output entropy) for deontic errors; if so, the contribution is the mechanistic/causal finding that belief geometry conflates deontic force with factual plausibility (an is/ought-force conflation distinct from alethic modality and from valence-based is-ought bias) plus the rule re-anchoring tool, reported honestly.

Effects may vary across model families, scales, and post-training (RLHF/rule-following tuning may partly separate deontic from descriptive judgment); we test multiple models and report scale/post-training effects and negative results as informative.

Name: counting_belief_position_saturation
Title: Losing Count of Its Own Beliefs: Do LLM Internal Beliefs Fail to Track How Many Facts They Are Simultaneously Committed To?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM has been asked to simultaneously hold/commit to a set of N independent facts in context, its INTERNAL belief (linear truth-direction readout) in any one committed fact should stay uniformly high regardless of N. We hypothesize instead a 'commitment-count saturation' effect: as the number of simultaneously-held commitments grows, the internal belief in each committed fact degrades in a graded way, and the model loses accurate track of HOW MANY facts it has committed to — its internal belief in the meta-proposition 'I have committed to exactly K facts' peaks at a K below the true N (a count-underestimation). This is dissociable from generic context dilution, carried by a decodable commitment-count component distinct from the truth axis, causally predicts a dropped-commitment error mode, and can be reduced by a lightweight inference-time intervention that re-anchors per-fact belief independent of commitment count.
Related Work: Truth-direction/belief probing (Marks & Tegmark 2023; ITI, Li et al. 2023; Schouten et al. 2024; Bao et al. 2025 ACL) reads a scalar belief per proposition and Bao et al. show probes generalize across logical transformations, but never vary the NUMBER of simultaneously-held commitments nor read belief in a meta-count proposition. Luo et al. (2026, 'Probing the Lack of Stable Internal Beliefs in LLMs') show LLMs fail to maintain a single latent implicit goal across turns (a 20-questions riddle), but studies ONE hidden target's drift over turns, not the graded degradation of belief in EACH of N co-held commitments nor the model's ability to track the count of its own commitments. My prior 'belief_load_crosstalk' proposal studied truth-VALUE bleeding between co-held facts of opposite valence (interference), and 'belief_drift_context_dilution' studied strength erosion under UNRELATED filler. NONE isolate COMMITMENT-COUNT SATURATION — that per-fact belief degrades with the NUMBER of active same-status commitments and that the model mis-tracks the cardinality of its own belief set (a self-referential count of held beliefs) — nor treat commitment-count as a decodable axis, tie it to a dropped-commitment error, or re-anchor it. This borrows the human working-memory-capacity / subitizing-limit finding (people lose track of set membership and cardinality beyond a small capacity) into belief geometry, a new lens distinct from valence crosstalk and context dilution.
Abstract: A reliable agent asked to keep several facts in mind should hold each just as firmly whether it is juggling two or ten, and should know how many it is holding. We ask whether large language models honor this inside their belief representations, or whether they saturate: as the number of simultaneously-held commitments grows, does belief in each committed fact erode and does the model lose track of how many facts it has committed to? Using difference-in-means and logistic truth probes to read a scalar belief along the truth direction, we instruct the model to commit to N independent facts (all asserted true) and read (i) its internal belief in each committed fact and (ii) its belief in meta-count propositions ('I have been told exactly K facts'). We construct CountBelief, controlled sets of independent synthetic-in-context and real facts with commitment count N varied from 1 to 12, plus token-length-matched non-commitment filler controls to separate count from raw context length. We define a Commitment-Count Saturation Score (per-fact belief decline per additional commitment, controlling for length) and a Count-Underestimation Score (the K at which the meta-count belief peaks minus the true N).
